10101-a-little-boy-lost:
W. H. Hudson's fantasy, illustrated by A. D. M'Cormick, follows a little boy lost on a great plain. Martin's home on the plain gives way to a spoonbill and a cloud, a chase after a flying figure, and rescue by a deaf old man.

Later chapters bring the people of the mirage, savages, and a great forest. There are a flower and a serpent, black people of the sky, wild horses, the lady of the hills, little people underground, and the great blue water. Hudson writes with naturalist wonder. Young readers get a dreamlike journey, where nature itself becomes the story.
10377-the-evil-guest:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu published this gothic novel in 1895, though its tale is set about sixty years earlier, near Chester. A gloomy old mansion called Gray Forest stands in rich, neglected woods, where moonlight makes glades look spectral. The house belongs to a younger son living on a narrow, encumbered income.

An evil guest enters this lonely life, and lust, sin, and death follow, as the book's biblical motto warns. Le Fanu builds dread through place, silence, and moral decay rather than sudden shocks. Readers get a dark, atmospheric tale of temptation and ruin in an old English house.
10379-at-love-s-cost:
Charles Garvice published this popular romance, opening with a man who curses his own folly for leaving a warm fire to chase a friend's wild plan. He rides seven hours by train, then drives through pelting rain toward the lakes in early June, asking why he ever agreed. The tone is comic, self-mocking, and brisk.

Love, pride, and a friend's scheme pull the hero into scrapes, misunderstandings, and at last a costly choice. Garvice, a best-selling romance writer, keeps the plot moving with talk and incident. Readers get a light, old-style love story, full of charm and period manners.
10432-aunt-jane-s-nieces-out-west:
Edith Van Dyne published this girls' novel in 1914, sending Patsy, Beth, and Louise out west with Uncle John. Caught by the camera opens the tale, as pictures, girls, and nonsense mix with a thrilling rescue and a mystery around a figure called A. Jones. The tone is bright, comic, and moral.

An invalid, a damsel in distress, a foolish boy, and Isidore Le Drieux add intrigue, while the yacht Arabella and a girlish notion carry the plot west. Uncle John is puzzled, doubts grow, and Maud makes a memorandum. Readers get a cheerful series tale of travel, film, and friendship.
10672-game-and-playe-of-the-chesse-a-ver:
William Caxton printed The Game and Playe of the Chesse in 1474, one of the earliest books printed in English, and this edition reprints that first text word for word. An introduction by William E. A. Axon, published in London in 1883, sets the old book in context. The reprint keeps Caxton's spelling and punctuation, with notes on the old letter forms.

Caxton uses the game of chess as a mirror of society, giving each piece a rank and a moral lesson, from kings and queens down to common folk. The book thus teaches conduct, duty, and government through play. Readers get a direct look at England's first printed prose and at how a medieval writer turned a game into a guide for life.
10736-children-of-the-frost:
Jack London published Children of the Frost in 1902, a book of ten stories about Native peoples of the far North. Its tales include "The Law of Life," "Nam-Bok the Unveracious," "Keesh, the Son of Keesh," "The Death of Ligoun," and "The League of the Old Men." The opening story sets the scene in forests beyond the last timber, in the Barrens of the Arctic.

London writes of hunger, custom, courage, and the clash between old ways and white newcomers, with the cold itself as a force in every tale. His sympathy lies with his Native characters, even when their laws seem harsh. Readers get early London at his strongest, telling Northern stories in plain, powerful prose.
10866-the-dolorous-passion-of-our-lord-j:
The Dolorous Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ gathers the meditations of Anne Catherine Emmerich, a German mystic, on the suffering of Christ. This text follows the twentieth edition, published by Benziger Brothers in New York in 1904, with a preface by the Abbe de Cazales to the French translation. Cazales met the book while traveling in Germany and found it simple, unassuming, and wholly submissive to the Church.

The meditations follow the Passion in vivid, devotional detail, inviting prayer rather than argument. Catholic readers have long used the book in Holy Week. It offers an intense, traditional account of Christ's final hours, as seen through a visionary's eyes.
10963-the-grip-of-desire-the-story-of-a-:
Hector France wrote this French realist novel about a village parish priest, translated into English with a portrait of the author. France warns readers at the start that he is a realist, not an idealist, and that his characters are not models of virtue. The story follows the poor, obscure cure through pastoral love, temptation, and the conflict between his vows and his feelings.

Chapters titled The Cure, The Confessional, The Parsonage, and The Temptation trace the priest's slow fall and its aftermath, with his servant Veronica at the centre of the drama. France paints what he saw, not what he dreamed, in plain, unsparing prose. Readers should note the book's frank treatment of desire and clerical life, unusual for its time.
10967-four-weeks-in-the-trenches-the-war:
Fritz Kreisler, the celebrated violinist, served briefly as an officer in the Austrian army and wrote this short memoir of four weeks at the front in 1914. He warns readers that his memories are uneven: some scenes stand out clearly, others blur, and the order of events often escapes him. Stress, uncertainty, and the strange mental state of the firing line, he says, explain the gaps.

Kreisler describes trenches, barbed wire, sappers at work, and a colonel's brief orders before an expected attack, with the tender concern behind the officer's martial manner. The book is short and personal, not a history of campaigns. It shows war through a musician's eyes, attentive to mood and human detail rather than strategy.
11084-sonny-a-christmas-guest:
Ruth McEnery Stuart wrote this 1911 Southern story about Sonny, a boy who arrives as a Christmas guest. A father, told by the doctor that the baby is a boy, refuses to look until the mother has seen him, fearing to drop the bundle and worrying where to lay it. The comedy of new fatherhood opens a warm family tale.

Later chapters follow Sonny's christening, schooling, diploma, keeping company, and wedding presents. At Miss Phoebe Kellogg's school, Sonny brings beasts and varmints, which she welcomes, finding books and clay modelling lessons for them, until his alligator in clay seems ready to creep away. Stuart writes in dialect with affection, celebrating a country boy's growth and a teacher's wisdom.
1109-love-s-labour-s-lost:
Four young lords of Navarre swear off women, wine, and sleep for three years of study, and four ladies of France arrive the same day to wreck the oath. William Shakespeare's early comedy turns on wit duels, love letters gone astray, and a pedant schoolmaster's pageant. The verse sparkles with puns and wordplay.

The lords woo in disguise, the ladies see through them, and the play ends not with weddings but with a death and a year's delay. That sober close sets it apart from other comedies. The play delights lovers of language, and it shows Shakespeare already master of comic form.
11106-the-girl-at-cobhurst:
Frank R. Stockton published this 1898 novel, The Girl at Cobhurst, in forty-four chapters. Dr. Tolbridge enters his warm hall one March afternoon, having stayed all night with the Pardell boy, found in desperate condition, and his wife greets him with delight at his return. The household of Cobhurst, with Miss Panney, Dora Bannister, and Miriam, forms the novel's centre.

Chapters follow Panneyopathy, a silk gown and a bottle, two girls and a calf, the teaberry gown too large and then donned, bombshells and bromide, a cry from the sea. Miriam wishes a girl with longings could know real country life, and thinks Dora would rather do the showing herself. Stockton's comedy of village manners, medicine, and courtship moves briskly through its many small crises.
11203-narrative-of-a-survey-of-the-inter:
Captain Phillip P. King, Royal Navy, published this narrative of a survey of Australia's intertropical and western coasts, performed between 1818 and 1822, in two volumes with plates, charts, and wood-cuts. King published parts of his journal to accompany the Admiralty's atlas of charts, as English colonies in Australia grew rapidly in importance for geography and natural history.

One result of the voyage was the occupation of Port Cockburn, between Melville and Bathurst Islands on the north coast. King recalls Burton's remark on Quiros's discovery of Terra Australis, doubting whether it was as true as Mercurius Britannicus or Utopia, yet likely to yield flourishing kingdoms. The narrative remains a primary source on Australian coastal exploration.
11223-big-timber-a-story-of-the-northwes:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published this 1916 novel, Big Timber, A Story of the Northwest, with a frontispiece by Douglas Duer. The book opens on the Imperial Limited swinging around the last hairpin curve of the Yale canyon into a timbered valley, where the Fraser River.

Estella Benton rides in the first coach behind the diner, nursing her chin and watching wooded heights lift green in place of barren cliffs. Chapters follow Mr. Abbey's arrival, halfway point, the toll of big timber, Jack Fyfe's camp, one way out, the plunge, a close call, the crisis, and a ride by night. Fyfe tells his wife his business netted twelve to fifteen thousand a year.
11244-a-project-for-flying-in-earnest-at:
Published in 1871 for twenty-five cents, this pamphlet argues that aerial navigation is finally within reach, despite the failure of the California experiment and earlier airships. It opens with an 1869 letter to the Tribune mocking a publicized machine. then claims a man living within twenty miles of Trinity Church in New York holds the true secret of flying in calm or storm, with or against the wind. Balloons, the author insists, are not the answer.

The pamphlet is booster literature, confident and vague about mechanics, and its promised inventor never delivered a working machine. Its value now is as a snapshot of pre-Wright aviation enthusiasm, when many inventors claimed the secret and none could prove it. Readers can enjoy its certainty while knowing how the story ended.
1135-the-tempest:
Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, lives exiled on an island with his daughter Miranda, ruling spirits and the wild Caliban by magic. When his enemies sail past, he raises a storm, wrecks them ashore, and stages his revenge, only to choose pardon in the end. William Shakespeare's last solo play is his most musical.

Ariel's songs, Caliban's curses, and Miranda's wonder at "brave new world" give the play its glow. Prospero breaks his staff and frees his servant, closing Shakespeare's career with a farewell to art itself. The play still enchants stage, film, and classroom alike.
11395-cheerful-by-request:
Edna Ferber's 1918 collection Cheerful By Request opens with its title story, in which an editor over lunch asks a writer for a fairly cheerful story. not pink but mauve, after a year swamped with drab realistic tales of dishwashers and fallen sisters ending in the East River. Josie Fifer's existence, mostly grey with a dash of pink, becomes the test case. Eleven more stories follow: the Gay Old Dog, the Tough Guy, the Eldest, That's Marriage, the Woman Who Tried to Be Good, and Shore Leave.

Ferber, author of Dawn O'Hara and Fanny Herself, writes with humor and sympathy about ordinary women. The collection's frame, an editor requesting cheer, doubles as a joke about wartime publishing. Readers of American short fiction will enjoy Ferber's brisk, humane voice.
11534-the-lions-of-the-lord-a-tale-of-th:
Harry Leon Wilson's 1903 tale of the Old West follows a Mormon convert through a hard country of dead cities, desert crossings, and new settlements. Chapter titles name the path: a wild ram in the mountains, a fair apostate, a revelation, and a march into the wilderness toward a promised land.

Brigham Young appears in the story, and questions of faith, pride, and obedience run through Joel Rae's trials. The novel mixes frontier action with religious feeling, and its Utah setting shapes both the journey and the choices its people make.
11720-fenton-s-quest:
M. E. Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret and Aurora Floyd, wrote Fenton's Quest as a cheap uniform edition novel. Contents open with the common fever, Marian's story, and an acceptance, then John Saltram, halcyon days, and a sentence of exile.

Later chapters bring a goodbye, a missing person, Jacob Nowell, a marriage at Wygrove, and a friendly counsellor. A scene near the end shows a man putting away selfish, vindictive thoughts, content to be his dear one's brother and friend, while the Grange stands sombre and flowerless. The novel is a Victorian sensation tale of love, loss, and a quest for truth.
11944-the-winning-of-the-west-volume-4-l:
Volume 4 of Theodore Roosevelt's Winning of the West, also dedicated to Francis Parkman, covers Louisiana and the Northwest from 1791 to 1807, with a map. Its preface describes a period that opened with a checkered but finally successful war, setting the tone for a narrative of expansion, conflict, and settlement.

Roosevelt follows American power as it reaches toward the Mississippi and beyond, through wars, treaties, and the movement of settlers into new country. Like the earlier volumes, this one joins military narrative to political history. It argues that the winning of the West was a continuous national story rather than a series of isolated frontier episodes.
12046-narrative-of-a-survey-of-the-inter:
Captain Phillip P. King, Royal Navy, fellow of the Royal and Linnean Societies and member of the Royal Asiatic Society, surveyed the intertropical and western coasts of Australia between 1818 and 1822. This second volume of his narrative continues the voyage, with an appendix on hydrography and natural history.

King's survey mapped harbors, rivers, and coasts that later settlers and traders would use, recording tides, winds, plants, and animals as he went. The narrative combines seamanship with science, in the tradition of Cook and Flinders. It remains a primary source for the early European knowledge of northern and western Australia.
12183-wau-bun-the-early-day-in-the-north:
Mrs. John H. Kinzie published Wau-Bun in Philadelphia in 1873, drawing on family journals, letters, and stories told by her husband relatives. The Ojibwe word of the title means dawn, or break of day, and the book covers the early American presence around Chicago and the upper Midwest.

Kinzie describes frontier households, fur traders, soldiers, missionaries, and Native neighbors, with scenes of travel, feasts, councils, and hardship winters. She writes as a participant rather than a historian, and her sympathies run with the settler community. Modern readers will note the limits of that view. Even so, the memoir preserves daily detail of a frontier that vanished within a generation.
12196-red-saunders-his-adventures-west-e:
Henry Wallace Phillips published these linked western stories in 1901, narrated by a friend of the hero, Red Saunders. Red, a red-haired cowpuncher with a quick temper and a soft heart, drifts between ranch work, town brawls, and romance.

Four long stories carry the book: a chance shot that starts a feud, a red-haired Cupid matchmaking, a golden ford, and a chinook wind striking Fairfield. Red drinks, fights, falls in love with a schoolteacher named Mattie, and promises to reform, with comic conditions. Phillips writes in cowboy dialect, full of tall talk and sudden tenderness. The stories helped fix the image of the good-natured western hero for later writers.
12405-frank-the-young-naturalist:
Harry Castlemon's 1892 boys' book opens the Frank and Archie series with Frank, a young naturalist at home with his museum. Chapters follow a race on the water, a fishing excursion, trout fishing, a duck hunt and a coon hunt. Alongside them come encounters with regulators, coast-guards and a man named Bill Lawson seeking revenge.

Frank's love of birds, fish and field craft drives the adventure, and his knowledge often saves the day. Castlemon writes for boy readers in a direct, outdoor style, mixing natural history with river and woodland scrapes. The book belongs to a popular series that carried Frank onward to gun-boats, prairies and the Mississippi in later volumes.
125-a-girl-of-the-limberlost:
Elnora Comstock collects moths in the Limberlost swamp to pay for her schooling. Gene Stratton-Porter's Girl of the Limberlost follows Elnora as she defies her bitter mother and earns her way. Philip Ammon helps her hunt, and Wesley and Margaret Sinton mother her.

Edith Carr, a city rival, tests Elnora's heart, while Freckles, now grown as Terence O'More, returns. Moth lore, swamp beauty, and the Golden Rule shape the story. Elnora's patience wins love and learning alike. The novel pairs with Freckles as a Limberlost classic. Nature writing and moral earnestness made Stratton-Porter's novels popular with young readers.
12615-the-song-of-our-syrian-guest:
William Allen Knight's 1904 Song of Our Syrian Guest, illustrated by Charles Copeland, retells Psalm Twenty-Three through a Syrian host's eyes. The psalm itself opens the book. The Lord is my shepherd, green pastures, still waters, soul restored, valley of shadow, rod and staff, table prepared, head anointed, cup running over, goodness and mercy following all life's days.

Knight then lets a Syrian guest explain shepherd life, hospitality and trust, so familiar verses gain Eastern colour. A salutation to the hand that held the tea-ball and to two little maids frames the gift book. The volume is a small, devotional classic, meant for reading aloud and for giving, gentle in tone and rich in local detail.
12826-the-air-trust:
George Allan England's 1915 novel The Air Trust, dedicated to Eugene V. Debs, imagines a monopoly that owns the very air people breathe. A billionaire's plot, a laboratory secret about oxygen, and a heroine named Catherine who defies the trust drive the plot through traps, trials, prisons, and escapes. Tiger Waldron and Flint scheme and counter-scheme.

A mid-book scene finds a hero noting a car's licence plate, 4622 New York, after a crash by a rocky river shore, then climbing to reach a telephone at West Point. England's socialist science fiction warns against unchecked corporate power. The novel remains a curious, earnest thriller of its age.
12894-sacred-books-of-the-east:
Epiphanius Wilson compiled Sacred Books of the East in 1900 as a one-volume gateway to world scripture. Selections from Vedic hymns, the Zend-Avesta, the Dhammapada, Upanishads, the Koran, and a life of Buddha fill the book, with critical and biographical sketches. The Buddha chapters follow birth, palace life, disgust at sorrow, leaving the city, and turning the law-wheel.

A passage on Mohammed's birth in 570, orphaned young and raised by a century-old grandfather who saw his lost son Abdallah in the boy, shows Wilson's narrative touch. The anthology aims to let English readers taste many faiths at once. It remains a useful, if dated, introduction to Eastern sacred writing.
1296-the-provost:
John Galt tells the chronicle of a Scottish burgh through its provost, Pawkie, a canny, self-serving magistrate who guides his town through fifty years of change. The tale moves from elections to riots, from new streets to old customs, all in Pawkie's own sly voice.

Galt writes Scots town life with humor and realism, and the provost's memoirs form a social history in miniature. The book, a companion to The Annals of the Parish, shows Galt's gift for local life. It suits readers who like Scottish chronicles and sly narrators.
12998-thankful-rest:
Annie S. Swan's 1889 tale, subtitled simply a tale, opens in a pretty Scottish homestead and follows a family through loss, change, and new hope. Its chapters move from unwelcome news at the parsonage to a new home, Sundays, a red house, days on a lake, and at last a wedding. Swan wrote for readers who liked domestic stories with a clear moral thread.

The plot turns on patience and kindness winning over hard hearts, as the book's opening verses promise. Young Tom and Lucy learn to bear waiting, and older folk learn to forgive. Five years after the wedding, the closing chapter looks back on sorrows eased by steady love. The tale is gentle, plain, and meant to comfort as much as to entertain.
13146-the-beauty-and-the-bolshevist:
Alice Duer Miller's 1920 novel, published by Harper and Brothers, sets a rich young woman against a radical editor in New York. The editor of the daily Liberty opens a pile of letters. Soon the story turns to Cord, a girl who doubts the luxury around her. Eddie, an older man, defends it. Illustrations show a raft, a Newport boat, and a little blue car.

Cord argues that a system by which she profits may still be wrong, and that wealth is not part of the Constitution. Eddie answers that she is young and has seen less of the world. A third voice, Moreton the reformer, agrees with Eddie that one class must govern, but holds that labor, not capital, should rule. The novel is a light, sharp debate on wealth and revolution, dressed as romance.
13166-the-psalms-of-david-imitated-in-th:
Isaac Watts's Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament, in this edition from an 1818 London printing, turns the psalms into Christian hymns. Watts takes David's songs and recasts them in New Testament terms for Christian worship. A transcriber's note warns that reprints differ, and that indexes were dropped since key words can be searched.

Psalm verses urge holy souls to rejoice, sing new songs, and trust God when plagues spread among ten thousand dead. Another psalm, on life's short span, asks God to teach the heavenly art of improving hours, so souls may live beyond the grave. Watts's versions shaped English hymn singing for generations, and this volume shows them in plain, singable form.
1320-criminal-psychology-a-manual-for-ju:
Hans Gross was an Austrian jurist who founded modern criminal investigation. He writes this manual for judges and lawyers on how minds work in court: how witnesses err, how suspects lie, and how judges deceive themselves. The book draws on cases and on the new science of mind.

Gross argues that law must learn from psychology if justice is to be just, and his chapters on memory, emotion, and proof still read with force. The manual shaped police work and legal study. It draws readers who like law, mind, and the roots of forensic science.
13227-the-lord-of-dynevor-a-tale-of-the-:
Evelyn Everett-Green's Lord of Dynevor, a tale of Edward I's time, opens at Dynevor Castle with a boy's call ringing down a valley and up a ravine: La-ha-hoo. Echoes take up the cry, but the boy, fair curls in mountain wind, watches a craggy ridge with keen blue eyes. His tale runs through brothers, the eagle's crag, Welsh wolves, and the king's judgment.

Later, Wendot rescues a girl left alone on a ledge where an eagle's eyry once stood, just as Maelgon's men come to seize her. Griffeth, his brother, wishes he had shared the peril, but Wendot praises his timely aid. Twin brothers, disguised for an attack on Carregcennen, care more for slaying hated Raoul than for who reigns after. The novel is a spirited Welsh border romance.
13296-promenades-of-an-impressionist:
James Huneker's 1910 Promenades of an Impressionist, published by Charles Scribner's Sons, strolls through modern art and music with a critic's flair. Contents run from Paul Cézanne, Rops the etcher, Monticelli, Rodin, Carrière, and Degas to Botticelli, six Spaniards including El Greco, Velasquez, and Goya, and Chardin. Huneker dedicates the book to Frederick James Gregg, quoting Stendhal on promenading prejudices.

On El Greco, he quotes Justi on craving for originality that bred mannerisms, and Stevenson on Spanish gravity of coloring never subtle or natural. Later, he defends Manet as a classic, whose power lies in broad, sabre-like strokes, not the niggling touches of impressionists, whose reductio ad absurdum is pointillism. The book is witty, learned criticism.
13460-how-to-become-like-christ:
A short devotional volume on likeness to Christ opens with Paul's image of believers reflecting the Lord's glory and changing from glory to glory. The writer insists that character is the one thing a person carries out of life, and that future good will vary with resemblance to Jesus.

Sermons follow on the Transfiguration, indiscreet importunity, shame at God's displeasure, Naaman cured, and the lame man at the temple gate. Peter's cry, Thou art the Christ, brings relief and keen satisfaction to his hearers. The book urges discreet prayer, patient resistance to evil habits, and a life guided toward the highest ends, step by step.
13532-kindred-of-the-dust:
Peter B. Kyne's 1920 novel Kindred of the Dust, illustrated by Dean Cornwell and dedicated to his foster sister Irene. Centres on Hector McKaye, owner of the Tyee Lumber Company and known as the Laird. In the living room of his home, the Dreamerie on Tyee Head, Hector holds court over family, timber, and old feuds.

Donald, his son, bows his head and tells his father he cannot give her up, while Nan takes in a man without a home. A lover returning from a tryst meets cronching figures with bludgeon ready, and Dirty Dan investigates a rich man's son who vanished without a trace. Kyne mixes lumber country, romance, and family pride in a western tale of kin and dust.
13801-harvest:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published Harvest in 1920, late in a long career as a novelist of English social life. Two old farm labourers open the book, walking from Great End Farm with bags on sticks. The elder still carries a look of youth despite grey hair and a stooping gait. Their talk sets a rural world of work, wages, and old age.

Ward follows farm families through harvest, love, and loss. She studies how custom, church, and new ideas pull at village life. Her sympathy lies with workers facing change and with women holding households together. The prose is steady and observant rather than flashy. Harvest offers a quiet portrait of English country life after the First World War.
13823-lady-merton-colonist:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published Lady Merton, Colonist in 1910, set in Canada and the Rockies. Elizabeth, Lady Merton, walks and climbs in the mountains, plunging spirit and sense into their beauty. A foreword explains Lake Elizabeth, a lake of dream with a real original discovered by Mrs. Schäffer of Philadelphia. An explorers' tent stands beside its broad expanse.

Ward follows Elizabeth from English society to colonial life, work, and love. A steward serves in a dining room while a tanned cook looks out from the kitchen. The novel weighs duty, faith, and the freedom of new lands. Ward's Canadian scenes praise landscape and settler energy. The book offers a late Ward romance with a colonial theme.
13859-boy-scouts-in-southern-waters-or-s:
G. Harvey Ralphson wrote Boy Scouts in Southern Waters in 1915, subtitled Spaniard's Treasure Chest. A collision in fog, a crippled boat, and a mysterious message start the adventure. Scouts wig-wag warnings, rescue a marooned boy, and capture a pirate prisoner. Jack is stricken by a bullet, and a night attack tests first aid and escape.

Treasure, a fort, and a burning cabin add mystery. One scout jokes about rocks where only sand exists, showing Ralphson's light humour. The story stresses Scout skills: signalling, boating, and teamwork. It belongs to a series that sent Scouts to sea, air, and motor boat. Young readers get thrills with a wholesome moral.
1409-the-soul-of-the-far-east:
Percival Lowell's study contrasts Western and Eastern ways of mind, drawing on life in the Far East. Eight chapters take up, in turn, individuality, family, adoption, language, nature and art, religion, and imagination. They argue that Eastern life rests far more on the group and on custom than on the single self.

Lowell writes as a clear-eyed outsider, noting manners, speech, and art with care, and he often turns the mirror back on Western habits too. The book is dated in some of its claims, yet it remains a readable early attempt to explain a whole culture through its daily forms and thoughts.
14261-alton-of-somasco-a-romance-of-the-:
Harold Bindloss published Alton of Somasco in 1905, a romance of the great northwest with pictures by R. Martine Reay. Chapters move from a first encounter and Townshead's ranch through Harry the teamster, Hallam of the Tyee, and the heir of Carnaby. Miss Deringham makes friends, Alton blunders, and a confederate, an undelivered message, and misplaced confidence complicate the trail to Vancouver and the Somasco Consolidated company.

A sickbed scene anchors the middle. Alton, grey-faced with steely eyes, demands a message Miss Townshead gave a messenger, only to learn it reached the lady instead. Whisky, sold stock, and a drunken errand explain the muddle. Later, a doctor watches over a sleeping pair while Alice Deringham rises with a soft glow, learning the worst has passed. Bindloss writes frontier business and romance with equal energy, and the northwest emerges as a place of deals, trails, and second chances.
14482-the-story-of-the-foss-river-ranch-:
Ridgwell Cullum's 1903 tale of the Canadian Northwest opens at a polo club ball, then plunges into a blizzard, a poker game, and the Foss River Ranch. Cullum wrote many popular frontier romances.

A villain called Lablache schemes for the ranch across muskeg and bad man's hollow, while half-breeds, traders, and a prairie girl complicate the fight. Chapters move from night terrors to open campaigns for the property. The novel is melodramatic and fast, full of snow, horses, and money-grubbing, in the tradition of the early western romance. Cullum's villains are as large as his landscapes.
14522-the-canterville-ghost:
Oscar Wilde's comic ghost story, in this illustrated 1906 Boston edition, tells of the ghost of Canterville Chase. His troubles begin when an American minister and his family move into his ancestral halls. Wallace Goldsmith supplied the pictures.

The ghost tries his classic haunts, from the bloodstain to the clanking chains, but the practical Otis family oils the chains, scrubs the stain, and pelts him with pellets. Only Virginia Otis treats him with pity, and her kindness frees him at last. Wilde's tale inverts the haunted-house story with wit, and it remains his most beloved short fiction.
14527-children-of-the-mist:
Eden Phillpotts's 1898 Dartmoor novel follows three books, from a boy's romance through an enterprise to a granite cross. Phillpotts, a Devon writer, knew the moor's farms and villages well.

Will and Phoebe Lyddon grow up among pixies' parlours, rivers, and granite, while Grimbal, a successful but unphilosophical man, sees his plan to possess Phoebe collapse and his life come adrift. The novel moves from childhood games to marriage, money, and loss. Phillpotts writes with local color and tragic force, and the moor itself broods over the story. His Dartmoor novels made the region famous among readers.
1453-the-alkahest:
Balzac's novel, also called The Quest of the Absolute, follows Balthazar Claes, a Flemish chemist. He ruins his family in search of the alkahest, a universal solvent that would turn base matter to gold. His wife watches their fortune melt in furnaces and experiments, while his children grow up in the shadow of his dream.

The book studies obsession with scientific patience: years of failure, brief hope, and a final discovery that comes too late to save the house. Balzac treats Claes with pity as well as awe. It is a powerful tale of genius, waste, and the price of a single consuming idea.
14555-william-lloyd-garrison-the-aboliti:
Archibald H. Grimké wrote this life of William Lloyd Garrison, the abolitionist, first published in 1891 and reprinted in 1974 from that edition. Grimké dedicated it to Anna M. Day.

The biography follows Garrison from obscure beginnings to the Liberator, the American Anti-Slavery Society, and his prophecy that Faneuil Hall would echo with his principles. Grimké presents Garrison as a hero for brave and true living in the republic. The book is a sympathetic nineteenth-century life, written by a Black scholar and diplomat of the next generation. Grimké himself later served as consul in Santo Domingo.
14581-the-just-and-the-unjust:
Vaughan Kester's 1912 novel, illustrated by M. Leone Bracker, opens with a fight against a man named Shrimplin and follows a gambler, a star witness, and a husband and wife through suspicion and love. Kester had written The Prodigal Judge.

Colonel George Harbison and Elizabeth anchor a plot of folly, screws put on, and a finger of suspicion, as Joe tells his story and light breaks in darkness. The novel moves between courtroom tension and domestic feeling. It is a solid popular romance of justice and marriage, written in the brisk style of its era.
14743-the-fun-of-getting-thin-how-to-be-:
Samuel G. Blythe's 1912 health book treats weight loss as a matter of sense, humour and habit, not miracle cures. He opens on fat itself, noting that half the comedy in the world rests on the paunch, and that fat people trying to get thin mirror thin people trying to get fat.

So-called cures come next, and Blythe is sceptical of them. Facing the tissue means facing one's own eating, drink and daily routine. Doctors may call fat fatal, he jokes, but comfort matters too. The book now reads as period advice, brisk and blunt, with the diet wisdom of its day and a cheerful refusal to moralise beyond common sense.
14858-the-man-thou-gavest:
Harriet T. Comstock's novel opens with passengers leaving a train one by one, while Truedale takes no heed. Dedicated to the MacDowell Colony at Peterborough, New Hampshire, and to her who understands, the book was largely written in a little studio deep in the pine woods.

A frontispiece shows a girl asking whether she is the sort to sell herself for anything, even for justice she thinks is his. That question drives the story: love, honour and sacrifice in a world where a woman's choices are judged harshly. Comstock writes with warmth and moral seriousness, and the pine-wood setting gives the romance a quiet, reflective frame.
1510-love-s-labour-s-lost:
In Navarre, a king and three lords swear off love, food, and sleep for three years of study, and then a French princess and her ladies arrive on state business. Vows crumble at once, and the play becomes a sparkling contest of sonnets, puns, and disguises between would-be scholars and witty women.

A pageant of the Nine Worthies ends in farce, and news of a death turns comedy sober at the close, with marriages deferred for a year of trial. The play is Shakespeare's most verbal comedy, full of wordplay and high spirits. It rewards readers who enjoy language as a game.
15323-the-green-eyes-of-ba-st:
Sax Rohmer's 1920 mystery, The Green Eyes of Bâst, opens with a narrator who sees the eyes. He then follows signs of the cat, a green image, and Isobel through interrupted suppers and velvet curtains. Chapters add Dr. Damar Greefe, a black doctor, a Nubian mute, and the secret of Friar's Park. Gatton's story widens the plot.

Egyptian cult, London fog, and a gray mist mix in Rohmer's popular thriller style, with a golden cat and a man on a tower near the end. The book trades on exotic mystery, in the manner of Fu-Manchu. Thriller fans will find it fast, lurid, and full of period atmosphere.
1540-the-tempest:
Shakespeare's late romance opens with a storm at sea, raised by Prospero, the exiled Duke of Milan, who rules a lonely island with his daughter Miranda and his spirits Ariel and Caliban. A ship carrying his usurping brother Antonio wrecks on the shore, and Prospero's magic sets a reckoning in motion.

Through love between Miranda and Ferdinand, Caliban's rebellion, and Ariel's songs, Prospero moves from vengeance to forgiveness and gives up his art. The play is brief, musical, and full of wonder. It is often read as Shakespeare's farewell to the stage, and a meditation on power and mercy.
15493-the-lancashire-witches-a-romance-o:
William Harrison Ainsworth published this romance of Pendle Forest in a third edition in London in 1854, illustrated by John Gilbert. It was undertaken at the suggestion of James Crossley, editor of The Discoverie of Witches in the County of Lancaster, to whom Ainsworth inscribes the book. That scholarly groundwork underlies a sprawling historical novel.

An introduction on the last abbot of Whalley leads into books on Alizon Device and Pendle Forest. Chapters cover a beacon on Pendle Hill, Whalley Abbey, a midnight mass, and the ordeal by swimming. Alice Nutter, Mother Chattox, the Asshetons, and a black cat and white dove populate the tale. Ainsworth mixes witch trial history with gothic romance, and the novel remains a vivid, if fanciful, retelling of Lancashire's famous witch panic.
1550-a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curi:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's historical romance, told as a history related by Mr Isaac Bickerstaff, follows Clorinda Wildairs, a lady of quality in the reign of William and Mary. From a wild girlhood in November 1690, Clorinda grows into a beauty of wit, temper, and daring, courted and quarrelled over by great men.

Through duels, marriages, and the fashions of the town, the novel traces a woman who refuses to be tamed by convention, yet longs for a love equal to her spirit. Burnett writes with colour and sympathy. The book is a lively costume romance, and a portrait of a heroine ahead of her age.
15540-across-india-or-live-boys-in-the-f:
Oliver Optic, real name William T. Adams, published this boys' travel novel in Boston in 1895, with Lee and Shepard, in the All-Over-the-World Library, third series. Adams dedicates it to his long-tried friend William Lee, senior publisher for more than a generation, with whom in forty years he never had a bicker or a shadow of unpleasantness. A frontispiece shows a figure in magnificent robes of India.

Chapters move from finding the longitude and a wreck in the Arabian Sea to first and second cutters to the rescue, titled gentlemen of Travancore, and an interview in the captain's cabin. Later parts treat India's geography, flora and snakes, population and people, and dinners at sea. Optic writes adventure with instruction, in the brisk style that made his hundred-plus volumes popular with American boys.
15673-the-day-of-the-beast:
A 1922 novel by Zane Grey, dedicated to American men who served in the Great War. Grey, best known for western tales, turns here to a soldier's return home. Daren Lane comes back with gassed lungs and a heart full of longing, only to find his country changed. Grosset and Dunlap published the book for a wide popular audience.

Lane sails up the Narrows past the Statue of Liberty, dreaming of orchards, ploughed earth, and his mother's kitchen. Home brings shock instead: new wealth, loose pleasure, and men like Swann who thrive on it. Lane clashes with this postwar world and fights to hold his own code. The novel stands as Grey's protest against a peace that seemed to forget the price of war.
15710-nicky-nan-reservist:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, known as Q, wrote this Cornish novel of the Great War's first months, in twenty-four chapters from how the children played to the first three recruits. News of war first reaches Polpier, a fishing village, where Nicholas Nanjivell, commonly called Nicky-Nan, pays small attention, preoccupied with his own affairs. The children, tragically concerned, take it gaily enough.

Polpier lives by the fishery, and scores of its fishermen passed through the Navy and now belong to the Reserve. They hold hazy notions of the Balance of Power in Europe, and few could explain it. Chapters follow a call to arms, how the men went, sermons, an anonymous letter, treasure trove, and business as usual. A broken pane, a vicar's misgivings, three pilchards, and first aid follow. Q writes a warm, comic chronicle of a village at war, seen through one stubborn fisherman.
1574-historic-girls-stories-of-girls-who:
E. S. Brooks's Historic Girls tells stories of girls who influenced the history of their times, written in an age of debate over women's equality and rights. The preface argues that women and girls, even in the distant past, proved themselves by action and endeavour, and each chapter follows one such girl through a crisis of her age.

The tales range across countries and centuries, with history retold as adventure for young readers. Brooks writes with earnest admiration. The book is a period work of girls' history, charming in its purpose and a window on how 1880s America taught heroism to girls.
16129-in-luck-at-last:
Walter Besant's novel In Luck at Last, published in New York by George Munro's Sons, opens with praise for second-hand bookselling. If everyone could choose the pleasantest way through life, the narrator thinks, many would run at once to the craft and mystery of the second-hand bookshop. It would be neither too lofty nor too mean, with a pitch to suit. Piccadilly, the Haymarket, and great collectors' shops set the standard he has in mind.

From bookish beginnings grows a tale of fortune turning at last, with London shops, odd characters, and second chances. Besant, a popular Victorian novelist, writes with warmth about ordinary people and their luck. Readers who love books about books will enjoy its shop talk and its hopeful plot.
16134-the-first-christmas-tree-a-story-o:
Henry Van Dyke's 1897 story, illustrated by Howard Pyle and published by Scribner, tells how the Christmas tree began. Four chapters carry the tale: The Call of the Woodsman, The Trail Through the Forest, The Shadow of the Thunder-Oak, and The Felling of the Tree. Winfried, the missionary woodsman, leads his people from the sacred oak of Thor to a little fir, and tells the story of Bethlehem beside it.

Pyle's photogravures picture the moonlit fields, Thor's hammer, and the moment the little fir is taken from its place. Van Dyke writes in a warm, reverent style for family reading at Christmas. The book remains a beloved telling of a holiday legend, short enough for one fireside sitting.
16249-bought-and-paid-for-from-the-play-:
Arthur Hornblow novelized George Broadhurst's play Bought and Paid For, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1912 with illustrations from stage scenes. Chapter one opens at a sickbed, where a tall, aristocratic wife with snow-white hair and eyes red from weeping begs the doctor for hope. The physician, just out of the sick chamber, hides what compassion prompts him to conceal, while a methodical nurse moves quickly nearby.

From that anxious room grows a domestic drama of marriage, money, and pride, in the popular theater's moral style. Hornblow turns stage dialogue into readable prose without losing its tension. Readers who like early Broadway melodrama will find a tense, old-fashioned story.
16289-the-fur-bringers-a-story-of-the-ca:
Hulbert Footner's 1920 novel The Fur Bringers, from the James A. McCann Company in New York, plays out in the Canadian Northwest. Contents run from June fever and Fort Enterprise through Colina, a meeting, an invitation to dine, Ambrose's camp, lovers, and Alexander Selkirk and family. Gathering shadows, a quarrel, Simon Grampierre, a plan of campaign, Colina commanding, and a bloodless capture follow.

Woman's weapons, undercurrents, the subtlety of Gordon Strange, a tea dance, fire and rapine, accusation and conviction, and a trap and a test carry the plot to its close. Footner writes brisk fur-trade adventure with romance and rivalry. Readers who like Northern yarns will find a colorful, fast-moving story.
16383-dotty-dimple-out-west:
Sophie May sends little Dotty Dimple west in this volume of the Dotty Dimple series. An October morning starts the trip, with a captain's son, a baby in a blue cloak, and a postponed pigeon pie along the way. Out west, Dotty goes nutting, wanders the woods, meets surprises, and even sniggles for eels.

The chapters are short and sunny, made for young readers. Dotty's chatter and small mishaps carry the story, with grown-ups kindly in the background. The book gives a gentle picture of a child's western holiday in the days when such trips were still an adventure.
16444-indian-unrest:
Valentine Chirol, reprinting and enlarging his Times articles with an introduction by Sir Alfred Lyall, surveys unrest in India in this 1910 book. Chapters cover swaraj on platform and in press, a Hindu revival, Brahmanism in the Deccan, the storm in Bengal, the Punjab and the Arya Samaj, Muslims, the Congress, and constitutional reforms. Depressed castes and native states get full treatment.

Chirol writes as a concerned imperial observer, mapping a vast land moving, in Morley's phrase, from the fifth century to the twentieth. The book is detailed and sober, aimed at readers who govern or study empire. It remains a key source on India on the eve of mass nationalism.
16477-florence-and-northern-tuscany-with:
Edward Hutton guides readers through Florence and northern Tuscany, with Genoa, in this second edition, illustrated in color by William Parkinson. The route runs from Genoa by Porto Venere, Carrara, Pisa, and Livorno to Florence, then through its squares, churches, and galleries: the Duomo, San Marco, Santa Croce, the Uffizi, and the Pitti.

Hutton writes as a learned, loving companion, mixing art history with walks and local lore. The book suits travelers who want depth, not mere lists. For lovers of Italy, it remains a classic guide to Tuscany's art and streets, rich in detail and affection.
16491-vergilius-a-tale-of-the-coming-of-:
Irving Bacheller sets this 1904 tale in Rome at the coming of Christ, when the city, in his image, had passed its summits and stood looking into a dark valley. Graves of Caesar, Cicero, Vergil, and Horace lie behind, while philosophers ask whether life is a misfortune and poets sing no more of pleasant trifles. Into that weary world comes the new faith.

Bacheller writes with rich, rolling prose, mixing Roman splendor with spiritual hunger. The tale is short and earnest, aimed at readers who love historical romance with a religious heart. It remains a fine example of early twentieth-century inspirational fiction.
1654-an-unsocial-socialist:
Sidney Trefusis is a rich young man who preaches socialism while living off the very wealth he denounces. This early Shaw novel tests him against the people around him. At an English country house he meets Agatha Wylie, a clever schoolteacher, and the pair trade arguments about class, marriage, and honest work.

Shaw uses the romance to stage debates: can a man be sincere while keeping his money. Can love survive when both partners insist on seeing through each other. The novel is talkative by design, and its comedy comes from Trefusis himself, a reformer whose sharpest opponent is his own comfort.
16551-the-girl-of-the-golden-west:
David Belasco's 1911 novel of California mining camps opens with the Girl riding back to the mines from Monterey, sole passenger on a stage piled with rebozos and silken souvenirs. Her mind, ripe for a lasting impression, reviews a week's delights in the old town. At Cloudy Mountain Camp, the boys hear not a word of her meeting until long after.

Belasco writes of a far western land where strangers from God knows where struggled, laughed, gambled, cursed, killed, and loved out strange destinies. The tale became a famous play and opera. Readers of western romance will find a vivid, theatrical story of the Girl and her camp.
1665-derrick-vaughan-novelist:
Edna Lyall tells this story through a friend of the title character, a young novelist whose talent grows out of sympathy rather than ambition. Derrick Vaughan spends his early years caring for a drunken father, and the patience that costs him shapes the way he writes about other people's lives.

The narrator, by contrast, admits his own selfishness, and the contrast between the two men drives the book. Lyall's point, borrowed from Lewes and Toynbee, is that a great artist needs deep feeling for others. The novel tests that claim in ordinary scenes: a sickroom, a country house, and a friendship that forces its teller to judge himself.
16785-our-catholic-heritage-in-english-l:
Emily Hickey wrote this 1910 book on Catholic heritage in English literature before the Norman Conquest, issued by Sands in London and Edinburgh with a color frontispiece of the death of St. Bede. It is inscribed to the Archbishop of Westminster by kind leave. Chapters open with the beginnings of English letters, Caedmon and Cynewulf, the Whitby monastery, and Caedmon's gift of song.

Hickey traces English verse from its monastic roots, through Genesis, Exodus, and the fall of angels, to later pre-Conquest writers. She writes for Catholic readers who want their literary past claimed with pride. The book gives a clear, short guide to early English letters, useful for students of Old English and of church history alike.
16911-the-romance-of-the-coast:
James Runciman wrote this 1883 book of coast sketches, issued by George Bell in London. He dedicated it to Frederick Greenwood, the editor who gave him his start away from political journalism. Chapters take up an old-school pilot, a fisherwoman, and a veteran. A fishing village heroine, silent men, and a cabin boy follow. A squire, a village preacher, a fisher's friend, a coastguard, and a suspected man close the set.

Runciman writes of sea folk with warmth and a sharp eye, praising hard work and plain virtue. Each sketch stands alone, drawn from life on the shore. Readers who love sea tales will find a humane, old-style book, full of boats, storms, and the small heroics of coast life.
17012-the-house-of-walderne-a-tale-of-th:
The Rev. A. D. Crake wrote this tale of the cloister and the forest in the days of the Barons' Wars, called The House of Walderne. Chapters move from a knight and squire and Michelham Priory into Kenilworth and the greenwood. Walderne Castle, Martin's first day at Oxford, and Hubert at Lewes Priory follow. Early Franciscans, spurs and desires, and May Day at Lewes appear. A crusader, outlaws, a preaching friar, and a medieval tyrant lead to the battle of Lewes and after.

Crake mixes monks, knights, outlaws, and schoolboys in a tale meant to teach history through adventure. His preface presents it as the twelfth of his series with pleasure. Young readers get a rich, old-style historical tale of medieval England, full of priories, castles, and battles, told with a clergyman's warmth.
1725-heart-of-the-west:
Texas ranches, border towns, and the camps of cowboys and rangers replace O. Henry's New York streets in these stories, though the last-page turn stays the same. A ransom is negotiated, a handbook of courtship is put to comic use, a princess meets a puma, and a call loan comes due at the worst hour.

The tales keep O. Henry's signature move — the last-page turn that reorders the whole story. But the ground is new: wide country, dry humor, and men who talk big and act bigger. Readers who know his New York stories will enjoy seeing the same wit at work under a western sky, with sentiment kept just short of soft.
1735-sophist:
How can anyone say what is false, if saying it means saying what is not. The Stranger from Elea takes that riddle as his starting point. The Eleatic Stranger leads the talk, with almost no description of time or place. The argument turns on verbs and nouns: no sentence can be formed without both, as in 'Theaetetus sits. '.

From that small point the dialogue builds a theory of being and not-being, and a way to separate the sophist from the philosopher. It is hard reading, but it is the dialogue where Plato's logic grows teeth. Readers who want the metaphysics behind the Republic's arguments about truth will find the groundwork laid here.
17467-effie-maurice-or-what-do-i-love-be:
Gall and Inglis of London and Edinburgh published this moral tale, Effie Maurice, or What Do I Love Best, for young readers. Chapters run from the first commandment and plans proposed, through New Year's Day, the miser, and the poor widow, to generosity and justice, the new book, and another of Mr. Maurice's lessons. A funeral closes the set.

The tale opens on a Sabbath evening in winter, when little Effie Maurice speaks with her mother about a neighbour's teaching. Readers get a didactic story in which each chapter tests a lesson in duty, kindness, and faith. The book suits readers of Victorian children's moral fiction and of the Sunday school tale.
17598-beth-norvell-a-romance-of-the-west:
Randall Parrish, author of When Wilderness Was King and Bob Hampton of Placer, wrote this western romance with a frontispiece in colour by N. C. Wyeth. A woman who never changes her posture, never seeming to notice the approach of dawn, opens the pictured scene, while Winston stands nearby. The chapters promise a chance meeting, a road company, a breaking of ice, and a new deal of the cards.

Later chapters bring open rebellion, the Little Yankee mine, a dismissal, a man who means fight, the force of circumstances, and a new alliance. Readers get a popular western of love, mines, and frontier conflict, in Parrish's sturdy style. The book suits readers of early twentieth-century romance of the West.
17609-our-deportment-or-the-manners-cond:
John H. Young, master of arts, compiled this guide to deportment from the latest reliable authorities, revised and illustrated, published in 1881 by firms in Detroit, St. Louis, Harrisburg, and Chicago. Copyright belonged to Freeman B. Dickerson in 1879 and 1881. Its full title promises the manners, conduct, and dress of the most refined society, with forms for letters and invitations and suggestions on home culture and training.

Young's preface holds that no subject matters more generally than the rules, usages, and ceremonies of good society. Readers get a Victorian etiquette manual, covering dress, calls, letters, and household training. The book suits readers of social history and of how Americans learned to behave in company.
17727-the-school-of-recreation-1696-edit:
Printed in London in 1696 for Henry Rhodes, this guide by R. H. teaches the pastimes of a gentleman of the age. Its title page lists hunting, hawking, riding, tennis, racing, bowling, fireworks, ringing, cock-fighting, fowling, defence, and angling, each with its own rules and tricks.

The preface vows that no one book had yet joined so many sports in one small volume. The text draws on the author's own practice plus the views of masters in each art. Readers learn how to cast a hawk, play at bowls, or set off fireworks, all in plain, old spelling. It is a rare, lively window on how English folk played, and played well, three centuries ago.
1803-wyoming-a-story-of-the-outdoor-west:
A rifle cracks from a clump of bushes a hundred yards away. The bullet cuts a line between Bannister on one side and Miss Messiter and her foreman on the other. The Lazy D ranch, a dance at Fraser's, and a party call carry the story into the range wars and cattle business of Wyoming.

Raine writes the outdoor west with the confidence of a man who knew its codes: loyalty to a ranch, quick shooting, and women who hold their own in a hard country. The novel moves fast, and its set pieces — ambushes, rides, and confrontations on open ground — give it the shape of the classic ranch romance.
18044-wine-women-and-song-mediaeval-lati:
John Addington Symonds translated Wine, Women, and Song, medieval Latin students' songs now first turned into English verse, with an essay, printed in London in 1884 by Chatto and Windus. Symonds dedicates the book to Robert Louis Stevenson, in memory of past symposia when wit flowed free.

Songs of drink, love, spring, and the road fill the pages, with the essay setting the scene of goliard life. The verse is bold, funny, and at times ribald, in the spirit of young clerks on the move. It is a lively, learned anthology, best for readers who like old songs with a modern, scholarly frame.
18054-the-zeit-geist:
L. Dougall wrote The Zeit-Geist as a novel of the Canadian fens, printed in a cheap one-volume library of complete novels. The tale opens at home in a small fen town, where the Ahwewee River falls thirty feet and dams have drowned wide woods and marshes.

The heroine returns to a town of green woods, breezy pastures, and stumps still standing, where the river runs shallow and swift. Dougall writes of place, kin, and the spirit of the age with a quiet, observant eye. It is a gentle, regional novel, best for readers who like slow, place-rich tales of Canadian life.
18149-conjuror-s-house-a-romance-of-the-:
Stewart Edward White published this romance of the northern forest in 1903. Its opening places a girl on a bank above a river flowing north, with a dozen whitewashed buildings at her back. Around the small settlement stretch balsams and spruce, birch and poplar, and beyond them vast muskegs and broken rock country.

Only trappers, native peoples, and beasts have trodden the wilderness around her. Once each summer a sailing ship from England feels its way through Hudson Strait to reach the post. The novel follows life at that remote edge, where the forest sets the terms and news from the outer world arrives once a year. It is a story of isolation, weather, and the pull of the wild.
18486-quiet-talks-on-following-the-chris:
S. D. Gordon, author of Quiet Talks on Power and Quiet Talks on Prayer, published this book of quiet talks on following Christ in 1913 with Fleming H. Revell in New York and London. Gordon writes in short, plain talks. His books aim at heart and practice.

Contents give the lone man who went before and the long rough road he trod. They give the pleading call to follow and what following means. A look ahead, the main road, valleys, and hilltops mark the way. Later talks ask shall we go, give finger-posts and fellow-followers, and end with the glory of the goal, face to face. Gordon opens with two young men on a Japanese liner debating whether belief has power to make a man live it. Readers get a devotional guide: following as friendship, road, and daily choice.
18529-august-first:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews and Roy Irving Murray wrote this story, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1915, with pictures by A. I. Keller. August First opens in stifling heat. A young clergyman pulls at his clerical collar and swings to the one window not wide open. He pushes it up three inches against dusty vines on the parish house wall. Black-gray clouds gather in the west, and a storm promises coolness.

The man gasps for breath, stares down a corridor to an open door to the street, and murmurs, if they are coming, why do they not come and get it over. He is the new minister, troubled beyond the heat on this first day of August. Readers get a story of a parish, a summer storm, and a young man's first test.
18653-the-mind-of-the-artist:
Mrs. Laurence Binyon collected this book of painters' and sculptors' thoughts at London in 1909 with Chatto and Windus, preface by George Clausen. Rather than famous treatises by Leonardo and Reynolds, she draws on letters, diaries, and memoirs for intimate working notes. Sayings run from Alfred Stevens and Fuseli to Leonardo on painting man's soul through limb and pose.

Permissions from families of Burne-Jones, Whistler, Watts, Rossetti, Millais, and Morris enrich the set, with translations from Durer, Cennini, and Corot. Pictures include Rembrandt's Polish Rider and works by Rubens, Raphael, and Gainsborough. The book gives artists' own views of their craft.
18680-practical-forestry-in-the-pacific-:
E. T. Allen, forester for the Western Forestry and Conservation Association, issued this guide at Portland, Oregon, in 1911. It sets out plain methods for guarding standing forests and growing new ones on the Pacific coast from Montana to California, for both the public and the lumberman. Allen notes that owners had begun to see timber land as a lasting source of work, not a mine to use up and leave.

Chapters cover fire prevention, taxes, regrowth, and tree planting by farmers, plus the public gain from a sound state forest policy. Figures come largely from the Forest Service, with thanks to J. F. Kummel for planting notes. The booklet is a practical early text on forest care.
18815-the-mark-of-the-beast:
Sidney Watson's prophetic novel, published by Fleming H. Revell in 1933 with copyright in 1918, asks what will follow the Lord's Second Coming for those left behind. Its publisher's note frames the questions: the Tribulation, the reign of Antichrist, and the meaning of the mark of the beast.

Chapters move from twenty-five years later and a super man through foreshadowings, the investiture, the abomination of desolation, the death of the two witnesses, and flight, pursuit, and martyrdom. Watson, who thanks Seiss and Campbell Morgan for thoughts on Judas and Antichrist, defends his fictional form by Bunyan, Milton, and Dante. The story aims to awaken careless Christians to a closer walk.
18903-the-last-harvest:
John Burroughs published this book in Boston and New York in 1922, with Houghton Mifflin. It belongs to his late work as America's best-known nature essayist, written at Woodchuck Lodge in Roxbury in the Catskills. A Wordsworth poem quoted at the front sets the tone: a quiet eye brooding on common things, gathering a harvest of random truths.

The essays observe birds, brooks, hills, and valleys with the patience of a lifetime outdoors. Burroughs finds meaning in solitude and in the outward shows of sky and earth. Readers get gentle, reflective nature writing from the end of a long career, suited to slow reading and to anyone who walks, watches, and thinks in the open air.
19074-italy-at-war-and-the-allies-in-the:
E. Alexander Powell, a correspondent of the New York World and later a captain, wrote this 1917 war book as volume four of The War on All Fronts. He reports from Italy and the western Allied lines during the First World War, with a focus on borders, trains, and troops on the move.

Powell describes frontier checks, secret service men, spies, and long rail runs along the Mediterranean shore from Genoa toward Pisa. His scenes show how war pressed on ports, towns, and ordinary travel. Readers get a first-hand wartime report, vivid on detail and firm in its Allied point of view.
19102-dearest:
H. Beam Piper wrote this short tale, first printed in Weird Tales in March 1951. Colonel Ashley Hampton, called Slaughterhouse Hampton in the Army, sits in his library at Greyrock among trophies of Indian, Filipino, and German wars, facing five people he counts as enemies. His nephew Stephen and wife Myra lead the hostile group.

Hampton hides a secret companion he calls Dearest, an unseen presence he speaks to in whispers learned at West Point, while old Sergeant Williamson senses something subtle in the house. The price of her company is eternal watchfulness. Readers get a sly, eerie tale of an old soldier, greed, and a ghostly friend.
19116-how-to-sing-meine-gesangskunst:
Lilli Lehmann wrote this singing manual, translated from German by Richard Aldrich. It was published in 1902. Lehmann, a famed soprano, insists that true artists need sound organs. They need a good teacher who can sing well. They need at least six years of study before the first work. Only such singers should teach.

She explains breathing in and out, the larynx, tongue, and palate. She covers the diaphragm and belly muscles that rule breath pressure. She covers the chest tension that drives tone through the vocal cords to head cavities. Readers get a thorough, demanding guide to the art of singing from a master of the stage.
19147-the-house-in-the-mist:
Anna Katharine Green wrote this mystery novel, issued in 1913 with a 1905 copyright. A young wayfarer, lost in raw mist on a dark night, follows a light to a strange house and steps inside. He hopes for shelter and perhaps for fortune beyond the next turning.

Inside he meets kin with sharp tongues, an old man with a pointed stick and a small boy guide, and guests whose talk hides old wrongs. Each arrival adds a thread to the puzzle. Readers get a moody, old-style detective tale where mist, manners, and family secrets cloud the truth.
19322-the-antichrist:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote The Antichrist, here translated from German with an introduction by H. L. Mencken, in a Knopf pocket edition of 1923. Mencken defends Nietzsche against democratic and clerical rage, arguing that his attacks carry learning and point, like bullets in a gun and teeth in a tiger. The book is fierce philosophy, not mere noise.

Nietzsche assails Christianity and democracy as forces that weaken life, praising strength, honesty, and a higher human type. His prose bites and provokes by design. Readers get a landmark of modern thought, best read as argument to weigh, not as doctrine to swallow whole.
19388-the-sagebrusher-a-story-of-the-wes:
Emerson Hough wrote this 1919 western, The Sagebrusher, with pictures by J. Henry, about Sim Gage at home. Sim, who wears all his clothes summer and winter, stands apathetic with foot turned over, longing for company yet arguing with his friend Wid Gardner not to hurry away. Cattle, a mule, and a willow creek frame his cabin.

Wid Gardner leaves by rail bars, calling Sim too dirty as he passes, while Sim chews a wisp of grass and watches him go. Wanted: a wife, fifty-fifty, and hearts aflame fill later chapters. Readers get a western tale of a shiftless man, neighbours, and the slow pull toward love and change.
19432-heart-and-soul-by-maveric-post:
Maveric Post wrote this book of plain reflections on life, put out in New York in the early nineteen twenties. He says frankly that he wrote it for himself, to set down thoughts that would not leave him alone, and only later shared them when friends urged him to print. Health, work, faith, and the lives of people near him are his themes.

One passage weighs an expert's rating of his own strength against how he feels day by day, a sign of the book's honest, first-person tone. It is not a system or a sermon, but a set of musings meant to help readers who wrestle with the same plain questions.
19507-lanier-of-the-cavalry-or-a-week-s-:
General Charles King wrote this cavalry tale of a young officer under a week's arrest, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Lanier stands accused of meddling with a sergeant's duty, hobnobbing with enlisted men, and lending civilian clothes to a protege for a wild escapade.

The charge sheet, read out with stern formality, frames a story of honor, friendship, and army discipline on a frontier post. King, himself a soldier, writes barrack life with ease, and the tale moves between courtroom talk and the bonds that bind officers and men.
19614-the-dark-forest:
Hugh Walpole wrote this novel of Russia in wartime, brought out by a New York house in the mid nineteen teens. Its first part follows a narrator from Petrograd station through schoolhouses, invisible battles, retreats, and a night flight, tired, dirty, and pursued.

The second part turns to lovers, Marie Ivanovna, and a forest where a door closes behind the fugitives. Walpole, who served in Russia, writes the Eastern Front as a place of fear and strange beauty, and the novel remains one of his most praised war books. Among the first part's chapters stands one named simply for Nikitin.
19694-a-smaller-history-of-rome-from-the:
William Smith wrote this smaller history of Rome, from earliest times to the empire. Eugene Lawrence continued it to the late empire. The New York edition of the late eighteen hundreds adds wood engravings and maps. It belongs to a student series made for school use.

Chapters follow Rome's kings, republic, and civil wars, including the clash of Marius and Metellus over an oath in the Senate. Smith's clear, compact narrative made Roman history open to generations of school readers. The opening chapter maps Italy's geography and early inhabitants, from Gallia Cisalpina to the Sabini and Marsi.
19877-jack-haydon-s-quest:
Jack Haydon's Quest is a school story of Rushmere School. Jack is prefect there and captain of the first fifteen. He walks swiftly out of the school gates one day. His leave takes him to Longhampton, three miles away. A day-scholar friend lies on the sick list there. The errand of friendship launches his quest in earnest.

School stories made prefects into knights of a small realm. Rugby, honor, and loyalty were their working virtues. A quest beyond the gates tests all three. John Finnemore wrote many such tales for boys. His schools run on fairness enforced by heroes. This opening is the genre in miniature. Readers of Tom Brown will know the country.
19967-beauty-and-the-beast:
Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, retold here anonymously. The merchant's family has fallen into poverty. With no servants, the girls must work hard, like peasants. The sons cultivate the fields to earn their living. All live roughly clothed and simply. That fall from wealth sets Beauty's story in motion. A stolen rose will carry her to the Beast's castle.

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont's version shaped this tale for children. Her Beauty is virtuous, dutiful, and brave in that order. The Beast's courtesy slowly disproves his appearance. Generations learned the tale in forms close to this one. Its lesson, that worth hides under roughness, never dates. This retelling keeps the familiar bones clean.
20018-evenings-at-donaldson-manor-or-the:
Maria J. McIntosh wrote Evenings at Donaldson Manor, also called The Christmas Guest. Its frame gathers guests for Christmas evenings of talk and tales. A quoted review praises McIntosh's Woman in America warmly here. She has written a clever book, the Protestant Churchman says. It contains much good word and truth, the review continues. American ladies are urged to consider her thoughts carefully. The manor evenings continue that improving vein.

McIntosh was a popular Southern writer of moral fiction. Her Christmas frame lets stories teach without sermonizing directly. Donaldson Manor's guests debate conduct, faith, and feeling nightly. The format suits holiday reading by the fire. American ladies were her declared audience and market. The book shows domestic fiction's respectable power.
20022-sequil-or-things-whitch-aint-finis:
Henry A. Shute wrote Sequil in 1904 as the sequel to his Plupy books. Its narrator Plupy keeps a diary in cheerfully bad spelling. He has forgot whether it was brite and fair since his last diry, he writes. Anyway, it is brite and fair today; lots of things have happened. Beany's father is a policeman now, which makes Beany feel pretty big. Plupy warns Beany had better not say much to him anyway.

Shute, a New Hampshire judge, wrote the Real Diary of a Real Boy first. Its misspelled boyhood became a national delight. Sequil continues Plupy's schoolboy wars, pranks, and loyalties. The comedy lives in the spelling and the deadpan alike. Grown readers remembered their own diaries in his. These books are American boyhood classics of their decade.
20198-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
George Borrow wrote Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, The Gypsy, The Priest. Lavengro tells, in part, of Borrow's own wild and bookish youth. He learned Romani, roamed with Gypsies, and sold Bibles in Spain. Critics praise how such writers pour their whole selves into their books.

Lavengro blends memoir, tale, and talk on language, roads, and faith. Its hero drifts between scholars, priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Few English books mix such worlds with so odd a charm. Readers get a classic ramble through words, roads, and Romani life. Borrow's own life, wild and learned, remains the book's true and lasting center throughout.
2033-the-unknown-guest:
Maurice Maeterlinck, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, writes on the unknown guest, the unseen presence that visits minds in dreams, premonitions, and strange coincidences. Maeterlinck, a Nobel laureate, treats the occult with philosophy. Maeterlinck won the Nobel Prize in 1911, for plays and essays on the unseen.

He asks whether such guests are spirits, thoughts, or powers of the mind itself, weighing evidence with calm curiosity. The book suits readers of mysticism who want speculation grounded in reflection, not mere marvels. His unknown guest, visiting in dreams and omens, asks whether mind reaches beyond body.
2055-two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana Jr., a Harvard student who shipped before the mast for his health, gives a firsthand account of life aboard merchant sailing ships in the 1830s. He sailed round Cape Horn to California, then a remote Mexican province. Dana left Harvard for the voyage in 1834, hoping sea air would mend his eyesight.

Dana describes hard work aloft, floggings, bad food, and the trade in hides, in plain language that sailors praised for its truth. The book helped reform seamen's conditions, and it remains the classic American memoir of common life at sea. His plain account of flogging and hard food helped reformers press for better laws for sailors.
20860-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Praise from the Pall Mall Gazette fronts The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast. Children, it notes, may spurn fine new picture books for plain old Goody Two-Shoes. That charm of the old and homely sets this slight book's tone.

William Roscoe's verse ball of insects dates to the early 1800s. Butterflies dance, grasshoppers feast, and small beasts hold a gay ball. The poem ranks among the first true picture-book verses for children. Its light lines and beast pageantry paved the way for the animal picture books children still love today.
21033-sketch-of-the-mythology-of-the-nor:
Desert sands, furnace blasts, floods, and fire rivers scour the lands in this mythology sketch. John Wesley Powell opens his study of North American Indian myth with nature's vast force. Fruits shrivel before starved men's eyes as rivers rage and mountains burst.

Powell, who ran the Colorado River, led the Bureau of Ethnology's early work. This first annual report sketch sorts native myths by the powers they name. Sun, storm, beast, and hero tales take ordered place in his scheme. Scholars have revised his frame since, yet the sketch stays a landmark of the field's bold, early reach.
21133-true-to-his-colours-the-life-that-:
Crossbourne, a quiet village among hills, is the scene of the Reverend Theodore P. Wilson's tale of a sceptic's home. Wilson sets his story some forty years before he wrote, in a place that seemed to hide from the roaring traffic around it. A stream runs restlessly through the village day and night.

True to His Colours argues, in story form, for the life that wears best: steady Christian faith over drink and doubt. Long sermons run through the narrative, as Wilson's readers expected from his temperance fiction. The village cast works out questions of belief, drink, and duty in their daily rounds and troubles.
21298-the-black-tor-a-tale-of-the-reign-:
Two teenage boys from feuding families meet among the wild hills of Derbyshire's Peak District. George Manville Fenn sets their tale in the reign of James the First, their families locked in a centuries-old feud. Each lives in a castle above the moors. A band of ex-soldiers camps on the hills and descends to rob the poorer folk.

The boys form a secret alliance, gathering their fathers' workmen into a small private army against the raiders. Their first attack fails badly. With better weapons and a better plan they try again. Fenn sets honour, inherited hate, and common danger against each other, letting the feud's youngest heirs end what their fathers could not.
21311-gil-the-gunner-the-youngest-office:
Gilbert Vincent goes out to India as a very young soldier in George Manville Fenn's long tale of the East. Schoolboy fights open the book before the regiment sails. In India, battles follow in quick order, and Gil is wounded, knocked out, and recovering as often as he fights.

At one point a wealthy local rajah captures Gil and treats him like an honoured guest, offering him any jewels he likes. Gil refuses, saying freedom to return to his father in the regiment is worth more than gems. The fighting aims at pushing the British out of India, and Fenn follows its cost on both sides.
21313-in-honour-s-cause-a-tale-of-the-da:
Frank Gowan, seventeen, is a page in the Prince of Wales's anteroom at the court of George the First. His father serves in the King's Guard, while fellow page Andrew leans Jacobite, like his father. George Manville Fenn fills the Hanoverian court with German and Dutch courtiers the king brought for comfort.

A German baron deliberately insults Frank's father, and their duel leaves the baron badly wounded. Though loyal to the king, Sir Robert Gowan is sentenced to lose his regiment and leave the country. Frank's search for his father runs through rooftop escapes, spies, and disguises around St James's Palace and its park.
21378-yussuf-the-guide-or-the-mountain-b:
Lawrence, a consumptive boy in his late teens with no relations, wishes aloud for a holiday somewhere hot and sunny. His doctor and a retired professor agree to take him to Asia Minor to see the antiquities, under his lawyer guardian's eye. George Manville Fenn sends the party first to Greece.

Dishonest ship crews sour the start, though their luggage went safely ahead. In Turkey they hire Yussuf, a charming and resourceful guide, and travel inland as helpfulness thins town by town. Mountain bandits capture the party at last and demand a ransom. Yussuf's skill becomes their best hope, in Fenn's tale of sickness, travel, and escape.
21384-afar-in-the-forest:
A young settler tells the tale in W. H. G. Kingston's Afar in the Forest, a short novel of life in the wild woods. He hunts game for the family store while his Uncle Mark fells tall trees around their home. Bit by bit, the two clear land at their new place.

Much of the book is Uncle Mark's own story, told by the fire at night. He tells why the family left home, how they landed safe, and how they found an old settlement in ruins. Lost kin, hidden ties, and two rescued children give the tale its twists. Kingston keeps the cast tangled on purpose, so close reading pays off.
2145-ben-hur-a-tale-of-the-christ:
Lew Wallace tells of Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince of Jerusalem wronged by his Roman friend Messala, sent to the galleys, and raised again through a sea fight and a chariot race. The tale runs beside the life of Christ. Wallace, a Civil War general, wrote Ben-Hur in the 1870s, and it sold for decades.

Wallace opens with wise men in the desert, follows Ben-Hur through Rome and Israel, and closes with faith and forgiveness. Ben-Hur became one of the best-selling novels of the nineteenth century, and a lasting popular epic. The chariot race, Ben-Hur's revenge on Messala, became one of fiction's most famous scenes.
21464-the-gilpins-and-their-fortunes-a-s:
Two school leavers talk over their futures at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Gilpins. One Gilpin boy dreams, with his brother, of farming in Australia like their hard-working father. The brothers sail, and their luck turns on a Sydney quay.
