There they save a family from a carriage with bolting horses, and win strong friends. The friends place them as overseers of a run-down sheep and cattle station past the Blue Mountains. The old manager was a crook, and many hands, sent out for crimes, are idle or worse. Mutiny brews before the brothers can set things right.
21493-twice-lost:
Godfrey Rayner's father, a half-pay naval lieutenant, joins a Bristol merchant house in W. H. G. Kingston's Twice Lost. The boy ships as a midshipman on the Heroine for the Pacific. There the tale's lost boy, Harry, first comes into view.

Islanders hold a shipwrecked sailor, and Harry proves to be an English boy used as a pearl diver. The crew takes him aboard and frees him from cruel masters. Years later the party settles in Australia, on the station next to Harry's own parents. Chance and grit drive this warm, tidy tale of loss and return.
21495-to-the-west:
Two young clerks quit a tyrant of an auctioneer in George Manville Fenn's To the West. They set their sights on British Columbia, far across the sea. The way there runs round Cape Horn to San Francisco, then up the coast.

On the road they meet folk good and bad, as Fenn's heroes always do. At last they reach the north and turn to hunting gold. Fenn draws places he never saw with striking life and care. The book runs long for him, some fifteen hours read aloud, and keeps its pace through storms, claims, and close calls.
21558-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
King Charles flees toward the New Forest as Captain Marryat's The Children of the New Forest opens. Marryat published the tale in 1847, his twenty-fourth book and the last of his lifetime. It was written for children and has stayed in print ever since.

When their father falls for the king, the Beverley children hide in a forester's cottage. They learn to farm, hunt, and live by their own hands. Roundhead foes and loyal friends test their courage and wit. The book's blend of history, woodcraft, and family love made it a lasting classic of children's fiction.
21676-confessions-of-a-caricaturist:
Oliver Herford confesses his art in Confessions of a Caricaturist, published in 1917 and dedicated to William Dean Howells. Short verses sit beside drawings of famed men, from Napoleon to Saint Paul. Herford likes Napoleon best, he says, since one hand hides in his vest.

Drawing hands, he owns, is not his knack, and Napoleon spares him the trouble. Roosevelt, Kipling, Shaw, Morgan, and Rockefeller take their turns in rhyme. Even Dante gets a joke about Benedictine and Chianti. Herford's light touch made him the wittiest pen-and-pencil man of his New York circle.
21734-the-golden-dream-adventures-in-the:
Gold in the far West draws the cast of this Ballantyne adventure across an ocean and a continent. The golden dream of the title is the hope of quick wealth that pulled thousands west in his century. Ballantyne knew the wild side of North America from his own years in Canada. He sets green newcomers against a land that tests every promise it seems to make.

The tale follows the party through travel, work, and danger in the western wilds. Greed, luck, and friendship pull the story in turn. Ballantyne keeps his moral steady: wealth found too fast can cost more than it pays. Young readers of his day took the warning with the adventure, gladly.
21753-the-norsemen-in-the-west:
Greenland eight or nine hundred years ago opens this Ballantyne tale of the Norsemen who reached America before Columbus. Two shaggy figures in bear-like dress creep over a ridge above a small hamlet of cottages, sheds, sheep, and boats. A sturdy settler plays with his small son outside the main cottage. The scene sets a whole lost world in motion.

Ballantyne follows the Norse settlers west from Greenland toward the new lands beyond the sea. Voyages, meetings with native peoples, and the hardships of a far colony fill the tale. He wrote it to give boys a true old story: that Europeans crossed the Atlantic long before Columbus. History and adventure sail in the same boat here.
21823-the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grass:
Tiny field creatures gather for a feast in this small book of verse by R. M. Ballantyne, published in 1874 for very young children. The gadfly blows his trumpet to call the company: beetle, emmet, gnat, and dragonfly all come in their colors. Predators lay aside their wars for the day and join the dance. A few over-eager dancers cause small mishaps, all safely mended.

Ballantyne wrote half a dozen such books for the youngest readers, some under the name Comus. This one is perhaps a twentieth the size of his sea novels. The rhymes are simple, merry, and meant to be read aloud. It shows the great adventure writer playing gently at the nursery door.
21871-adventures-in-the-far-west:
Young Britons cross the North American West in this short, picture-filled adventure by W. H. G. Kingston. Twenty-nine illustrations crowd the book, including a striking scene of a witch doctor visiting a sick man. The party travels among grizzly bears, wolves, and tribes who do not want them there. For much of the tale they live with a friendly tribe, whose ways Kingston describes at length.

Near the end, the heroes help rescue an emigrant wagon train attacked by a hostile tribe. A young lady has been seized and carried off, and the chase is on. Charley Fielding's cry at the campfire opens the action. Kingston's style, the editor says, is as excellent as ever. It is a brisk western in his classic mold.
22042-christmas-its-origin-and-associati:
William Francis Dawson set out to trace Christmas from its beginnings to his own day. His Christmas: Its Origin and Associations gathers customs scattered through many older authors. He found that some great Christmas feasts marked turning points in English history. He also saw the yearly feast as a link in the chain of Christian evidence across nineteen centuries.

Dawson moves from Roman and pagan roots through medieval revels to Victorian family practice. Holly, mistletoe, carols, feasts, and charity all get their histories. The book is earnest, well stocked, and proud of its subject. It suits readers who want the story behind the holiday's familiar trimmings.
22277-darry-the-life-saver-or-the-heroes:
Frank V. Webster wrote Darry the Life Saver, or The Heroes of the Coast, in 1911 for boy readers. Webster supplied many volumes to the cheap series trade under his own name and others. His hero Darry belongs to the surfmen who guarded America's coasts. The book opens on a brigantine battered by a Caribbean hurricane, staggering along like a wounded beast, her masts gone by the board.

From that wreck the tale builds rescues by breeches buoy and lifeboat. One picture shows a woman lowered safely and stowed away. The Life-Saving Service, forerunner of the Coast Guard, supplies real practice behind the thrills. Darry's adventures honour men who rowed out when others ran from the sea.
2241-love-s-labour-s-lost:
A king of Navarre and three lords swear off women, food, and sleep to study for three years, just as the Princess of France arrives with her ladies. Love's Labour's Lost watches the oath crumble in a festival of puns, songs, and love letters, with the pedant Holofernes and the clown Costard adding to the wordplay. Wit is the real subject here, and everyone competes at it.

Unlike most comedies, the ending defers marriage: the ladies demand a year of proof before they will wed. The play's verbal fireworks and bittersweet close make it a favorite of readers who love language itself. Its songs and jokes reward a slow, attentive reading.
23094-the-boy-nihilist:
Allan Arnold recruits a bright young fellow in The Boy Nihilist. Friends knew his talents well. So did members of the secret societies scattered across Ireland, Germany, and Russia. They knew him as a bright young fellow with brains, pluck, and enthusiasm, which, rightly directed, would make him valuable to any secret organization having the people's liberty at heart.

Beyond that, nothing particular was known of him, which is exactly how dime novels like their conspirators. Plots, bombs, and disguises fill this entry in the era's anxious literature of anarchism. Arnold writes the secret-society scare as boys' adventure. The book survives as a period artifact, showing how 1890s headlines about nihilists were repackaged for young readers hungry for danger.
23155-western-characters-or-types-of-bor:
James Hall apologizes for a gap in Western Characters, his types of border life in the western states. A sketch or two, Hall admits, might have been fuller had certain new books reached him in time. Schoolcraft's large work on Indian history and character heads his list of missed sources.

Hall, an Ohio judge and editor, sketched the frontier's human types while the frontier was still news. Hunters, settlers, preachers, and Native leaders pass through his pages as specimens of a vanishing world. The Schoolcraft aside shows his method, a working writer stitching authorities into firsthand sketches. Published in the 1850s, the book preserves border life described by a man who lived on that border and helped invent its literature.
23179-frictional-electricity-from-the-sa:
Max Adeler's Frictional Electricity is a comic tale that first reached readers through the Saturday Evening Post. An inmate of an asylum begs a visitor to hear him out. He says no nurse will listen to him, though telling his story would do him good after the hard use he has had.

His whole ruin, he claims, came from frictional electricity, a thing his listener admits he does not know. The patient wishes he had stayed just as ignorant, pointing to his own broken state as proof. Adeler frames the piece as a tall, rueful confession, played for laughs and pity at once.
23188-michael-penguyne-or-fisher-life-on:
Michael Penguyne, or Fisher Life on the Cornish Coast tells a story of men and boys who earn their living from the sea. An older fisherman works his sails with one eye on the shore below them. He keeps glancing toward the south-west, where heavy clouds are piling up fast.

Between tasks, he casts a look of approval at the boy with him. That small glance carries the book's world: skill learned by watching, weather read at a glance, and danger judged early. Readers get fisher life as daily work, not as scenery, on a coast where storms build quickly.
23254-the-cobbler-in-the-devil-s-kitchen:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Cobbler in the Devil's Kitchen comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. The Kitchen has a natural tiny fireplace on its east side, a couple of feet high. Cedar foliage screens it from the lake wind, and there Owen, the cobbler, cooked his meals.

His hearth had no flue, yet the smoke generally found its way out. Fish then crowded the straits, and Owen had only a short cast to reach deep water. Catherwood sets a solitary tradesman inside a wild, well-stocked place. Readers get a quiet tale of making do, alone, on the lakes.
23287-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the:
Lavengro, subtitled The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest, is a life story told by its own hero. The narrator begins with his father, a Cornish man and the youngest of seven brothers. The family were gentlemen of a modest kind, not very wealthy, yet holders of a coat of arms.

They lived on their own land at Tredinnock. The name means the house on the hill, and the house and its acres had been in their possession from time beyond memory. Readers get an autobiographical tale of learning, wandering, and Romany life, rooted in one old Cornish family's pride and decline.
23311-beauty-and-the-beast:
This version of Beauty and the Beast, printed in Cincinnati, tells of a merchant once rich, forced by losses to retire to a country cottage with his three daughters. The elder two grumble at poverty, but the youngest, Beauty, stays sweet and kind.

When her father must repay a beast's hospitality, Beauty takes his place and learns to love beyond looks. The tale's moral, that kindness outlasts wealth and beauty, has kept it a nursery favorite for centuries. The tale teaches that kindness outlasts wealth, beauty, and fine dress. Beauty asks her father for no rich present, only a rose, which he finds in an elegant garden on his way back.
23355-the-little-violinist:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich wrote this short, sad tale about James Speaight, a child violin player known on stage as Young Americus. Born in London and brought to America at four, the boy played concerts in many large cities, winning wonder for skill far past his years.

Aldrich says the tale is no invention: the events came to his hand ready made, and he tells them with a tender, plain voice. The story follows the small player through praise, travel, and the strain of a life spent before crowds. Its power lies in pity for a child made famous too soon, and in the quiet grief of those who watched his gift burn bright and brief.
23366-a-philanthropist:
Josephine Daskam set this comic tale among reform workers, as Miss Gould tells her lodger about a man she took for Tom Waters of the Reformed Drunkards' League. Hopes ran high when the man asked that the League meet at his house, a sign, she thought, of true change of heart.

The visit ends in farce: Miss Gould, late and lost on the way, finds the room in an uproar, with rival songs sung at once and order gone. Daskam uses the mishap to poke gentle fun at good works done with more zeal than sense. The tale asks, with a smile, whether a philanthropist serves people best by plans and meetings, or by seeing them as they truly are.
23443-unspecialist:
Murray F. Yaco wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in nineteen sixty. It rests on a bold claim: a machine can be built to do any well described job better than a man. A man's edge lies in the unexpected, undescribed, emergency job, if he has not been trained into a machine himself.

Banner, the hero, rips open his orders, curses at the phone, and sinks into a chair as the receiver dangles and coils, while a knock at the door brings fresh trouble. Yaco plays the idea for both thrills and laughs, as rigid plans meet a problem no rule covers. Readers who like sharp, idea driven science fiction will enjoy its brisk style and its defence of the generalist in a world of specialists.
23479-eight-illustrations-to-shakespeare:
Only the title matter, certificate, and captions for Walter Crane's eight illustrations to Shakespeare's Tempest are present here in text form, with no full play text. Duncan C. Dallas, who engraved and printed the plates in Dallastype facsimile, certifies six hundred and fifty copies, with plates destroyed after printing.

Captions name scenes such as Prospero on fortune's bounty, the dance of nymphs and reapers, and a noise of hunters, each tied to act and scene. The set, printed by J. M. Dent in London and Copeland and Day in Boston, suits lovers of Crane's art and of the play's island magic, as a plate book to view rather than a text to read.
23498-the-pirate-slaver-a-story-of-the-w:
Harry Collingwood wrote this West African sea tale as if by a midshipman aboard a British warship patrolling the Congo coast to stop the slave trade. Portuguese slavers seek to carry captured Africans across the Atlantic to Cuba in wretched conditions, and the patrol seeks to thwart them.

Harry Dugdale, the hero, is seized in action and would have been killed but for the slaver captain's son, who takes an interest in him. A bargain follows: Harry will help with navigation and watch keeping, but must go below when fighting starts. Collingwood writes the sea with skill, and the action rivals Kingston at his best. Readers will find a stirring, if period bound, tale of duty, captivity, and the fight against a cruel trade.
23677-the-moving-picture-boys-on-the-coa:
Victor Appleton, creator of Tom Swift, sent Blake and Joe to the seashore in this volume of the Moving Picture Boys series. The two young camera operators make their living filming real events, and the coast gives them plenty: surf, ships, and the perils of the deep promised by the subtitle.

Their automatic camera, left running on its own, plays a part in a rescue, and the boys aid in the work of saving life while still getting their pictures. For readers of the period, the book doubled as a window onto early film work. It shows what a moving-picture crew carried, how it shot, and how fast it had to move when danger struck.
23693-the-blue-birds-winter-nest:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy published The Blue Birds' Winter Nest in 1916, another volume about the Blue Bird girls. Aunt Selina, a peevish old lady in a fine old mansion, opens the story by calling for Sally. From that household beginning, the girls form plans for winter work, inspired by Uncle Ben's business talk.

Chapters follow the founding of the Bobolink Boys, a winter nest council, and the making of a magazine, the B. B. and B. B. Magazine, built by Blue Birds and Bobolinks together. Along the way come Aunt Selina's Civil War story, a tale of Yankees taking possession, and an Alaskan trip. It is a warm girls' club story about work, friendship, and earning success.
23730-the-promise-a-tale-of-the-great-no:
James B. Hendryx published The Promise in 1915, a tale of the Great Northwest in the tradition of his Connie Morgan books. Its hero, known as Broadway Bill, moves through a crooked game, a wreck, and a frame-up, then hits the trail northward toward the tote-road and the country beyond.

Chapters named The Pace, Love or Hate, At Bay, The Werwolf, and A Fire in the Night show the book's pace and temper. Bill finds new friends, takes a job, faces a test, and meets Daddy Dunnigan and the ghost-seeing Creed. At its heart is a promise kept against hard odds, in a land of lumber camps, rivers, and men who settle debts with their fists.
23985-peter-the-priest:
Maurus Jokai's Peter the Priest, translated by S. L. and A. V. Waite and published in New York in 1897, opens in a monastery. Six monks besides the prior and abbot receive a sealed letter in Latin from their most gracious patroness. None likes it: one of them is bidden to court to educate her only son.

The boy is a little devil, the abbot says. He talks and whistles in church, insults saints and departed souls, and torments animals. Chapters follow the fools of the castle, the lords of Madocsany and Mitosin, the bishop's wedding, and the temptation. An ice-blocked flood, a ghost's hour, and a grave of gold lead to a feast of death. Jokai's romance is grand, dark, and Hungarian to the core.
24010-the-gods-are-athirst:
Anatole France's The Gods Are Athirst, translated by Mrs. Wilfrid Jackson and published by John Lane in 1914, is a novel of the French Revolution. Its hero, Évariste Gamelin, is a painter, a pupil of David, and a member of the Section du Pont-Neuf, formerly Section Henri Quatre.

Gamelin goes at an early hour to the old church of the Barnabites, meeting place of the section's general assembly since May 21, 1790. Above the doorway stand the Republican words Liberty, Equality, Fraternity or Death, and the religious emblems have been battered to pieces. Saints dragged from their niches give way to red-capped patriots electing magistrates. France's novel watches idealism harden into terror.
24423-fifty-years-with-the-revere-copper:
S. T. Snow, treasurer of the Revere Copper Company, read this paper at the stockholders' meeting on March 24, 1890, printed by Samuel Usher in Boston for the stockholders. Snow begins with a word: his first appearance in the company's office, then at Number 22 Union Street, came on Monday morning, March 23, 1840. Saturday night last completed fifty uninterrupted years of service. He cannot expect the record to be repeated by himself, nor duplicated for a long time.

No other stockholder's certificate predates 1881, and nobody in the office looks back twenty years. The company was incorporated and organized in 1828, and in 1840 all the original corporators were living. Though by now every one of them, and later stockholders from their families, has passed away. No one else living has dealt daily with the company's members from its very beginning. Readers get fifty years inside one Boston firm.
24556-mr-faust:
Arthur Davison Ficke wrote this modern verse drama, published at New York in 1913 in the Modern Drama Series edited by Edwin Bjorkman. Its inscription tells Goethe, Marlowe, and Lessing to calm their fears: no one plots to steal their laurel wreaths. Ficke's Faust is his own, for a new century.

The play retells the old bargain with the devil in modern dress, with lyrics, one reprinted from Poetry magazine. Ficke, a poet and playwright, gives his hero wit and feeling rather than old-fashioned grandeur. Readers who know the classic Fausts will enjoy this lively American answer to them.
24793-blow-the-man-down-a-romance-of-the:
Holman Day published this coastal romance in 1916, opening with a sea shanty as its motto. Captain Boyd Mayo works his way out of soundings into deeper waters, both at sea and in life: fishing shares, tavern talk, a yacht, and a girl with a debt of honor. Chapters move from the schooner Ethel and May to storms, wrecks, and a tempest that turns the cards.

Day writes with a salty tongue and a warm heart for coast folk, their work, and their codes. Mayo grows from a young skipper into a man tested by loss and hard proof. The book suits readers who like sea tales where character matters as much as weather, and where a man's job is done well or not at all.
24900-the-annual-catalogue-numb-ii-1738-:
The Annual Catalogue, number two, for 1738, lists every new book, pamphlet, and print published from January 1, 1737, to January 1, 1738, with prices and booksellers. Sold for sixpence by Worrall, Corbett, Ward, and Chandler of London, it aimed at gentlemen, ladies, and country booksellers who lived far from town.

Entries run through history, divinity, law, poetry, plays, novels, painting, and architecture, naming each seller and his shop. A letter from Jenny Diver in Drury Lane sits beside histories of the ancient Germans and answers to deist tracts. The catalogue gives book historians a full, priced snapshot of London print in a single year.
24929-the-green-rust:
Edgar Wallace wrote The Green Rust, a thriller that opens with the passing of John Millinborn and the drunken Mr. Beale. Some suspect Beale of being a detective, and he plants registered envelopes on poor old White, while his plain words to others mark him as a man to watch. Chapters follow Punsonby's discharge, letters that were not there, and the house near Staines.

Behind the small crimes looms the Grand Alliance, a crime against the world itself, and the green rust that gives the book its name. Wallace keeps his usual pace, with short scenes and sharp talk. Readers who like his mystery stories will find a tense tale of conspiracy, spies, and a secret that threatens more than one life.
24971-travels-in-the-far-east:
Ellen M. H. Peck's 1909 travel volume, published by Thomas Y. Crowell, follows her journey from Milwaukee through Chicago and New York toward the Far East, opening with Shelley's Ozymandias as its epigraph. The Azores mark the first foreign landfall, and the route runs on through Egypt and India, with Peck noting temples, palaces, and daily life as she goes. She dedicates the book to her daughter, writing from Milwaukee in December 1908.

At Tanjore she describes an immense palace built about 1550, with a great Durbar room holding bas-reliefs and a white marble Flaxman statue of Raja Shah Foji, once Flaxman's pupil. Nearby sits an unusual library of eighteen thousand Sanskrit manuscripts, half written on palm leaves. The volume reads as a well-to-do American's wide-eyed tour, observant and unhurried.
2503-myths-and-legends-of-california-and:
This collection gathers the myths and legends of California and the Old Southwest, from Native American creation stories to Spanish and Mexican tales of the borderlands. The volume preserves stories of Coyote, of lost mines, and of haunted missions, told in a plain style for general readers. The legends map a region's imagination.

The book's value lies in its range: many peoples' stories side by side. Modern readers should note its early twentieth century framing. Folklore lovers will find a rich regional treasury. The legends include stories from many Native peoples of the region.
25104-ocean-steam-navigation-and-the-oce:
Thomas Rainey's Ocean Steam Navigation and the Ocean Post, published in New York in 1858, argues for fast, regular steam mail service across the Atlantic. Dedicated to Postmaster General Aaron Venable Brown, it treats ocean steamers as a matter of commerce, politics, and national standing, not merely of engineering.

Rainey weighs the costs of high speed, compares paddle wheels with screw propellers, and warns that cheap freight and rapid mail are different problems. His careful figures and policy arguments make the book a useful record of how mid-century Americans thought about shrinking the ocean by steam.
25159-two-on-the-trail-a-story-of-the-fa:
Hulbert Footner's Two on the Trail, published in 1911, is an adventure novel of the far Canadian Northwest. The story opens in a restaurant, introduces an unknown lady, and soon sets its travelers on a hard trail through stopping houses, river landings, and Caribou Lake.

Chapters follow Natalie as she tells her own story. A ninety-mile portage, a fight in a storm, a blizzard, and a marooned companion follow, with a wounded heroine and a clue to a missing girl named Rina. Footner writes with a brisk, outdoors pace, and the novel offers readers a rugged trek across a country of water, forest, and winter.
25478-the-boy-artist:
This Nelson tale for the young follows Raymond, a boy artist, and his patient sister Madge. Raymond paints Madge by firelight, begging her to hold her head still though the blaze scorches her cheek and the toast waits. His resolve carries him through fever, a kind friend, and an invitation that brings surprise and success. Mr. Smith, their patron, offers his Isle of Wight country house and promises to be a father to them for the time.

Madge worries at leaving home, yet lights up at the thought of country, sea, and her brother's recovery. The volume adds a second tale, Town Daisies, about a lonely life and transplanted flowers. T. Nelson and Sons published the book in London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1872, from the author of Hope On and King Jack of Haylands.
25732-the-faust-legend-and-goethe-s-faus:
H. B. Cotterill, editor of Goethe's Iphigenie and Dante's Inferno, writes this study of the Faust legend and Goethe's Faust, published in London by Harrap in 1912. A Latin tag opens the book, claiming ridicule often cuts great matters more strongly and better than force.

Cotterill traces Faust from folk legend and puppet plays to Goethe's great drama, weighing how a scholar's pact with the devil became a symbol of human striving, knowledge, and damnation. Greek words in the text appear in transliteration, and the study suits readers who know Goethe's play or meet Faust for the first time.
25771-a-nobleman-s-nest:
Iván Turgénieff writes A Nobleman's Nest, translated from Russian by Isabel F. Hapgood and published in New York by Scribner's Sons, with a 1903 copyright and a 1924 printing. The novel stands among Turgénieff's collected novels and stories, beside Rudin, On the Eve, Fathers and Children, and Smoke.

Turgénieff, a master of Russian realism, follows a nobleman returning to his estate, where love, duty, and the changing Russian countryside test his hopes. Hapgood's translation, made for American readers, keeps the novel's quiet tone and careful portraits of country gentry, servants, and women caught between old ways and new.
25800-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Cecil Hallett, of Magdalen College, Oxford, writes this short history of Ripon Cathedral and a description of its fabric for Bell's Cathedrals, with fifty-three pictures. Ripon Cathedral from the north fronts the book, and transcribers kept original spelling quirks, listing changes at the end.

Hallett traces the church's history from early foundations through medieval building to modern use, describing stonework, windows, and monuments in plain, scholarly prose. The guide suits visitors walking the cathedral and students of church architecture seeking a compact, accurate account. Hallett writes with a scholar's care for builders and monuments.
25801-the-girl-scouts-in-beechwood-fores:
Margaret Vandercook writes The Girl Scouts in Beechwood Forest, in her Girl Scout series, following her Ranch Girls and Red Cross Girls series. A flame ascending in a spiral of smoke opens chapter one, with Donald and Lance McCla looking backward in chapter two.

Girl Scouts in a beechwood forest face camp life, trails, and mysteries, with Vandercook's usual mix of outdoor skill, friendship, and service. The series gives girls heroines who cook, hike, signal, and solve problems together, in a story meant to mirror real scout work and play.
25811-the-automobile-girls-in-the-berksh:
Laura Dent Crane writes The Automobile Girls in the Berkshires, or The Ghost of Lost Man's Trail. She had written The Automobile Girls at Newport and Along the Hudson. Altemus published the book in Philadelphia in 1910. A splash descending on unsuspecting Bab fronts the book.

Chapters open with a reunion, where Barbara cries that Mollie Thurston and she are lost. New light on old papers follows. Happiness and another scheme come next, with days in the heart of the Berkshires, woods, and the great white also, as motor girls chase a ghost trail through New England hills.
25872-girls-of-the-forest:
L. T. Meade, the prolific English writer born in Cork in 1854, tells a schoolgirl tale of high spirits and new rule. A party of girls bursts into Mr. Dale's study in a rush, with Verena and Pauline at the front, and Miss Tredgold follows on what she calls a call of duty. She means to stay as long as she is wanted, to bring order out of chaos and turn hoydenish girls into ladies.

The clash between the girls' wild woodland freedom and Miss Tredgold's firm hand drives the book. Meade, who wrote her first book at seventeen and edited the Atalanta magazine for six years, knew girl life well and drew on East London scenes in much of her work. Here the forest girls test their guest, and she tests them, in a tale of fun, pluck, and growing up.
25904-john-the-baptist:
F. B. Meyer writes the life of John the Baptist for his Biographical Series, printed in London in 1911. Meyer says the Baptist's portrait in the Gospels had long held him, and study of it gave rest from life's fret and strain. Chapters follow John from the house of Zacharias through his schools and schoolmasters to his first ministry, his baptism unto repentance, and his witness to the Messiah.

The book stresses John's cry that he must decrease while Christ increases, and his summons before Herod's court. Herod, Meyer writes, judged John a just and holy man, yet reasons of state kept the king from the Jordan, so a chamberlain fetched the prophet to speak before the court. The life closes as a burning and shining light, spent in witness and sealed by a king's prison.
25979-sonnets-of-shakespeare-s-ghost:
Gregory Thornton procures the words and Willem Blaeu makes the ornaments for Sonnets of Shakespeare's Ghost, printed at Sydney by Angus and Robertson in 1920. The conceit is plain: Shakespeare's spirit, vexed by critics who say his sonnets feigned love from toys of the brain, answers in his own rhyme. Dedicated to the only begetter of these ensuing sonnets, the book renews the verse wherein he was most excellent in life.

The ghost denies that his love was a shadow born of naught or an apish rhyme. He asks why the wise world would turn each word to falsehood and do his lady double wrong. Later sonnets muse on clouds that hide the sun's warmth, blaming the rack of cloud, not the sun, for cold days. The book is a playful, learned homage to the sonnets.
25980-footprints-in-the-forest:
Edward S. Ellis sends Jack Carleton and the Shawnee scout Deerfoot through forest perils in Footprints in the Forest, number eight of the Log Cabin Series, printed in 1886. Contents run from a retrospective and a valuable ally to the camp of strangers, a quarrel, Shawanoe versus Pawnee, a double failure, and the flight of Deerfoot. Pawnees are astonished, a situation reverses, and Indian honor is tested.

One scene shows a man darting like a deer among trees despite a stinging arm, while Jack wrings Deerfoot's hand and cries what a fine fellow he would be in a story. Deerfoot's even white teeth and sparkling black eyes mark his good spirits. Later chapters bring Lone Bear's revelation, a fight and retreat, and a startling close. Ellis writes of woodcraft and friendship with zest.
26-paradise-lost:
John Milton retells the Fall of Man in blank verse across twelve books. Paradise Lost opens in Hell, where Satan rallies his fallen angels after defeat. The poem then follows creation, temptation, and exile from Eden.

Milton states his aim plainly: to justify the ways of God to men. Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit, lose Paradise, and face a hard world with hope. Satan's pride and rhetoric make him a vivid, troubling figure. The epic stands as the great English poem on sin and grace. Poets and readers have debated Satan's appeal ever since, making the epic a living argument.
26009-adventures-of-a-young-naturalist:
Lucien Biart tells the adventures of a young naturalist in Mexico, edited and adapted by Parker Gillmore and printed by Harper in 1871 with one hundred and seventeen pictures. Gillmore's preface calls Mexico the most interesting country on earth for science and travel, lavish in nature's gifts, from volcanic peaks and lagoons to giant rivers and vast forests. Much still waits to be learned of its trees and beasts.

The young hero explores with Sumichrast, catching Hercules beetles that buzz from bushes and strike branches hard. A beetle slips his grip and flies on, and the boy cries that the beetle is stronger than he is. Sumichrast smiles that the name Hercules is earned. The book mixes natural history with boyish adventure in a rich, strange land.
26059-the-ascent-of-denali-mount-mckinle:
Hudson Stuck, archdeacon of the Yukon, tells the first complete climb of Denali, the highest peak in North America. The party travels by dog sled through the Alaskan interior, then works up the glaciers toward the mountain. Ice falls, broken snow ridges, and cold shape every stage of the climb.

An earthquake had shattered the lower ice, forcing a high traverse around a peak before the party reached the horseshoe ridge of snow that leads to the summit. Stuck records camps, routes, and the slow labor of the final ridge in plain detail, with notes on the Yukon rivers crossed on the way in. The account stands as both a climb record and a portrait of travel in early Alaska.
2607-psmith-journalist:
P. G. Wodehouse sends his elegant hero Psmith to New York in this comic novel, and opens by warning London readers that New York life runs on different rules. Gangs there, he explains, murder not on impulse but on commercial lines, at so many dollars per murder.

Psmith takes over a newspaper and turns journalist, using wit, nerve, and perfect manners against gangsters and corrupt bosses. Wodehouse writes with his usual lightness, and the jokes never quite hide the danger. The book delights as a farce of a very English gentleman tidying a very American mess.
26162-peking-dust:
Ellen N. La Motte's Peking Dust, published in New York in 1919, gathers letters she wrote from Peking in October and November 1916 and again in February and March 1917. Early letters describe old China, race feeling, spheres of foreign influence, and the Lao-hsi-kai affair, while later ones cover an opium scandal, a dust storm, and walks on the city wall.

As the months pass, the letters track a sharp turn: fear of war, the German reply, the breaking of diplomatic ties, and a meeting with President Li Yuan-hung. Written with a nurse's sharp eye and a traveller's candour, the book gives a first-hand view of China on the edge of the First World War, seen from inside its capital.
26175-a-successful-shadow-or-a-detective:
Old Sleuth's dime novel continues the adventures of detective Jack Alvarez, fresh from the solved mystery of Two Wonderful Detectives. A prologue recalls a missing beauty and a widow's tale, then new chapters send Jack into a gambling room, an opera house, and a brushwood crime scene. A baron, a Spanish millionaire, and a forged acceptance all cross his path.

Jack's task turns on motive, not just on clues, and the book praises his patient shadowing above all. The chase builds through betrayals, schemes, and a hurried message toward a confession that clears the mystery. It is a fast, old-style detective yarn, written to thrill readers who liked a hero who never lost the trail.
26189-a-spoil-of-office-a-story-of-the-m:
Hamlin Garland's A Spoil of Office, here in a new and revised edition of 1897, follows Bradley Talcott, a young western man of humble means who sets out to win political success. Garland keeps close to Bradley's own view throughout, and he warns readers not to mistake Bradley's judgments for his own. Ida Wilbur, for one, appears only as Bradley sees her.

The background draws on three great farm movements: the Grange, the Alliance, and the People's Party. Scenes move from Rock River to law study at Iowa City and work under a judge. Dedicated to William Dean Howells, the novel treats farm politics as fit matter for fiction, and it tracks one man's rise through the hopes and limits of the modern West.
26244-cavanagh-forest-ranger-a-romance-o: Hamlin Garland's 1910 romance of the mountain West is named for Cavanagh, a forest ranger. Garland, already known for The Captain of the Gray-Horse Troop and Main-Travelled Roads, issued it with Harper and Brothers in New York and London. The title page presents it as a romance, a tale of adventure and feeling set among rangers and mountain folk. Its hero's calling places the story in the high country, where a ranger guards forests, trails, and remote settlements.
26779-the-ghost:
Wm. D. O'Connor set this Christmas tale on Beacon Hill, the rich and respectable West End quarter of Boston. Its streets wear an air of stony, well-fed dignity, and one old street broods over a wrong: given to the city before the Revolution by Mr. Middlecott, it bore his name until he was dust, then took the grander name of Bowdoin. Rumor whispered that the ghost of its father walked there at night, pausing at corners to read signs that no longer bore his name.

Published by G. P. Putnam and Son in 1867, with two pictures by Thomas Nast, the story turns that slight against the living into a haunting. A pale, thin woman calls on Dr. Renton in his library, and the respectable quarter must face what its ingratitude has raised.
26907-the-cornwall-coast:
Arthur L. Salmon's 1910 guide walks the reader along the whole Cornwall coast, from Plymouth in the east around to Land's End and the Scilly Isles. Written for walkers, cyclists, and motorists, it pairs routes with notes on which Ordnance Survey maps to carry for each stretch.

Chapter by chapter it covers fishing ports and resorts such as Looe, Fowey, Falmouth, and Penzance, with warnings about tides that can trap the unwary. The book mixes practical road advice with history and local color, and it still works as a portrait of the Cornish shore before mass motoring.
27014-trade-and-travel-in-the-far-east:
G. F. Davidson's Trade and Travel in the Far East, published in London in 1846, recalls twenty-one years passed in Java, Singapore, Australia, and China. Davidson wrote the sketches on a long voyage from Hong Kong to England in 1844, paper on his knee, with three young children lacking amusement beside him.

Drawn entirely from memory, the book claims nothing but truth in its incidents, from crossings in forty different square-rigged vessels to trading posts and colonial towns. It reads as a merchant traveler's notebook, candid about its defects and rich in firsthand observation.
27139-a-leaf-from-the-old-forest:
John D. Cossar's A Leaf from the Old Forest, published in London in 1870, gathers poems rooted in the Scottish border country. The title poem asks for a leaf from the forest of beauty and song, following the Ettrick's sweet waters through woods and fair meadows.

The index lists King Nimaera, Lord Henry of the Eden-side, My Mother's Death, The World's End, and The Sabbath Day, with an orphan boy and a stolen kiss among the shorter pieces. Cossar writes in a plain, musical voice, fond of oak, chestnut, holly, and old friendships.
27256-a-pioneer-railway-of-the-west:
Maude Ward Lafferty's A Pioneer Railway of the West records the restoration of part of the first track of the Lexington and Ohio Railroad. Now the Louisville and Nashville, it was laid at Lexington in 1831. Dedicated to men of forethought and courage who pioneered railroad development in America, it was marked by exercises on May 30, 1916, at the University of Kentucky.

In July 1915, workmen rebuilding Louisville and Nashville freight yards unearthed old rail stones and strap iron rails. They belonged to the old Lexington and Frankfort Road, believed the earliest railroad beyond the Alleghany Mountains. Lafferty hurried downtown before her train to see the relics on display, and three military companies escorted the dedication.
27270-india-s-problem-krishna-or-christ:
John P. Jones's India's Problem, Krishna or Christ, published by Revell in 1903, comes from a missionary of Southern India with the American Board. Jones opens with the land and the people: physical features, economic conditions, social life, education, politics, and the government of India.

A chapter surveys the religions of India, from Judaism, Mohammedanism, and Parseeism to Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, and Hinduism. The contrast covers their initial conceptions, their ultimate aim or goal, and the agency and means each faith recognizes and appeals to. Jones then contrasts Hinduism and Christianity on incarnation, atonement, spirituality, eschatology, and faith, closing with missionary organization, problems, and results.
27394-a-new-guide-for-emigrants-to-the-w:
J. M. Peck of Rock Spring, Illinois, published this practical guide in Boston in 1836 for families thinking of moving west. It sketches Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, and Michigan, with the territories of Wisconsin and Arkansas and the adjacent parts, and it speaks from a man living in the country he describes.

Chapters cover the Mississippi Valley in general, climate and how to preserve health, and the character and manners of planters, farmers, hunters, trappers, and boatmen. They also cover the public lands: surveys, townships, land offices, and pre-emption rights. Anyone studying westward migration gets a firsthand handbook of what settlers needed to know.
27437-desert-dust:
Edwin L. Sabin published this western novel with George W. Jacobs in Philadelphia in 1921, illustrated by J. Clinton Shepherd. The first-person narrator tells his own story, from a pair of blue eyes and a rise in favor through a grand tour, a rendezvous, and stakes laid on the queen.

Later chapters narrow and fork the trail, bring voices in the void, and end with the queen winning and a summons waited upon. Scouts gallop through the illustrations, and desert country frames the action. Sabin writes the West as a place of movement, risk, and loyalty, and the tale moves at a steady, adventurous pace.
27444-starman-s-quest:
Robert Silverberg published this science-fiction novel with Gnome Press in Hicksville, New York, in 1958. He notes in a later preface that it was his second novel, written when he was nineteen in his junior year at Columbia. Readers tracing a writing career's early layers, he says, will find much to explore here.

The prologue opens at the dawn of the Space Age, when the Lexman Spacedrive changed all human history. It ranked second among the theoretical feats of those exciting years, and it altered the pattern of social development on Earth. From that premise Silverberg builds a story of space travel and its human costs. It is early Silverberg, energetic and ambitious.
27504-lorimer-of-the-northwest:
Harold Bindloss, author of By Right of Purchase, published this Canadian novel with A. L. Burt in New York in January 1909, from a Frederick A. Stokes copyright, with a frontispiece by Alfred James Dewey. Its prologue opens at Fairmead in Western Canada on a still, hot autumn day.

Lorimer's story runs from a first sowing, a church parade, and the land of promise through an unpleasant apprenticeship, a bid for fortune, harvest home, and a hold-up. It goes on to railroads, rising waters, stolen cattle, a race with time, the gold trail, a trial, the Day Spring Mine, and a bountiful harvest. A canoe shooting a rapid toward eternity fronts the book. It is a vigorous tale of prairie settlement.
27584-baseball-joe-in-the-big-league-or-:
Lester Chadwick published this Baseball Joe novel with Cupples and Leon in New York in 1915, illustrated throughout. Joe Matson, the young pitcher, faces his hardest struggles as he moves toward the big league, with his sister Clara at his side in the opening chapter.

Chapters run from Two Letters and To the Rescue through An Appeal, The Threat, and Joe Is Drafted, to Off to St. Louis and Going Down South. Later come stage fright, a queer message, a lame arm, a tight game, and Shalleg's downfall. An illustration shows Joe beating the ball by a narrow margin and declared safe. Young readers get baseball adventure at full stretch.
27776-the-methodist:
Evan Lloyd's 1766 poem The Methodist, reprinted here by the Augustan Reprint Society, satirizes the Methodist movement of its day. The reprint, issued by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library, frames the poem with scholarly notes.

Two short passages from the poem were later anthologized in The Penguin Book of Satirical Verse, a sign of its lasting bite. Readers get both an eighteenth-century satire and a modern edition's apparatus for understanding its targets and context. The reprint's introduction notes survey Lloyd's work and an unpublished dissertation on the poet. The reprint lists general editors from the Clark Library and the University of California.
27819-round-games-with-cards-a-practical:
Baxter-Wray wrote Round Games with Cards, a practical treatise on the most popular round games, with their variations and hints for practice, published in 1891 and 1897. Contents also include Nap, Loo, Poker, Vingt-un, Commerce, Speculation, Pope Joan, Cassino, Spoil Five, and Loto.

The book opens with Napoleon, or Nap, introduced from the United States about 1865, in which one player's hand stands against every man's. Clear rules and variations make the volume a useful handbook for family and club play in the age before bridge took over the card table.
27902-a-bird-lover-in-the-west:
Olive Thorne Miller published A Bird-Lover in the West in Boston and New York with Houghton, Mifflin in 1900, after an 1894 copyright. The studies were made in Colorado in 1891, Utah in 1893, and the Middle Country of southern Ohio in 1892, with several chapters first appearing in the Atlantic Monthly.

Contents follow camping in Colorado, an uproar of song with meadow-larks and horned larks, cliff-dwellers in the canyon, and four o'clock in the morning with grackles, doves, and cardinals. Miller writes with a naturalist's ear and a poet's eye, and the book remains a charming record of western birds.
27913-the-quadroon-adventures-in-the-far:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Quadroon, adventures in the far west, opening with a lyrical address to the Mississippi, the Father of Waters. The narrator recalls leaping its tiny stream in the land of a thousand lakes, launching a birch-bark boat, and floating south past wild rice meadows.

The journey continues past the falls of St. Anthony, where conifers give way to oaks, elms, and maples, and the river takes on a livelier, deciduous dress. Reid's romance of the river and the frontier blends travel description with adventure, in the manner that made him a favorite of young readers.
282-eothen-or-traces-of-travel-brought-h:
A. W. Kingslake crossed from Europe into the Ottoman East and wrote the journey down. Eothen, or Traces of Travel Brought Home from the East, in the 1898 Newnes edition, opens at Semlin on the Danube. Belgrade's fortress looms across the river, dark and historic.

Kingslake notes how two frontier towns, a cannon shot apart, hold no communion. Hungarian, Turk, and Serb live asunder across the Save. Later chapters carry him through Turkey, Syria, and Egypt with wit and observation. The book became a classic of Victorian travel writing. Kingslake's wit and eye for contrast made Eothen a travel classic.
28434-the-astronomy-of-milton-s-paradise:
Thomas N. Orchard, a member of the British Astronomical Association, published The Astronomy of Milton's Paradise Lost in 1896. He asks what John Milton actually knew about the heavens, and how that knowledge shaped the images in his great poem.

Early chapters sketch the history of astronomy and science in the seventeenth century, including Milton's links with Galileo. Later chapters work through the seasons, the starry heavens, and each celestial object named in Paradise Lost, with diagrams of the Ptolemaic system and Milton's own division of space. The book suits readers who love both poetry and the history of science.
28446-uncle-terry-a-story-of-the-maine-c:
Charles Clark Munn's 1900 novel Uncle Terry opens on a stormy Maine night. Uncle Terry comes in from the shed warning that waves are breaking over White Horse Ledge. His household, including the young girl Telly, settles by the stove as the storm shakes the little house.

The story that follows weaves together orphans washed up by the sea, a miser, village gossip, a country school, legal sharp practice, and quiet acts of kindness along the coast. Munn writes in the dialect and rhythms of Maine shore life. At the book's heart is Terry himself: weather-beaten, kindly, and steady through every turn of fortune.
28464-epistle-sermons-vol-2-epiphany-eas:
Luther's Epistle Sermons, Volume II, translated by Professor John Nicholas Lenker and published in Minneapolis in 1909, forms volume eight of Luther's complete works in English. It gathers Martin Luther's sermons on the epistle readings for the seasons of Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost.

Lenker's foreword links the volume to the evangelization of the world, arguing that the Reformation, missions, and emigration each carried the gospel to new peoples. The sermons themselves expound the biblical texts Sunday by Sunday in Luther's direct style. The book serves pastors, students, and lay readers interested in Luther's preaching.
28579-the-homesteaders-a-novel-of-the-ca:
Robert J. C. Stead's 1916 novel, published by the Musson Book Company of Toronto, follows settlers facing the Canadian West. Its opening scene shows a schoolmaster dismissing six pupils on an Indian summer day, erasing the blackboard, and deciding he will not teach past spring. He walks toward a lake, and the story turns from the schoolroom to open country.

Later chapters carry the settlers into the wilderness, across prairie land, and through rough living. They meet the lure of easy money, a fight in the foothills, and an inquest with explanations that follow it. The novel shows how hope, hard work, and sudden trouble shaped life on a new frontier.
28690-the-empire-of-the-east:
H. B. Montgomery's The Empire of the East, published by Methuen and Company of London in 1908 with nineteen illustrations, surveys Japan. Its epigraph borrows St. Francis Xavier: this nation is the delight of my soul. Montgomery opens by doubting a handbook claim of twenty-five centuries of written history and an unbroken dynasty since 660 B.C., since most Japanese history is legendary.

Chapters cover the country's physical features, race and language, religions, constitution, daily life, trade, finance, education, and army and navy. Art, architecture, posts, law, literature, newspapers, morality, China, Europeans, Buddhist temples, and the Ainos follow. Readers get an Edwardian portrait of Japan as it stood and where it might go.
28813-the-electronic-mind-reader-a-rick-:
John Blaine wrote this 1957 Rick Brant science-adventure story about a mind-reading machine and the trouble it brings to Spindrift Island. Rick Brant, his sister Barby, and his friend Don Scott are drawn into a plot. It involves a million-dollar gimmick, a security check by Janig, a wandering barber, and a device that seems to read thoughts. Chapters move from surveillance with cereal to brain waves, vanishing mermaids, and a one-man boarding party.

The book mixes boy detective work with 1950s science wonder, as Rick tests what the machine can really do and who is using it. Grosset and Dunlap published it as part of a long-running series for young readers who liked gadgets, codes, and danger. It remains a brisk period adventure, full of slang, science talk, and cliffhangers.
2900-the-age-of-invention-a-chronicle-of:
Holland Thompson wrote The Age of Invention as a chronicle of American inventors, warning that no short book could catalog every nineteenth-century invention. Instead he sketches the personalities behind the machines, leaving technical detail to encyclopedias. The story includes the Waltham mill, where Paul Moody of Amesbury helped build looms, carding, drawing, and roving machines under one roof.

By the autumn of 1814 the Waltham works combined every step of clothmaking in a single American mill, one of the first in the world to do so. Thompson uses such scenes to show invention as teamwork, business, and craft together. The book suits readers who want the human history of American machinery rather than a parts list.
29128-david-dunne-a-romance-of-the-middl:
Belle Kanaris Maniates wrote this 1912 romance, David Dunne: A Romance of the Middle West, published by Rand McNally in Chicago and New York, with pictures by John Drew. The story opens with a dusty, tousle-headed, freckle-faced boy in a suit made from overalls and a woman's shirtwaist, crossing lots to the Brumble farm in search of Miss M'ri. He looks in kitchen, henhouse, dairy, and flower garden, then calls her name in a treble voice.

Later pictures show Dave's little gal, David walking beside a stiffly starched little girl, and a man standing at bay before floating banners. Maniates writes a middle-western romance of boyhood, friendship, and growing up. Readers get a warm, old-fashioned novel of farm country, told with humor and affection for its people.
29228-the-contrast:
Royall Tyler wrote this comedy, extracted here from Representative Plays by American Dramatists, volume one. Tyler lived from 1757 to 1826, and the volume's introduction calls The Contrast the first American play written by a native author to gain anything like a run. William Dunlap, called the father of the American theatre, recorded its success in his history of the stage.

Tyler, steeped in New England life, built the play around the contrast of its title: American plainness against imported fashion and manners. The comedy's types and dialogue made it a landmark. Readers get the founding comedy of the American stage, still readable for its wit and for its picture of a new republic deciding what kind of people it would be.
29288-the-unknown-life-of-jesus-christ:
Nicolas Notovitch published this book in New York in 1890, translated by J. H. Connelly and L. Landsberg, presenting what he called his 1887 discovery. Notovitch claimed that during a journey in Tibet, through Cashmere and Ladak, he found a manuscript life of Saint Issa, whom he identified with Jesus, in a Buddhist monastery. The claim has never been accepted by scholars, and readers should treat it as Notovitch's account, not as established history.

Contents follow a journey in Tibet, Ladak, a festival in a gonpa, the life of Saint Issa, a resume, and explanatory notes. Notovitch entered a railway car at Lahore on October 14, 1887, bound for Rawalpindi. Readers get a famous fringe text, valuable for its influence and its story, and for the debate it sparked about Jesus's so-called lost years.
2938-yeast:
Thomas Henry Huxley chose yeast as the subject of a popular lecture for three reasons, simplicity, familiarity, and the chance to explain without diagrams. Yeast is among the simplest and most familiar objects of household life, and its phenomena can be put plainly without turning away to pictures. The lecture follows sugar as it breaks down under fermentation.

Huxley reports that refined analysis accounts for at least ninety-nine percent of the sugar, split into carbonic acid and three other products. He speaks with hesitation before his friend Professor Roscoe, lest he trespass on chemistry's province. The lecture remains a model of popular science, turning a kitchen substance into a lesson about living processes.
3033-the-passing-of-the-frontier-a-chron:
Emerson Hough wrote The Passing of the Frontier, a chronicle of the Old West, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Chapters cover the frontier in history, the range, cattle trails, the cowboy, mines, pathways of the West, Indian wars, cattle kings, and the homesteader. Hough opens by calling the frontier the most stirring, intimate, and beloved word in English, carrying the elan of the French En avant.

The narrative follows gold discoveries in Montana, doubly found by men from California and men heading west, with Francois, called Be-net-see, finding gold on Gold Creek in 1852. News lay dormant until 1857, since the wild country had small ingress or egress. The book gives a romantic yet detailed history of the West's closing, written by a novelist-historian.
3139-the-dove-in-the-eagle-s-nest:
Charlotte M Yonge sets this historical romance in a fierce noble household, where a gentle girl must live among hawks. The Macmillan edition of 1890 reprints a story first issued in two volumes in 1866. W J Hennessy supplied the illustrations. Yonge, a favorite Victorian writer for young readers, builds her tale on contrast: softness against pride, patience against force.

The dove of the title is a girl whose temper refuses the eagle's ways. The nest is a castle world of feud, honor, and hard rule. Readers who enjoy Yonge's moral romances will find her usual strengths here. A firm heroine, a vivid past age, and a plot that tests character under pressure all serve a steady sense of right.
3202-moby-thesaurus-list:
This file holds the Moby Thesaurus, a public domain word list released by its author in January 2001. The documentation notes describe it as the unabridged main thesaurus file, distributed in plain ASCII for the MSDOS systems of its day. Vocabulary files arrive in ordinary text form, so any program can read them without special tools.

A thesaurus of this kind groups words by likeness of meaning, giving writers and software a stock of alternatives for any term. The Moby lists became a standard resource for word games, writing aids, and early language software. Readers opening the file will find data, not prose: long runs of related words, built for lookup rather than for reading straight through.
3203-moby-part-of-speech-list:
This file holds the Moby part-of-speech list, a public domain resource released by its author in January 2001. The documentation describes a part-of-speech file in plain ASCII, distributed for MSDOS systems and meant to be unpacked and read by any program. Its entries tag words with their grammatical roles: noun, verb, adjective, and the rest.

Writers of software use such lists to parse sentences, check grammar, and build language tools. The file gives tags rather than definitions or prose, word after word in plain text. Readers opening it will find a working tool, not a book. It is a plain list from the early age of free language data, still handy wherever a program must know what job a word does.
3204-moby-hyphenation-list:
Where may a long word break at the end of a line? The Moby Hyphenator list, public domain since January 2001, answers that question entry by entry. The documentation describes a hyphenation file in plain ASCII, distributed for MSDOS systems and meant to be unpacked and read by any program. Its business is a single practical question: where may a word be broken at the end of a line?

Typesetters, word processors, and text tools use such lists to divide long words cleanly across lines. The file gives break points rather than definitions or prose, entry after entry in plain text. Readers opening it will find data built for machines and for printers: a working tool from the early age of free language data, still useful wherever text must be laid out well.
3205-moby-pronunciation-list:
Written words become spoken sounds in the Moby pronunciator list, a public domain resource from January 2001 built on the CMU dictionary. The documentation describes a pronunciation file in plain ASCII, built from the CMU dictionary list and distributed for MSDOS systems. Its entries pair written words with their spoken sounds, in a phonetic spelling a program can read.

Speech software, rhyming tools, and reading aids use such lists to turn text into sound. The file gives pronunciations rather than definitions or prose, entry after entry in plain text. Readers opening it will find data for machines: a plain, practical list from the early age of free language data, still useful wherever a tool must say a word aloud.
3323-the-ward-of-king-canute-a-romance-o:
Ottilie A Liljencrantz sets this romance in the Danish conquest of England. The fall of the house of Frode opens it, with Randalin, Frode's daughter, at the center. Where war-dogs kennel, when royal blood is young blood, and before the king follow, leading to the training of Fridtjof the page and the game of swords. Taken captive and the young lord of Ivarsdale carry the tale on.

King Canute himself presides over the story's world: a Danish king ruling an English land, with wards, hostages, and loyalties to settle. Liljencrantz writes the eleventh century as adventure, with courts, camps, and swordplay. Liljencrantz's eleventh century runs on courts, camps, and swordplay, with a page growing toward lordship under a conqueror's eye.
3457-the-man-of-the-forest:
Zane Grey sets this western in the White Mountains, where a lone hunter moves under great fir and spruce trees at sunset. Old Baldy, the highest peak, stands bare and gold in the last light, and the forest seems to swallow the man as he glides through it. He is friendly with an Indian hunter, but he hates the sound of white men's horses in those fastnesses.

The trouble comes from a gang of bad men hidden in the woods, and the novel follows pursuit, ambush, and rescue among the peaks. Grey writes the landscape in rich color and keeps the action moving. Readers who like classic westerns will find his familiar mix: a strong silent hero, a wild country, and a fight between lawless greed and solitary honor.
3547-see-america-first:
Orville Hiestand, working with Charles Herr, offers wayside sketches of American scenery in this outdoor book. The dedication thanks the Herr family, whose love of the great out of doors made the sketches possible. The introduction quotes Emerson on morning light, cloud bars like golden fishes, and nature as medicine for bodies cramped by work.

Hiestand urges readers to see America first, rather than crossing the sea for famous views. His sketches follow hilltops at sunrise, woods, and open horizons, arguing that a day outdoors restores tone to mind and body. The book suits travelers, nature lovers, and readers who enjoy early twentieth century praise for the American landscape.
3660-out-of-the-triangle-a-story-of-the-:
Mary Bamford writes a collection of stories from far places, opening in Alexandria, Egypt. A voice rings through a street, crying that sinners should keep their eyes to the ground, while Heraklas walks by Lake Mareotis, mourning his brother Timokles lost in the desert. Other stories in the book include The Squash of the Esvidos, Comale's Revenge, At the Panaderia, Miss Stratton's Paper, and The Victory of Quang Po.

Bamford writes for young readers, with clear morals and vivid foreign settings, from Egyptian lakes to Chinese villages and Arctic igloos. Her tales mix adventure with lessons in honesty, courage, and kindness. The book suits families who enjoy old fashioned story collections that travel the world in a single volume.
3727-maurice-guest:
Henry Handel Richardson sets this long novel among the music students of Leipzig in the 1890s. Maurice Guest, a young man from abroad, stands before the new Gewandhaus as crowds pour out of a rehearsal, and soon he is caught in a love affair that unmakes him. He adores Louise, a gifted and restless fellow student, who in turn loves the brilliant violinist Schilsky and waits in vain for his letters.

Practice rooms, concerts, boarding houses, and long walks frame a study of obsession, as Maurice watches Louise pine, excuse, and hope against all sense. Richardson writes with close care for mood and music, and the novel grows darker as pride and longing wear the hero down. Readers who like serious fiction about art and passion will find a demanding book that earns its length.
4081-the-alchemist:
Ben Jonson's comedy The Alchemist follows three rogues who run a fake philosopher's stone business from a London house while its master is away. Face, Subtle, and Dol Common promise dupes gold, love, and long life, with chants of hum and buz to sharpen the five senses.

A gull named Dapper must bathe his fingers, wash his eyes, and pay twenty nobles among her grace's servants, dressed in a clean shirt for luck. Jonson's plot spins through greed and gulling at a furious pace. Readers who enjoy sharp, crowded comedy will find a masterpiece of trickery and talk.
4277-two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana wrote this classic of sea life from his own time before the mast. A Harvard student who shipped as a common sailor, Dana sailed from Boston around Cape Horn to California in the 1830s. He worked aloft, handled hides on the coast, and lived under harsh captains and harder weather.

The book made its mark by telling the sailor's life plainly, without romance. Readers learn how a ship was worked, how crews were fed and punished, and what the California hide trade meant in daily labor. It remains a firsthand record of the forecastle, and a text that later reformers quoted for the sailor's cause.
4298-the-paying-guest:
George Gissing built this short novel on a simple domestic idea. Mumford sees an advertisement and suggests taking a paying guest, to keep his wife company during the day. Emmeline, startled, weighs the plan: the rent is heavy, and so is the cost of Clarence's season ticket, but their house at Sutton has room to spare.

The air at Sutton has improved mother and child since they left London, and the guest promises company as well as income. Gissing then shows how a stranger in the house changes a marriage, a household, and its small economies. It is a compact study of suburban life, told with Gissing's dry, watchful humor.
452-lavengro-the-scholar-the-gypsy-the-p:
George Borrow tells his own wandering youth in this partly true, partly fancied memoir. Lavengro, scholar and would-be writer, roams England, learns tongues, meets gypsies, and talks with priests, tinkers, and horse dealers. Isopel Berners, a tall gypsy girl, stands out among his roadside friends.

Borrow writes in careless, vivid prose, full of talk, quarrel, and sudden charm. An introduction by Augustine Birrell praises the book's elixir of life and motion. The memoir charms as a picaresque portrait of England on foot, where learning and vagabond freedom share the same road.
4589-all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur published All's for the Best in 1869, gathering twelve sketches. Their titles run from Faith and Patience and Is He a Christian? through Rich and Rare Were the Gems She Wore, Not as a Child, and Angels in the Heart, to Cast Down but Not Destroyed, Good Ground, and Giving That Doth Not Impoverish. Later pieces ask Was It Murder, or Suicide? They add The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman.

The opening sketch meets a doubter who trusted human prudence, walked by his own light, and lost his way, confessing he has no faith in anything. A gentleman answers that he has faith in God, though the doubter shakes his head in bewilderment. Readers get a set of earnest Victorian tales about faith, patience, and conduct. Each is short enough to read alone, and each aims to steady a reader in doubt or sorrow.
4676-outpost:
J. G. Austin, author of Dora Darling, or The Daughter of the Regiment, published Outpost at Boston in 1867. Its contents open with sunshine, the little wife, Cherrytoe, and the children of Merrigoland. They go on to a runaway, Mother Winch, Teddy's little sister, the Fayver, and the night-watch. An empty nest, a trace and a search, Teddy's temptation, and the Cachuco follow.

Later chapters bring Giovanni and Pantalon, a pink-silk dress, beginning a new life, wholesale murder, and Dora Darling herself. A chamber of memories, a letter and an offer, Giovanni's room, and a confession lead to Teddy losing and finding his home. Burroughs' business, man versus dog, a visitor for Mrs. Ginniss, a new patron, and welcome home close the tale. Readers get a long Victorian domestic adventure, full of children, secrets, and second chances.
4701-the-ethics-of-the-dust:
John Ruskin, Slade Professor of Fine Art, wrote The Ethics of the Dust as ten lectures to little housewives on the elements of crystallisation. He dedicates the book, at Christmas 1875, to the real little housewives whose gentle listening and thoughtful questioning enabled him to write it. An old lecturer, of incalculable age, talks with girls named Florrie, Isabel, May, Lily, Kathleen, Lucilla, Violet, Dora, and Egypt.

Lectures run from the valley of diamonds and the pyramid builders, through crystal life, orders, virtues, quarrels, caprice, and sorrows, to home virtues and the crystal rest. Ruskin uses crystals to teach order, patience, and moral conduct, mixing science with fable. Readers get a charming, unusual Ruskin book, where geology becomes a lesson in character, for young readers and for adults who like science told as story.
4702-the-flaming-forest:
James Oliver Curwood opens The Flaming Forest with David Carrigan, sergeant in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, humming softly under a blue northern sky and thanking God he is alive. He blesses McVane, superintendent of N Division at Athabasca Landing, for detailing him to his mission. Glad to travel alone in deep forest, he expects weeks carrying him deeper into his beloved north.

Making noonday tea over a fire at a river's edge, Carrigan concludes for the hundredth time that it is nice to be alone in the world. Green forest crowds like an inundation on three sides of him. His comrades call his task a bad assignment, and danger waits ahead. Readers get a northern police adventure of forest fire, pursuit, and romance, with Curwood's usual snow, rivers, and lonely trails, and a hero who loves the wild he polices.
5301-the-imperialist:
Sara Jeannette Duncan's Imperialist, published in 1904, is set in the Canadian town of Elgin. Old Mother Beggarlegs presides like a venerable stooping hawk over a market stall of gingerbread horses, round cookies, and brown sticky taffy. Children speculate about her past, but she will never tell, and only children have time to wonder.

From that small-town opening, Duncan builds a novel of Canadian politics, imperial loyalty, and the pull of Britain against the United States. The book offers a sharp, witty portrait of a young dominion arguing about its future, through characters rooted in a single Ontario town.
5315-told-in-the-east:
Talbot Mundy's Told in the East, published by Bobbs-Merrill in 1920. It was reprinted in the omnibus Romances of India, and gathers three stories: Hookum Hai, For the Salt Which He Had Eaten, and Machassan Ah. Hookum Hai opens with a blood-red sun resting on a low mud wall, above dried acacia trees, in a landscape of heat and dust.

Mundy writes of India with the colour and pace of popular adventure, following soldiers, traders, and local rulers through loyalty, salt, and honour. Readers get three linked tales of British India, in which oaths and debts matter. Desert roads shape the action, from a writer who knew the region's stories well.
560-mr-standfast:
John Buchan returns Richard Hannay to war work in this sequel to Greenmantle, dedicated to South African troops. Hannay, cured of dyspepsia yet restless, hunts a German spy ring through English villages, Picardy chateaus, and Alpine passes. Andrew Amos, Blenkiron, and a cage of wild birds mark the chase.

Buchan writes with warm, steady vigor, mixing spy craft with Bunyan echoes in chapter titles. The tale ends with an exile's return and a summons for Mr. Standfast himself. The novel stands as a strong wartime adventure, where duty, friendship, and faith carry a man through.
5772-ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
George William Russell, known as AE, writes on theosophy and mysticism in AE in the Irish Theosophist. Contents include a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society. The Twilight Hour, The Mask of Apollo, and The Secret of Power follow. The Priestess of the Woods, A Tragedy in the Temple, and essays on waking, dreaming, and deep sleep complete the set. Verse by AE closes the collection.

Readers meet Irish mysticism at its most poetic, where myth, vision, and spiritual practice blend. Russell treats consciousness as a landscape to explore, with gods and symbols as guides rather than dogmas. The book suits readers of Yeats's circle, Irish literature, and esoteric thought, offering short, luminous pieces that reward slow, reflective reading.
5952-the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-great-west:
Laura Lee Hope takes the Bobbsey family west for a new round of holiday adventures. Bert and his small brother Freddie appear early, full of plans for snowmen and snowball games, while Flossie and the rest of the household share the trip. The book stands late in a long series of Bobbsey tales.

The western setting gives the children fresh ground to explore and fresh scrapes to get out of. As in the houseboat book, the pleasure lies in family company and small, lively incidents. Young readers follow a familiar set of siblings through unfamiliar country.
6067-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-rockies-:
Frank Gee Patchin opens with love of a horse, as Tad Butler begs Walter Perkins for two minutes on his pony. Walter hesitates, Tad insists he knows how to ride, and Chunky, whose well-rounded cheeks earned his nickname, backs him up with tales of Texas ponies and a broncho barely saddled once.

The Pony Rider Boys ride the Rockies in search of a lost secret, with Stacy Brown, Ned Rector, and Professor Zepplin along. Patchin writes brisk boy adventure, where riding skill, camp talk, and mountain trails matter most. The boys' pride in the saddle carries them into country that tests it.
6102-from-jest-to-earnest:
E. P. Roe dedicates From Jest to Earnest to his friend of youth and maturer years, Reverend A. Moss Merwin, a missionary in a foreign land who left every earthly ambition open at home. The novel begins with a practical joke and its victim, puzzled and interested, then a little pagan and plain talk.

A sleigh ride and something more, another spell than beauty's, finding one's level, and the other set follow. Midnight vigils, a preacher taught by the pagan, and the dawning light carry Hemstead toward earnestness. Roe turns jest into conversion, showing how a joke can open a life to serious faith.
6384-that-printer-of-udell-s-a-story-of-:
A dying mother prays in broken dialect for Dick, fearing a tough time for him when she is gone. She has had no show and has kept scratching to provide for herself and her boy. Her man is mostly no count and trifling, except when he drinks, and then, she says, God knows how he uses them. Dick, a hollow cheeked wisp of a boy crouching like a frightened animal, creeps to the bed and touches her wasted hand.

Harold Bell Wright's middle western story follows that printer's boy from such a start into print shop life at Udell. A body viewed for identification, a disfigured hand, and a missing little finger raise questions of letters and papers hidden. Dick asks in a whisper whether search was thorough, for people hide important documents. Wright writes uplift through work, faith, and a friend who hoped when others lost hope.
6471-the-children-of-the-new-forest:
Captain Marryat, Royal Navy, sets The Children of the New Forest in 1647, when King Charles the First, defeated after nearly five years of civil war, lay prisoner at Hampton Court. Cavaliers were dispersed, and Cromwell's parliamentary army began to control the Commons. In November, Charles escaped with Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg, riding fast toward Hampshire and the New Forest, hoping friends had provided a vessel to France.

No vessel waited, and disappointment followed. A mid passage shows Edward and Humphrey in the forest, laying a body in a grave from a cart before calling their sisters, then debating prayers for the dead. They are not in the Bible, Edward says, so some portion of the Bible must be read instead. Marryat writes a children's story of war, hiding, and family duty in the forest.
6479-lady-mary-and-her-nurse-or-a-peep-i:
Mrs. Traill writes Lady Mary and Her Nurse, subtitled A Peep into the Canadian Forest, as a child's guide to forest life told through a nurse's stories. The flying squirrel opens it, with its food, a story of a wolf, an Indian village, and wild rice. Sleighing, sleigh robes, fur caps, otter skins, an old snow storm, otter hunting, and otter slides follow, with Indian names and remarks on wild animals and their habits.

Lady Mary then reads Mrs. Frazer the history of the squirrel family: grey squirrels on Pine Island, their poor relations the chitmunks, and Velvet Paw at the mill by the rapids. Later chapters add Indian baskets, maple sugar, racoons, Canadian flowers, porcupine, and beaver architecture. A mid passage shows blue jays, blackbirds, field mice, squirrels, and chitmunks busy in wheat fields, filling cheeks with grain. Traill writes Canada for children, creature by creature.
6516-the-suppressed-gospels-and-epistles:
Archbishop Wake gathers writings that early Christian groups held dear, yet later councils set aside from the New Testament as most readers know it. Mary, the infancy tales, Nicodemus, letters of Paul and Clement, Barnabas, Hermas, and the notes of Ignatius all appear here, each with its own chapters. The long title states the case plainly: these books were once prized, then barred after sharp dispute.

Wake adds notes on where each text came from and why its standing was questioned, so a reader can judge the claims for each one. The volume thus serves both as a set of old writings and as a record of how a canon took shape. It suits readers who want to see what the early church read beyond the books that stayed in.
6769-the-people-of-the-mist:
H. Rider Haggard dedicates The People of the Mist, first published in 1894, to his godsons, as a record of primeval and troglodyte imagination and barefaced, flagrant adventure.
