Chapters bear titles like The Sins of the Father, After Seven Years, The Last Vigil, Otter Gives Counsel, and The Tale of Soa. Leonard swears on the blood of Aca, and a midnight marriage follows.

From a yellow devil's nest to the temple of Jâl, the tale moves through vengeance, disillusion, and a people's strange rites. Haggard writes with the gusto of his African romances. The People of the Mist is a thrilling, old-style lost-world adventure, full of danger and wonder.
6808-woman-on-the-american-frontier-a-va:
William Fowler argues that history, as usually told, records men's deeds in war and statecraft, while women appear only as queens or schemers for power. The story of women's work in great migrations, he says, has been told only in lines where it should fill volumes. His book aims to fill that gap, with heroism, adventures, privations, captivities, and noble lives and deaths of pioneer mothers.

Illustrated with many engravings, the history gathers tales of women on the frontier, from cabins to captivity. Fowler's tone is admiring and earnest. Woman on the American Frontier is a valuable, early tribute to pioneer women, still moving in its rescue of their stories.
6813-lost-in-the-backwoods-a-tale-of-the:
Mrs. Traill's tale of the Canadian forest, first called The Canadian Crusoes, returns in 1882 under a new, more descriptive title, Lost in the Backwoods. Young readers had loved it at first, and the publishers hoped it would please a new generation as well. The opening verse paints a Canadian morning, bright streamers on high, dazzling white snow, and ocean waves on shore.

Children lost in the woods must learn to live by wit, work, and courage, in a romantic adventure of the northern forest. Traill writes with a settler's knowledge and a storyteller's warmth. Lost in the Backwoods is a classic Canadian children's adventure, full of woodcraft and pluck.
6972-lays-from-the-west:
Stella, whose full name appears as M A Nicholl, sings lays from the west in a volume dedicated with gratitude to Missus Spotiswood Ash of Bellaghy in Ireland. A prefatory verse pictures a spirit taking her songs as tiny germs and bidding them root among coming hours and grow into flowers. The opening poem, In the Northwest, sets prairie flowers, blue sky, and sweet air against love of a native land far away.

The poet dreams of broad beech shade in glens beside Lough Neagh, even while poplars quiver and the tall iris blooms by a blue lake. The lays that follow hold that double vision, of a new western home and an old Irish shore. Nicholl writes with simple feeling for exile, landscape, and memory.
6998-the-spanish-chest:
Edna Brown's Spanish Chest opens with a foreword comparing books to a sketch whose painted figures walked out of the picture. Brown says books grow because someone thinks hard about their characters, and her own little book grew that way. It is dedicated to Florence and Clara, who shared a winter in the Channel Islands and have since gone on a longer journey, with verses confessing lines washed in with tears.

An illustration asks what a tiny dotted line across the grounds can mean, as Win inquires into a mystery. Photographs and drawings by John Goss adorn the tale, which mixes nonsense, mocking fears, and feeling. Brown wrote not for critics but for friendly eyes, and the chest at the center holds more than old things.
7074-beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont tells Beauty and the Beast as a tale for juvenile readers, ornamented with elegant engravings. A rich merchant with six children, three sons and three daughters, spares no cost for their education and gives them all kinds of masters. His daughters are extremely handsome, above all the youngest, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, a name she keeps as she grows.

Her sisters, proud because they are rich, give themselves ridiculous airs and will visit only persons of quality. The youngest, handsome as she is, proves better than her sisters in temper and heart. A frontispiece shows the Beast attacking the merchant, and the tale that follows turns pride, patience, and love into a household classic.
7107-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This closing part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter thirty six, once all are reckoned asleep. Huck and Tom slip down the lightning rod, shut themselves in the lean to, and bring out fox fire to work by. They clear four or five feet along the middle of the bottom log, right behind Jim's bed, and plan to dig under it, hidden by Jim's counterpane hanging near the ground.

They dig with case knives till near midnight, hands blistered, with hardly a mark to show for it. Huck jokes this is no thirty seven year job but a thirty eight year job, while Tom sighs and falls to thinking. The closing chapters leave Tom still planning while Huck digs through the night.
722-james-otis-the-pre-revolutionist:
John Clark Ridpath tells the life of James Otis, the Boston lawyer whose speeches against writs of assistance helped spark the American Revolution. Otis argued that taxation without representation broke English liberty. Otis argued against writs of assistance in 1761, a speech John Adams called the start of independence.

Ridpath follows Otis from his early career to his fiery courtroom stand and his later decline, placing him before the better-known patriots. The short life serves as an introduction to a founder whose ideas outlived his mind. Ridpath, a popular historian, wrote the life for general readers, not for scholars alone.
7237-roving-east-and-roving-west:
E. V. Lucas roves east and west in this travel book, opening in India with noiseless feet, the sahib, and the passing show. Birds, towers of silence, and garlands follow, then Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, a tiger, the sacred city, and Calcutta. Japan follows, with its little land, its rope trick, and its quiet scenes, and the contents promise a traveller's eye in both worlds.

Lucas dedicates the book to his host at Raisina and quotes Johnson on the two objects of curiosity, the Christian world and the Mahometan world, with Wordsworth close behind. His sketches favour people, streets, and small encounters over grand sights. The result reads like a notebook kept by a friendly wanderer.
7347-the-lincoln-story-book-a-judicious-:
Henry L. Williams compiled the Lincoln Story Book as a judicious collection of the best stories and anecdotes of the great president, many appearing here for the first time in book form. His preface contrasts two Lincolns. One is the Chicago statue's typical Westerner of forum, rostrum, and tribune at his inauguration under the war-cloud in 1861. The other is the Lincoln dear to common people, the speaker of household words.

That second Lincoln appears long and gaunt, divided between two chairs for comfort, head bent forward, smiling broadly at a tale of his own. Williams gathers the jokes, sayings, and human moments that made that figure beloved. The book preserves Lincoln the storyteller beside Lincoln the statesman.
7352-first-and-last:
H. Belloc's First and Last gathers essays whose contents range from weighing anchor and the reveillon through cheeses, the captain of industry, and the inventor. The views of England, the lunatic, the inheritance of humour, and an old gentleman's opinions on historical evidence complete the first sweep. The absence of the past, St Patrick, lost things, the reading of history, victory, and reality follow. Jose Maria de Heredia, Normandy and the Normans, old things, Hastings, and Roman roads in Picardy join them, with the decline of the book among them.

Belloc's table reads like a mind wandering a library and a landscape at once, sure in opinion and rich in phrase. The reward of letters, eye-openers, the public, entries, companions of travel, and sources of rivers close a miscellany with no dull corner. Readers get Belloc at his most various and dogmatic.
7474-the-ancient-east:
D. G. Hogarth, Keeper of the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, wrote this short history for the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. He starts by fixing what his title means, since older writers used direction words in their own way. For Herodotus and Greeks of his day, the southern lands were Egypt, Arabia, and India. The northern lands were Thrace and Scythia, while Hither Asia counted as the East.

Beyond that East, those writers pictured only a fabled stream, Ocean, ringing the world. Hogarth then follows his region through time, with chapters on the years 1000, 800, 600, and 400 before Christ, closing with the victory of the West and an epilogue. Maps show the region and its main divisions and the Asiatic empire of the age. It is a compact survey of the ancient Near East before Alexander, written while archaeology was remaking the field.
8094-certain-noble-plays-of-japan-from-t:
Ezra Pound chose and finished these noble plays of Japan from the manuscripts of Ernest Fenollosa, with an introduction by William Butler Yeats. Yeats explains that he asked Pound for the plays because they might help explain a possibility of the Irish dramatic movement. And he writes with his imagination stirred by masks and head-dresses seen in the studio of Edmund Dulac. The plays are Noh dramas, with their masked actors, choruses, and ghosts.

Pound's versions brought Japanese classical theatre to English readers for the first time in this form, and they influenced modernist poetry and drama deeply. The volume is short but historic, a meeting of Japanese tradition and European experiment. For readers of Pound and Yeats, it is essential, and for theatre lovers, a doorway into Noh.
8122-legends-of-the-northwest:
H. L. Gordon, author of Pauline, gathered these legends of the Northwest after years spent studying the language, history, traditions, customs, and superstitions of the Dakotas. His contents include a prelude on the Mississippi, The Feast of the Virgins, Winona, and The Legend of the Falls. All legends of the Dakotas, plus The Sea-Gull, the Ojibwa legend of the pictured rocks of Lake Superior, and Minnetonka. Gordon notes that Dakota means alliance or confederation, and that Sioux was a name given by French traders.

The legends are retold in verse and prose, preserving stories of love, sacrifice, and landscape. Gordon writes as a respectful student of the peoples he describes, though through nineteenth-century eyes. For readers of Native American legend and Midwestern lore, the volume remains an early and earnest collection.
8143-the-shadow-of-the-east:
E. M. Hull published The Shadow of the East in 1921, opening on an American yacht brilliantly lit off Yokohama harbour. With the full moon glittering on the water to the steps of the landing-stage. Coloured lamps along the sea wall transform the Japanese town into fairyland, though by day the scene is blatant and tawdry. The epigraph, from Ezekiel, warns that the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge.

Hull, famous for The Sheik, writes a romance of the East in which past sins shadow the present. Her heroine moves between yacht society and eastern mystery, and the novel's glamour carries its melodrama. For readers of romantic adventure fiction, it is a vivid example of the genre at its height, and a period portrait of Yokohama.
838-jasmin-barber-poet-philanthropist:
Samuel Smiles wrote this life of Jacques Jasmin, the barber-poet of Agen in southern France. Born poor, Jasmin cut hair by day and wrote verse in Gascon by night, winning fame for songs that moved the people. Sainte-Beuve praised him as a poet whose influence might have spared France revolutions.

Smiles follows Jasmin from boyhood in Agen to his triumphs as a singer and giver, for he spent his earnings on the poor. The life is a Smiles lesson in self-help through art and charity. The book gives English readers a vivid portrait of a folk poet, and of the France he sang for.
8389-lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-lates:
Robert G. Ingersoll, the Great Agnostic, filled lecture halls across America, and this volume gathers his later lectures. Contents include Thomas Paine, Liberty of Man, Woman and Child, Orthodoxy, Blasphemy, and essays on heretics, the Bible, Voltaire, and myth and miracle. Ingersoll argues, with courtroom polish, that reason and kindness outrank creed, and that doubt is honest.

His lectures made freethought respectable to middle-class audiences, and his defense of Paine helped restore a founder long smeared as an infidel. Readers get oratory rather than scholarship: jokes, stories, and rolling periods aimed at a live crowd. The volume still reads as a landmark of American secularism, from its most famous voice.
8745-wulf-the-saxon-a-story-of-the-norma:
G. A. Henty tells the Norman Conquest through Wulf the Saxon, arguing in his preface that Hastings. Though its immediate results may seem less than those of other great battles, has in the long run influenced mankind's destiny more than any similar event. The admixture of Saxon, Danish, and British races called English, he says, lagged behind Europe, distracted by internal dissensions. Broad divisions between north and south under weak kings.

Wulf, a young Saxon thane, serves Harold, fights at Hastings, and lives through conquest, resistance, and settlement under Norman rule. Henty mixes real kings and battles with a hero's adventures, teaching the Conquest as personal story. Boys' adventure and history blend in the usual Henty manner, partisan toward Saxon courage. The novel remains a lively introduction to 1066 for young readers, and a period piece for adults.
8873-the-isle-of-unrest:
Henry Seton Merriman sets The Isle of Unrest in Corsica. Opening with Richard Lovelace's lines on going to the wars: tell me not I am unkind to fly from a quiet breast to war and arms. A new mistress, the first foe in the field, and a stronger faith in sword, horse, and shield. Contents promise the moving finger, chez Clement, a by-path, a toss-up, the Rue du Cherche-Midi, neighbours, journey's end, Vasselot, the promised land. Thus far, before surprise, summons, war, and gossip.

Merriman, popular novelist of adventure, uses Corsican vendetta, French politics, and a love story to build a tale of unrest literal and personal. The island's wild beauty and fierce loyalties drive the plot. Readers who enjoy late Victorian romance with a strong sense of place will find a brisk, atmospheric novel.
9300-jennie-baxter-journalist:
Robert Barr wrote this lively novel in 1899 about Jennie Baxter, a young woman journalist in London. Jennie makes her toilette, meets a porter, and confers with two important editors. She interviews a frightened official, learns of a princess's diamonds, and meets a great detective. Soon she solves the diamond mystery herself.

Later chapters mix Jennie with the elite of earth, dodge an offer of marriage, and brush a government secret. Barr writes with humor and pace, letting his heroine outwit men at their own game. The novel still delights as an early tale of a working girl reporter.
9376-the-forest:
Stewart Edward White wrote this book of the north woods, from the calling to the science of going light. Chapters teach making camp, lying awake at night, open-water canoe travel, and walking through woods. Flies, habitants, rivers, hills, and woods Indians all get their turn, with a fish caught and a man who walks by moonlight.

White writes from camp life itself, with practical hints and poetic feeling joined. An outfit list aids the reader who would follow. The book remains a classic of outdoor writing, a guide and a love letter to the forest at once.
9385-the-incomplete-amorist:
E. Nesbit wrote this novel in 1906, in four books: The Girl, The Man, The Other Woman, and The Other Man. Its Balzac epigraph holds that to birth a desire, nurse it, grow it, and satisfy it is a whole poem. Chapters run from the inevitable and irresistible to the prisoner, the criminal, and the escape, then to seeing life and rescue.

On Mount Parnassus, love and Tupper, and interventions lead to truth, and truth with a vengeance. Nesbit, famed for children's books, writes here for grown-ups with wit. The novel remains a clever, modern romance of desire and its discontents.
9390-fifteen-years-with-the-outcast:
Florence Roberts, called Mother Roberts, wrote this memoir in 1912 of fifteen years with the outcast, meaning the poor and despised. Its preface contrasts two speakers at one assembly: a missionary fresh from India, telling of converts and persecution for leaving idolatry, and a noted English hunter just back from Bengal.

Roberts chose the harder field at home, among those society casts out. Her pages tell of rescue, patience, and faith put to work in slums and streets. The memoir remains a vivid record of Christian social work, earnest, plain, and full of human faces.
942-green-mansions-a-romance-of-the-trop:
W. H. Hudson wrote this romance of the tropical forest, about Abel, a Venezuelan traveller who flees into the wild and finds Rima, a mysterious girl of the woods. Rima, who speaks with birds and lives among green mansions of trees, becomes Abel's love and his guide to a world apart from men.

Hudson writes the forest with lush, poetic prose, full of birdsong, mist, and danger. The romance turns tragic, as Abel's world and Rima's cannot both survive. The book, praised by its foreword writer as beyond his power to do justice, remains a beloved classic of nature romance, haunting and beautiful.
945-dust:
Mr. and Mrs. Haldeman-Julius wrote this novel whose chapters trace dust through a life: the dust is stirred, dust in her heart, dust begets dust, dust in his eyes, and Martin battles with dust. Martin's son shakes off the dust, the dust settles, and the dust-bin waits at the end.

The novel uses dust as a figure for the grime of poverty, toil, and small-town life, and for the hope of shaking it off. Its prose is earnest and plain, aimed at readers who know hard work. Dust stands as a period piece of American social fiction, where a family's fate is told through a single, homely image.
9788-ned-myers-or-a-life-before-the-mast:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Ned Myers, or A Life Before the Mast, in 1843, the true life of an old shipmate. Cooper holds that any man's life, faithfully told, would interest and instruct readers. Myers, a common sailor, tells his voyages, perils, escapes, and opinions from the forecastle. Cooper hopes Myers's experience and moral change may sway young minds for good.

The book follows a foremast Jack through storms, ports, and hard service, with the tang of true sea talk. Cooper, famed for sea tales, here lets a real sailor speak. A reader gets a vivid, honest sailor's life, and a window on the merchant navy of the early republic.
9905-a-deal-in-wheat-and-other-stories-o:
Frank Norris published this story collection in 1903, three years after his great wheat novel The Octopus. The title tale follows a Chicago wheat corner, where a bear broker and a bull fight over prices while farmers and small traders pay the cost.

Other stories cross the old and new West: a wife on the frontier, a bargain with a peg-legged man, and a sudden death remembered in a memorandum. Norris writes with force about money, land, and luck. The book is a strong short introduction to his belief that markets, like weather, crush the little people first.
a-girl-of-the-limberlost:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this novel about Elnora Comstock, a poor Indiana girl who pays for her schooling by collecting moths and butterflies in the Limberlost swamp. The character list at the front describes her plainly: she collects moths to pay for her education and lives the Golden Rule. Her mother, embittered by her husband's death in that swamp, withholds money and love alike.

Across twenty-five chapters Elnora enters high school in hand-me-down shame. With help from the kind Sinton neighbors, she builds her collection into a livelihood. She also sets her heart on a violin and a full education. Philip Ammon, a young visitor, joins the moth hunts and falls in love. The book mixes nature study of the vanishing swamp with a story of endurance at home.
a-lady-of-quality-being-a-most-curious-h:
Frances Hodgson Burnett frames her historical novel as a curious history related by Mr. Isaac Bickerstaff, in the 1896 Frederick Warne edition used here. It begins on November 24, 1690, at Wildairs Hall, where the loud, choleric Sir Jeoffry prepares to hunt. His daughter grows up wild, beautiful, and proud in Queen Anne's England.

Twenty-four chapters follow Mistress Clorinda through horse breaking, suitors, a marriage to an earl, and a deadly war of reputation with a rival beauty. A hidden miniature and a night meeting in a rose garden mark key turns. Burnett mixes costume splendor with a study of a woman too strong for her age's rules.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
The final chapters of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, chapters 36 to the last, give Tom Sawyer full command of Jim's escape, and the work proceeds by his book-learned rules. Digging with case-knives quietly swapped for picks, a rope ladder baked in a pie, and warnings written in blood. Jim, patient and chained in his cabin, endures a glory he never asked for.

The escape ends in a night chase, a bullet in Tom's leg, and Jim risking his freedom to nurse the boy. Then the revelation that Miss Watson had already freed Jim in her will. Aunt Polly arrives to untangle the boys' names, Tom pays Jim for his trouble, and Huck, dreading adoption and sivilizing, plans to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest.
ae-in-the-irish-theosophist:
AE in the Irish Theosophist collects the early writings of George William Russell, who signed himself AE, from the journal of Ireland's theosophical circle. Russell opens with a word on the objects of the Theosophical Society, the movement that joined Eastern religion, occult study, and moral renewal. Twenty four prose pieces follow, and a set of thirty nine verses closes the gathering.

Titles map his young mysticism: The Mask of Apollo, The Secret of Power, The Priestess of the Woods, and A Tragedy in the Temple. Essays take up concentration, the element language, and the states of waking, dream, and deep sleep under their Sanskrit names. Tales and meditations turn toward Ireland in The Legends of Ancient Eire and At the Dawn of the Kali Yuga. Russell later became a poet, painter, and agricultural reformer; here his otherworldly Ireland is still being invented, page by page.
all-s-for-the-best:
T. S. Arthur gathered All's for the Best in Philadelphia in 1869, twelve tales of faith under trial. The opening piece, Faith and Patience, argues with a doubter of fifty. Mr. Fanshaw confesses he has no faith in anything at all. His friend Wilkins answers with talk of internal sight, the mind's eye.

Other chapters ask Is He a Christian and weigh cast down, but not destroyed. Giving that doth not impoverish praises open-handed charity. Was It Murder, or Suicide darkens the collection with a mystery. The Nursery Maid, My Father, and The Christian Gentleman close the set. Arthur's Swedenborgian faith, trust in divine order behind appearances, shapes every tale. The title is his doctrine: rightly seen, all works for the best, even sorrow.
an-unsocial-socialist:
George Bernard Shaw begins at a girls' school in an old English country house, where a sensible teacher's quiet evening is broken by a strange arrival. Sidney Trefusis, a rich young widower, has walked out of his marriage and his class to preach socialism. He hides near the school under a false name and stirs every mind he meets.

The schoolgirls, their teachers, and the local gentry all collide with Trefusis's talk about property, marriage, and labor. Shaw fills the novel with debates, letters, and comic scenes at the school and on a model farm. It is fiction used as a platform, written with the wit that later made Shaw famous on the stage.
apess-son-of-the-forest:
William Apess, a Pequot Methodist preacher, published A Son of the Forest in 1829. It is the first published autobiography by a Native American. Apess wrote it himself and issued it at his own cost.

He tells of a poor childhood, beatings by white guardians, service in the War of 1812, and his turn to preaching. Throughout, he protests the theft of Native land and the abuse of Native people. His faith and his anger speak side by side. The book opened a path for Native writers and still stings today. Later editions carried his name as Apess, the spelling used here in the title.
beauty-and-the-beast:
Marie Le Prince de Beaumont's Beauty and the Beast is the classic fairy tale, written for the entertainment of juvenile readers and ornamented with elegant engravings. A very rich merchant has six children, three sons and three daughters, and spares no cost for their education.

The youngest daughter, admired from childhood as the little Beauty, is as good as she is handsome. Her two elder sisters pride themselves on their wealth and keep company only with persons of quality. When fortune turns, Beauty's kindness is tested by the Beast's enchanted castle. Readers of every age will recognise this telling as the source of the tale's most familiar form.
ben-hur-a-tale-of-the-christ:
Lew Wallace built Ben-Hur around Judah Ben-Hur, a Jewish prince of Jerusalem under Roman rule, and his boyhood friend Messala, now a Roman officer. A falling tile injures the Roman governor, and Ben-Hur is condemned to the galleys while his mother and sister vanish into prison. At sea he saves the Roman commander Quintus Arrius, who adopts him and makes him rich.

Freed, Ben-Hur trains Arab horses and beats Messala in the great chariot race at Antioch. His search for his family leads through leper caves to the crowds following Jesus of Nazareth. Wallace frames the revenge story inside the Gospel story, ending at the Crucifixion. The novel became the best-selling American religious epic of its century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Vaast describes an abbey at Arras, ancient capital of Artois, founded in 667. St. Vaast, born about 453, lived as a recluse, was ordained by St. Remi of Reims, and prepared Clovis for baptism before becoming first Bishop of Arras in 499.

Vaast's labours in planting the faith were blessed by many miracles, and he also took charge of Cambrai for ten years. He died in 540 and was laid in his Arras cathedral. In 667 St. Auburt, the see's seventh bishop, began building a Benedictine abbey on the site of a little chapel Vaast had raised to St. Peter, and Vaast's relics were transferred to the new house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agony-of-chri:
Agony of Christ, from agonia, a struggle, means in profane literature athletes' physical struggle or the mental excitement before conflict. In Scripture it occurs only once, Luke 22:43, for Our Lord's anguish in the Garden of Gethsemani. Remarkably, only Luke mentions the sweat of blood and the angel's visitation.

The authenticity of verses 43-44 narrating these details has been questioned. They are absent not only from the other synoptists but even from Luke in several ancient codices, notably the revised Sinaiticus and codices A and B. Their presence in most manuscripts, uncial and cursive, has sufficed to retain them in critical New Testament editions. Their acceptance by Tischendorf, Hammond, and Scrivener seems to settle authenticity beyond doubt. The sweat of blood is read literally by almost all Catholic exegetes, with medical testimony cited that such haematodrosis, though rare, is neither impossible nor preternatural.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-hoh:
Alexander von Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst was a titular Bishop of Sardica, famous for his supposedly miraculous cures, born at Kupferzell in Württemberg in August 1794 and dead at Vöslau in November 1849. He studied at Vienna, Berne, Tyrnau, and Ellwangen, and was ordained a priest in September 1815, serving at Stuttgart and then Munich. After a pilgrimage to Loreto, he became councillor in 1817 and canon of Bamberg in 1821.

About 1821 the cures began. Hohenlohe was healed of a throat pain at Hassfurt through the prayers of a peasant, Martin Michel. In June 1821 he cured the paralytic Princess Mathilda von Schwarzenberg by prayer joined with Michel's. The pope told him to attempt no more public cures, but he continued in private. He named times of prayer for applicants across Europe, England, Ireland, and America, including Ann Mattingly of Washington in 1824. Rome passed no judgment on the supposed miracles, and Catholics were divided.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antichrist:
Antichrist, Greek Antichristos, bears the prefix anti, with varied meanings: antibasileus, an interregnum king; antistrategos, a propraetor; anthoupatos, a proconsul; Homer's antitheos, godlike, elsewhere hostile. By analogy antichristos might mean one resembling Christ; safer to define it by biblical and ecclesiastical usage. Antichrist occurs only in John's Epistles, with parallels in the Apocalypse and Paul's Epistles, fainter ones in the Gospels and Daniel.

St. John supposes early Christians acquainted with teaching on Antichrist's coming. The figure is described more fully in 2 Thessalonians. The day of the Lord will be preceded by revolt and the man of sin's revelation. He will sit in God's temple as God, work lying wonders by Satan's power, and seduce truth's rejecters. But the Lord Jesus shall destroy him with the brightness of His coming. Antichrist will be a human person, perhaps of Jewish extraction, not a demon nor the devil incarnate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archpriest:
An archpriest, or chief of the college of presbyters, aided and represented the bishop in liturgical and religious duties. Much as the archdeacon stood out among deacons as the bishop's special assistant, so the archpriest stood out among priests. Found since the fourth century in many dioceses, the archpriest was as a rule, above all in Rome, where the custom began, the oldest presbyter raised to the rank. In the Greek church his appointment often lay with the bishop. By the seventeenth rule of the Fourth Synod of Carthage he shared with the bishop care of the poor.

After the full Christianization of Roman and Germanic peoples, the West gained another kind of archpriest for rural districts. There scattered people's spiritual needs multiplied too fast for city clergy to meet alone. The entry tracks two archpriests: the bishop's senior priest in the city, and the rural head serving country parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assistant-pri:
The assistant priest, in Latin presbyter assistens and formerly called capellanus, is the first and supreme in dignity among ministers assisting the bishop in pontifical functions. Where cathedral chapters exist, ordinarily the first dignitary serves as assistant priest, yet if the bishop only attends a service, the first canon after the dignitaries ought to serve instead. If a priest preaches at pontifical Mass, that preacher must also be assistant priest.

A cardinal bishop serves as assistant priest for the pontiff. By privilege, prothonotaries de numero, or of the number, and mitred abbots may keep an assistant priest at pontifical Mass. So, with restrictions, may supernumerary prothonotaries and prothonotaries ad instar, or after the pattern. Certain dignitaries and canons hold the same right by ancient custom, and the Congregation of Rites allows an assistant priest at a priest's initial solemn Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bathurst:
Bathurst is a diocese in New South Wales, west of the Dividing Range, founded as a town in 1824. Population filtered slowly into its rich plains until gold was found in the district in 1851. Its first church was a bark hut, replaced in 1861 by a fine cathedral built for £12,000 under Dean Grant.

In 1865 Bathurst became the center of a vast new diocese, served at first by six priests, seven churches, and six schools with 492 pupils. Its first bishop, Matthew Quinn, consecrated at Dublin in 1865, arrived in 1866 with five priests and seven Sisters of Mercy. By 1907 the diocese counted 89 churches, 242 nuns, 4,298 schoolchildren, and about 27,000 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-fores:
Blessed John Forest, a Franciscan martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1471, probably at Oxford, he suffered on 22 May 1538. At twenty he took the habit of the Observant Franciscans at Greenwich, studied theology at Oxford nine years later, and became chaplain and confessor to Queen Catherine of Aragon.

As provincial of the Observants from about 1525, he defended Catherine's marriage and the pope's authority against Henry VIII. Imprisoned for refusing the royal supremacy, he was burned at Smithfield, chained over a fire fed with a statue of a Welsh saint. The entry presents a friar who would not bend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bukarest:
Bukarest, archdiocese of the Rumanian kingdom outside Moldavia, counts about 56,000 Latin Catholics, 4,000 to 5,000 Uniat Rumanians, and a few hundred Uniat Armenians. Its capital city, with 285,445 people in 1905, holds some 202,000 Orthodox Greeks and 43,000 Jews. The city lies on a swampy plain astride the Dimbovitza, crossed by about a dozen bridges, with stately buildings, gardens, and bright domes giving its old quarters a half-Oriental air.

Its chapter holds four canons and honorary canons, and forty priests serve twenty-four parishes and forty-five churches. The archiepiscopal seminary trains nineteen students with four professors, while six more study abroad. Catholic schools fill every parish, Christian Brothers teach 1,028 pupils, English Ladies run boarding and primary schools for over 2,000 girls, and the Dames de Sion teach 133 boarders. The Gothic cathedral of Saint Joseph, finished in 1884, stands as the country's largest Catholic church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burghard-frei:
Burghard von Schorlemer-Alst, a Westphalian social reformer, organized peasants into a Christian union that outlived the Kulturkampf. Born at Heringhausen on 21 October 1825, he trained as a cadet at Dresden's Royal Saxon Military College, served as a Prussian Uhlan officer, and fought in Baden in 1849. Leaving the army in 1852, he married Countess Droste zu Vischering and took the Alst estate near Burgsteinfurt.

His 1862 pamphlet on the Westphalian peasant's plight proposed an independent peasant union, and two societies rose that year, spreading until nearly 10,000 members stood enrolled by the late sixties. He led the Prussian agricultural board, founded schools at Ludinghausen and Herford, and sat in the Prussian Diet and Reichstag for the Centre party, fighting the Church's foes with acuteness and humor. The united Westphalian Peasant Union of 1871 counted 20,500 members in 1890 and over 30,000 in his last years. He died at Alst on 17 March 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinals-191: Members of the College of Cardinals in 1913 fill this roster. Each cardinal appears with his see or office, from the Bishop of Albano and the Archbishops of Toledo, Seville, Paris, and Bordeaux to the Patriarch of Venice. Archbishops of New York, Milan, Baltimore, and Armagh appear too. Jesuits, Franciscans, and Benedictines number among the orders named. The list runs through Europe, the Americas, and beyond to Prague, Gran, and Rio de Janeiro.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celsus-the-pl:
Celsus the Platonist was an eclectic philosopher and polemical writer against Christianity who flourished toward the end of the second century. Little is known of his life beyond that he lived under Marcus Aurelius, worked between 175 and 180, and wrote a book called The True Word attacking the Christian religion. Celsus ranks among several second-century writers named Celsus who opposed Christianity, and he was probably the Celsus known as a friend of Lucian.

That identification is doubted. Lucian's friend was an Epicurean, while the author of The True Word shows himself a Platonist. His knowledge of Jewish religion and Egyptian customs leads some historians to place him in the empire's eastern half. Others explain it by travel or by contact with foreigners in Rome. He owes his fame largely to Origen, who received a copy of his work about 240 and answered it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-character-of-:
The character of Jesus has won acknowledgment from varied witnesses. Kant praised His ideal perfection, and Hegel saw the human and the Divine joined in Him. Sceptics did Him homage, Spinoza called Him the truest symbol of heavenly wisdom, and Voltaire stood overawed by His life's beauty and grandeur. Napoleon at St. Helena found no comparison between Jesus and anyone else.

Rousseau, Strauss, Renan, and Mill each praised Him in turn. They called Him a god beside Socrates the sage, religion's highest object, God's most beautiful incarnation, and a man charged with a unique commission from God. These views matter less for theology than for the impression Christ's history made. The article then examines Jesus in His relation to men and to God, in reason's light and faith's, His sanctity and His divinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronology-of:
An entry on the chronology of the life of Jesus Christ, seeking both its absolute and its relative order. Absolute chronology fits certain facts to universal history, while relative chronology arranges the rest of the life by the links between its parts. The datable points are the year of the Nativity, the start of the public ministry, and the death.

Matthew places the birth in the days of Herod. Josephus dates Herod's death by his thirty-four years of actual rule and an eclipse of the moon in March of the year 750 from Rome's founding. Since Herod slew children up to two years old, the birth likely falls in 747, 748, or 749. The ministry is dated from Luke, Josephus on the Temple, and the fifteenth year of Tiberius. The entry also weighs the census under Quirinius and a Pisces conjunction of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commemoration:
Frederick Holweck's entry covers a feast kept on the Tuesday after Sexagesima. Its aim is devout remembrance and honor of Christ's sufferings for human redemption. Feasts of the instruments of the Passion, the Arma Christi, arose in the Middle Ages. This commemoration came later. It first appears in the Breviary of Meissen of 1517, as a simple feast for 15 November. That book also held feasts of the Holy Face and Holy Name. All three vanished with the coming of Lutheranism.

In the appendix of the Roman Breviary the feast traces to Saint Paul of the Cross, who died in 1775. Thomas Struzzieri, Bishop of Todi and Paul's faithful associate, composed its Office. Holweck calls that Office rich and full of pious feeling, though its hymns run rather modern. The entry thus joins a late medieval local feast to its modern Roman form, through the Passionist founder and his bishop friend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dioceses-supp:
This supplemental list gathers dioceses that came into being after the Catholic Encyclopedia itself had begun. Pope Pius the Tenth, following Leo the Thirteenth, raised new sees and vicariates each year as railways, steamships, and emigration opened new regions. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives a brief account of each new diocese and notes shifts in the bounds of older sees.

The list opens with Aimer, raised from a prefecture in Rajpootana on 22 May 1913, answering to Agra. It runs through missions and provinces across Asia, Africa, and the Americas, ending with Simla, whose province was completed in 1913. For readers tracking a fast-growing church, it is the update that keeps the main diocese articles current.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-disciples-of-:
The Disciples of Christ are a sect founded in the United States by Alexander Campbell. Campbell was born in County Antrim, Ireland, on 12 September 1788, of Scottish and Huguenot stock, to parents of deep piety and high learning. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his father from a ministry in Ireland to America, where he pursued the dream of uniting all Christians in one communion on a purely scriptural basis.

That effort, the entry argues, could only breed fresh division, against the will of its founder. The Disciples take the Bible as the full revelation of God's will and reject all binding creeds. They keep both Testaments as equally inspired, though not equally binding, and they observe the Lord's Supper as a memorial feast rather than a sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-histori:
Early historical documents on Jesus Christ fall into three classes, pagan, Jewish, and Christian, and this entry studies them in turn. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns that pagan sources are few and stained by hatred and prejudice. Galilee lay remote, Jews passed for a superstitious race, their God seemed unknown to pagans, and Christians were often mistaken for one sect among many.

The entry weighs what pagans, Jews, and Christians each preserve about the life of Jesus. These sources do not yield a full biography, but they account for the rise of Christianity through its founder. Questions of Gospel authenticity and of the Synoptic problem are left to their own articles, while this entry maps the ground outside the Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-symbols:
Early symbols of the Eucharist hold first place among the signs with which first-age Christians adorned their tombs. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry finds the weightiest monuments in the underground cemeteries of early Rome, the catacombs. Their discovery and reopening in the later nineteenth century shed light on dim allusions in early Christian writings. Catholic theology thus gained fresh evidence on belief in the Eucharist and on its celebration in the age after the apostles.

Wilpert, a leading scholar of Christian archaeology, guides the reading of these symbols. The entry draws on Kraus, Marucchi, and Northcote and Brownlow to show how fish, bread, and cup spoke the mystery to the buried faithful. For readers of the catacombs, it is a key to pictures that taught before books were common.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eucharist:
Eucharist, from Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving, names the Blessed Sacrament of the Altar as sacrament and Sacrifice of Mass, in which Christ is truly present under bread and wine. Other titles are used, such as Lord's Supper, Table of the Lord, Lord's Body, and Holy of Holies, to which may be added Agape, Eulogia, Breaking of Bread, and Synaxis. But the ancient title Eucharistia, appearing in writers as early as Ignatius, Justin, and Irenaeus, has taken precedence in the Church's technical terminology.

The expression Blessed Sacrament of the Altar, introduced by Augustine, is now largely restricted to catechetical and popular treatises. This extensive nomenclature alone proves the central position the Eucharist has held from the earliest ages, in Divine worship and in the life of faith animating the Church's members. The Church honours the Eucharist as one of her most exalted mysteries, yielding in nothing to the Trinity and Incarnation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangelist:
Evangelist is a New Testament word found only three times in that form, at Acts 21:8, Ephesians 4:11, and 2 Timothy 4:5. It seems to mark a function rather than a rank in the early Church. The Apostles were evangelists in that they preached the Gospel, and Philip was both deacon and evangelist, while Saint Paul urged Timothy toward an evangelist's work. From the scattered notices, evangelists appear as traveling missionaries, at times solemnly set apart, who preached to those who had not heard the faith and paved the way for pastors and teachers.

Later the word changed sense and came to mean the writers of the Four Gospels alone, the sense of modern speech. The Latin Church at last fixed Matthew as man, Mark as lion, Luke as ox, and John as eagle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eve-of-a-feas:
The Eve of a Feast, or Vigil, was the night before a feast when the faithful kept watch in prayer. In the first ages they gathered in the evening in the church where the feast would be kept and readied themselves with prayers, readings from Scripture, and at times a sermon. Mass was also said in the evening, and toward morning the people waited in streets and houses near the church for the morning services. 

The morning break led to abuses, as people feasted and danced around the church, and councils moved against the night vigils. A synod at Rouen in 1231 banned all but patronal vigils, and bishops replaced night watches with a vigil-eve fast. After the eleventh century the vigil's fast, Office, and Mass moved to the day before.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exorcist:
Exorcist means two things. In general it is anyone who exorcises or claims to exorcise demons. In particular it is one ordained by a bishop for that office, the second among the Western Church's four minor orders. Early on, exorcism was not confined to clerics, and Origen attests that even the simplest faithful at times cast out demons by prayer. The Western orders arose not long before the middle of the third century.

At Rome, Pope Cornelius counts fifty-two exorcists, readers, and door-keepers. The Fourth Council of Carthage in 398 fixed the rite, giving the book of exorcisms and bidding the man lay hands on energumens. Exorcists took part in daily baptismal exorcisms and cared for energumens haunting the church. The East never set up such an order. Later the office faded into major orders, so now only priests use the power, with the bishop's leave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-d-a:
Louis d'Ailleboust was the third governor of Canada under France. He reached the colony in 1643 and helped to found Montreal. As governor from 1648 to 1651, he faced the violent destruction of the Huron missions. He also saw the first French grain sown in the colony's soil.

His wife Barbe taught the Algonquin language and founded a confraternity in 1663. D'Ailleboust laid the foundation stone of Ste Anne de Beaupre in 1658. He died at Montreal on 31 May 1660, after long years of public service. His nephew Charles Joseph later served as judge of Montreal until 1693.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fast:
Fast, in this article, means abstinence from food or drink for a set time. The strict fast allows one full meal a day, taken about midday. A small evening collation is also permitted by custom. Before Communion, a complete and total fast was required.

The article lists fasting days in the United States, Britain, and Ireland. Lent, Ember Days, vigils, and the Fridays of Advent head the list. Moralists ground fasting in natural law and the mastery of appetite. Positive church law then fixes the days and the manner of keeping them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Holy Winding Sheet feasts honour burial cloths linked to Christ's entombment. One sheet reached Besancon in 1206, and its feast falls on 11 July. Another, the famed Turin shroud, came from Lirey in Burgundy to Chambery in 1432. Its feast, approved in 1506, is kept on 4 May.

A third feast at Compiegne honoured a winding sheet brought from Aachen in 877. The Turin sheet moved to its royal chapel in the Turin cathedral in 1578. Since 1831 a general feast, tied to no relic, falls on the Friday after Lent's second Sunday. The Office for that feast comes from the Turin Proprium.

The Prayer of Christ feast falls each year on the Tuesday after Septuagesima. It recalls Christ's prolonged prayer in Gethsemane in our behalf before the Passion. The Office stresses the great importance of prayer itself. Lent's start makes the feast a call to make prayer the heart of Lent.

Bishop Struzzieri of Todi probably composed the Office for the feast. St Paul of the Cross first suggested it, and Pius VI approved it. Rome adopted it in 1831, and many other dioceses followed after Rome. It has not yet entered the Baltimore Ordo's calendar.

The Transfiguration falls on 6 August, recalling the manifestation of Christ's glory on Mount Thabor. Matthew records the manifestation of divine glory to Peter, James, and John. Armenian tradition credits Gregory the Illuminator with the feast's origin. He is said to have replaced a pagan feast of Aphrodite.

The Latin Church adopted the feast slowly, mostly from the tenth century onward. Callixtus III spread it to the Universal Church in 1456 after Belgrade's victory. Hunyady's defeat of the Turks on 6 August prompted the extension. It is the titular feast of Rome's great Lateran Basilica today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-ver:
Ferdinand Verbiest was a Belgian Jesuit missionary and astronomer at Peking. Born in 1623, he reached China in 1659 with thirty-five new missionaries. Called to Peking, he assisted and eventually replaced Adam Schall. In 1668 his astronomy triumphed over China's in a public imperial test.

Verbiest then headed the Bureau of Mathematics and built great brass instruments for the emperor. His brass quadrant, sextant, and globes still stand in Peking's palace tower. He cast cannon, taught mandarins and bureau students, and tutored Emperor K'ang-hi. He died at Peking in 1688, famed for science, service, and mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-kerri:
Francis Kerril Amherst, born in London on 21 March 1819 and dead at Kenilworth on 21 August 1883, was Bishop of Northampton in Victorian England. Eldest son of William Kerril Amherst of Essex, he entered Oscott College in 1830. He left after eight years with no thought of the priesthood, returned in 1841, and was ordained by Cardinal Wiseman on 6 June 1846. He joined the Third Order of St. Dominic, taught at Oscott, and served the mission at Stafford.

On Bishop Wareing's resignation he was appointed to Northampton and consecrated on 4 July 1858, and in 1862 he was made Assistant at the Pontifical Throne. Ill health forced him to resign his see in 1879, and the next year he was transferred to the titular see of Sozusa. The entry gives a short, factual record of a bishop whose career moved between college, parish mission, and diocesan leadership in the restored English hierarchy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genealogy-of-:
The Genealogy of Christ faces the hard task of matching Matthew's and Luke's lists of Jesus' forebears. The article grants the puzzles outright, refuses despair, and studies each genealogy alone, then side by side, then against the exceptions that test their harmony. Matthew's list descends from Abraham in three sets of fourteen names.

Patriarchs, kings, and private men fill Matthew's three fourteens, yet gaps show. Three kings drop between Joram and Ozias, Joakim falls between Josias and Jechonias, and nine links span five hundred thirty years from Zorobabel to Joseph. Luke counts eighteen for the same stretch, a pace closer to ordinary generations. The entry weighs lacunae and harmonies with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holocaust:
Holocaust, from Greek words meaning whole and burnt, designates an offering entirely consumed by fire. Jews and some pagan nations of antiquity used such offerings. In the Vulgate the word answers to two Hebrew terms. Holah means that which goes up to the altar or to heaven in flame, and kalil means entire or perfect, a synonym for an offering wholly consumed.

At whatever time and by whomsoever offered, holocausts ranked as the highest outward expression of reverence to God, because they were the most complete. Some modern critics read the prophets as rejecting sacrifice outright, holocausts included. The entry calls that a partial view, mistaking an attack on abuses for an attack on the institution itself, and refers readers to its article on sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-ghost:
This article sets out the Catholic doctrine of the Holy Ghost as part of the mystery of the Holy Trinity. St. Augustine warned that in no other subject is error so easy, progress so hard, or careful study so fruitful. The dogma holds that the Holy Ghost is the Third Person of the Trinity, really distinct from Father and Son yet consubstantial with them, God like them, sharing one divine essence.

He proceeds not by generation but by spiration, from Father and Son together as from a single principle. The entry then surveys chief errors against the doctrine, from second- and third-century Monarchians onward, showing how every attack on the Trinity also threatened faith in the Holy Ghost. Readers get both the dogma stated plainly and its history of dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-host:
The host is the bread destined for Eucharistic consecration, though the term may also embrace the sacrifice's bread and wine. It is reserved above all to the bread. Ovid derived hostia from hostis, enemy, since ancients offered vanquished enemies as victims, but hostia may instead come from hostire, to strike.

In the West the term spread chiefly through the Vulgate and liturgy. There it named Christ, the immolated victim, and, looking ahead, the still unconsecrated bread destined to become his body. In time liturgical use wore away the original sense of victim. The host also went by many other names, such as buccellae, circuli, and coronae, and the entry surveys its names, forms, and handling across the ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imitation-of-:
The Imitation of Christ, sometimes called the Following of Christ, is a devotional work that trains the soul toward Christian perfection with Christ as its model. Written in plain, conversational Latin, it offers counsels of perfection across four books. Those books cover useful advice for a spiritual life, advice on spiritual things, interior consolation, and the Blessed Sacrament.

Next to the Bible, it may be the most widely read spiritual book anywhere. People have argued over who wrote it since its anonymous first printing in 1418. Names put forward include Bernard and Bonaventure, Innocent III, and Henry of Kalkar. Others were Walter Hilton, John à Kempis, Giovanni Gersen, and Jean Charlier de Gerson. Recent scholarship has fully upheld the claim of Thomas à Kempis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-incest:
Forbidden sexual relations between close kin are defined here in moral and canon law terms. The entry draws the line at blood kin and kin by marriage within the fourth degree, as canon lawyers counted degrees. It treats both completed acts and incomplete acts as carrying guilt. Its focus is why the act counts as a distinct wrong, not just a breach of chastity.

That distinct wrong, the entry argues, lies in the offense against the love and respect owed to parents and, in lesser degree, to other kin. For parent and child the ban rests on natural law itself, while for wider kin it rests on church law barring marriage within those limits. Readers get a compact statement of the rule, its grounds, and how theologians graded the offense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-interest:
Money charged over and above the return of borrowed capital is the topic of this moral and economic entry. Interest applies to a loan for consumption. Such goods the borrower may spend or destroy, returning an equal amount of the same kind. Hire differs from interest. Hire is the price paid for using a thing that must itself come back. Corn, wine, oil, and fruit can all be lent in this way, though money is the usual case.

Three kinds are sorted: moratory interest, a penalty or make-good for late payment. Compensatory interest covers the lender's risk of loss and gain forgone while parted from his capital. Lucrative interest is profit the lender would not gain without lending. The entry gives readers the moral vocabulary behind centuries of debate over what a lender may fairly charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ite-missa-est:
Go, the Mass is ended — in Latin Ite missa est — is the deacon's dismissal chant at Mass's close, after the post-Communion prayers. This old formula of dismissal, the apolysis, survives in every liturgy, and it counts among the most ancient Roman formulas, shown by its archaic and awkward shape. All three oldest Roman ordines contain it.

The first Roman ordo pictures the rite. Once the post-Communion prayer ends, a deacon chosen by the archdeacon looks to the pontiff for a sign. Then he tells the people Ite missa est. They answer Deo gratias. Medieval commentators puzzled long over the strange wording, guessing a missing word or reading est as “is now accomplished.” The entry settles the phrase's age before its meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-joest:
Dutch painter Jan Joest, also called Van Kalkar, was born at Calcar about 1460. He died at Haarlem in 1519. He was practically unknown until 1874, when Canon Wolff and Dr Eisenmann established his identity. His great work, painted between 1505 and 1508, shows scenes from Christ's life on the high altar wings of St Nicholas church at Calcar. Critics knew the work but not the painter.

Canon Wolff found many references to Joest in his hometown archives, proving the masterpiece's date and that in 1518 Joest worked at Cologne for the important Hackeney family. After leaving Cologne, Joest seems to have gone to Italy, visiting Genoa and Naples. Returning to Holland, he settled at Haarlem, where he painted St Willibrord for St Bavon's church. A rediscovered master of the Calcar altar, his name came back with his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jesus-christ:
Jesus Christ is treated here not as a single narrative but as a cluster of linked studies, each announced in turn. The entry opens with the name itself, Jesus and Christ, and the honour paid to the Holy Name as a reminder of blessings through the Redeemer.

Further sections weigh early documents on Christ, pagan, Jewish, and Christian; fix the chronology of his life. They trace his character toward men and toward God; and set out the Incarnation, the Resurrection, devotion to the Sacred Heart, and Christology, the doctrine of his person and works. Together they form a compact sum of Catholic teaching on Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-georg-:
Johann Georg Herbst, a German Bible scholar born at Rottweil in 1787 and died in 1836. He was schooled at home, at Saint Peter's in the Black Forest, and at Freiburg from 1806. After maths and philosophy he mastered Eastern tongues and Bible science under Hug.

Ordained in March 1812, Herbst taught at Ellwangen seminary and held its Hebrew and Arabic chair, then Oriental languages and Old Testament exegesis. When Ellwangen's faculty moved to Tübingen in 1817 he added Scripture introduction and biblical archaeology. Occasional lectures on New Testament, church history, and pastoral care followed, amid a young faculty that included Drey, Hirscher, and Möhler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-host:
Johann Host, one of seven Dominicans famed for fighting Luther at Cologne, was born on a Westphalian farm about 1480 and died at the turn of 1532 and 1533. His companions were Hoogstraten, Collin, Luxemburg, Pesselius, Smeling, and Slotanus, men of like stamp.

Host joined the Dominicans at sixteen, studied at Bologna from 1516 to 1519, and in 1520 joined Cologne's theology faculty, whose orthodoxy policed German faculties. Amid controversy he edited works on the Holy Land, against Luther's Babylon, and on the Psalms, and left many polemical writings of his own. His last book, a priests' handbook, appeared at Cologne in 1532.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bapst:
John Bapst was a Swiss Jesuit missionary in Maine whose work survived a Know-Nothing mob's tar and feathers. Born at Fribourg in 1815, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1835, was ordained in 1846, and reached New York in 1848. Though he knew neither English nor the local Indian tongue, he was sent to Old Town, Maine. There Indians left twenty years without a priest welcomed him with joy.

He labored for their reform, founded temperance societies, and built up missions across the state, drawing converts and attention. At Ellsworth in 1851, hated as a priest and for his Catholic school, he was dragged from a parishioner's house. He was tarred and feathered, then ridden on a rail out of town by order of the town council. He recovered, built Bangor's first church in 1856, later led Jesuit houses in Boston, Canada, and New York, and died in Maryland in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-fust:
John Fust, also called Faust, was the Mainz financier whose capital launched Gutenberg's printing press. Of a wealthy Mainz family, he became Gutenberg's partner in 1450, furnishing the money and taking a mortgage on tools and materials. The partnership broke in 1455, when Fust sued Gutenberg for his advances and took possession of the printing apparatus.

With his son-in-law Peter Schoffer he continued the business. They issued the magnificent forty-two-line Latin Bible, known as the Mazarin Bible from the copy found in Cardinal Mazarin's library, and an indulgence of 1454. Their Psalter of 1457 was the first book printed with a complete date. It was followed by Durandus in 1459 and Cicero's De Officiis in 1465, the first printed classical author. When Mainz was sacked in 1462, his scattered workmen carried the secret art abroad, and Fust died at Paris about 1466.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knowledge-of-:
Knowledge of Jesus Christ surveys the mind of Christ, not a summary of facts about him. Since Christ holds two natures, the article treats his divine mind and his human mind as separate questions, the first being simply God's own knowledge.

Arians and Agnoetae, who denied Christ's full divinity or mixed his natures, are shown attributing ignorance even to the Word. Catholic teaching instead grants omniscience to the divine intellect. The human intellect, the article's main concern, knew in three ways. First came the beatific vision, seeing God face to face from the start. Then infused knowledge, poured in by divine light. Last came experience gathered over time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludwig-windth:
Ludwig Windthorst was a German Catholic statesman, born near Osnabruck in 1812 and dead in 1891. From a family of Lower Saxon lawyers, he proved industrious, shrewd, cautious, and quiet at school, traits he kept for life.

A lawyer at Osnabruck from 1836, he won clergy trust and became president of Hanover's Catholic board for churches and schools in 1842. There he learned how Protestant states squeezed Catholic freedom after 1803, and brokered a Hanover settlement while other states slid toward the Kulturkampf. Elected to Hanover's Diet in 1848, he became the Centre Party's master debater and organizer, defending church, schools, and law against Bismarck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lust:
Lust is the disordered craving for, or indulgence in, the carnal pleasure of the organs of generation. Its wrong lies in seeking sexual satisfaction outside marriage, or inside it in a way against the laws of marital life.

Every such deliberate act, says Paul in Galatians, bars the doer from God's kingdom, and counts as mortal sin when fully voluntary. Other faults often admit lighter degrees, but impurity holds the grim mark that direct, conscious surrender always brings grave guilt. Where consent is indirect, through a cause once posited, guilt may shrink to venial, judged by danger foreseen and power to excite passion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-le-sa:
Maurice le Sage d'Hauteroche d'Hulst, a French prelate, writer, and orator born at Paris in 1841, died there in 1896. After the College Stanislas he studied at St-Sulpice and Rome, earning a divinity doctorate. He served as curate at St. Ambrose, volunteered as an army chaplain in the war of 1870, and in 1873 joined Cardinal Guibert's diocesan administration.

His chief labour was the free Catholic University opened at Paris after the 1875 law on higher education. As rector from 1880 for fifteen years, he built it across every branch of learning, guarding orthodoxy while meeting scientific progress. In 1891 he took Monsabre's pulpit at Notre-Dame, preaching six years of Lenten conferences on Christian morals and the Decalogue. Elected deputy for Finistere in 1892, this royalist by birth loyally backed the republic at Leo XIII's request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monogram-of-c:
The Monogram of Christ most often means the Chrismon, formed by joining the first two letters of Christ's name in Greek, Chi and Rho. Constantine the Great set it on his military standards, and Eusebius describes it on the labarum, the imperial banner carried before the army.

Two other monograms existed as well, one for the name Jesus and one combining both names, with many variants appearing on fourth- and fifth-century monuments. The letters also turn up on pre-Christian coins and in Greek manuscripts as shorthand for other words, but there the Chi stands upright, while in Christ's monogram it lies on its side. The entry sorts the forms, their variants and their uses in early Christian art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-the-:
The Order of Christ in Portugal rose from the suppressed Templars, whom Portugal had welcomed first in Europe in 1128. Portuguese Templars helped win the Algarve and stood acquitted by Lisbon's church court, yet Clement V suppressed their order in 1312 and King Dinis mourned useful allies lost.

Dinis founded the Militia of Christ in 1317, John XXII approved it in 1319 under Calatrava's rule and Alcobaça's oversight, and in 1323 gave it the Portuguese Templar estates. Many Templars joined, and the order sailed with Henry the Navigator's age of discovery. Many former Templars hastened to become Knights of Christ after the new order’s founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-the:
The Orders of the Holy Ghost grew from Rome's great hospital into a network of care across Christendom from the thirteenth century. La Porte du Theil called the hospital the most beautiful, largest, and best-ordered in civilized Europe, and even Virchow, an unbeliever, praised Innocent III for spreading its charity methodically.

Earlier hospices sheltered travelers and pilgrims, treating the sick at home, but the Holy Ghost order gathered the sick under infirmarian communities. The entry follows its houses, rule, and medical work through medieval and modern Europe. Virchow praised Innocent III for diffusing charity methodically to every sphere of social life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pentecost:
Pentecost is the Christian feast of the Holy Spirit's descent on the Apostles, fifty days after the Resurrection. It fell on the old Jewish feast of weeks, and its English name, Whitsunday, came from the white robes of those baptised at its vigil. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces a feast that reaches back to the first century, though no early evidence proves its observance as clearly as Easter's.

Tertullian already treats it as established, a Gallic pilgrim describes its solemn keeping at Jerusalem, and the Apostolic Constitutions stretch it to a week. Whether it should carry an octave stayed debatable into Berno of Reichenau's day. Now it ranks with Easter Sunday. The entry also covers its vigil baptisms, its single Nocturn through the week, and the singing of Veni Creator at Terce.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pentecost-jew:
The Jewish feast of Pentecost ranked second among the great festivals of Israel. Its Greek name marked the fiftieth day counted from the Passover sabbath, and the Old Testament calls it the feast of harvest, the feast of weeks, and the day of firstfruits. A sheaf of barley opened the harvest; loaves from the new wheat closed it. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the feast's timing, offerings, and later meaning.

Timing itself was disputed. Most teachers counted from Nisan 15, the first day of unleavened bread, while Sadducees and later Karaites counted from the weekly sabbath inside Passover week. The entry leaves the ancient dispute undecided, noting that all Jews later fixed the feast fifty days after Nisan 16. Since biblical times a new layer of meaning has grown onto the harvest rite, one Scripture never hints at.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-handmaid:
The Poor Handmaids of Jesus Christ are a community founded by Catherine Kasper of Dernbach in Germany. Born on 26 May 1820 of humble parents, she resolved early to consecrate her life to God, joining Mary's contemplative spirit to Martha's active service. She and two companions took vows as Poor Handmaids on 15 August 1851, with Sister Mary Kasper as mother-general until her death in 1898.

The community first served the sick and needy, above all orphans, then took up teaching in parochial schools, academies, boarding schools, kindergartens, and industrial schools. The Kulturkampf forced it from parochial schools, but other charity continued, and Pius IX approved its constitutions in 1870, Leo XIII confirming them. From 1863 it worked in America, opening a German orphan asylum at Chicago and a hospital at Fort Wayne, reaching 3,500 members, 500 in the United States.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priest:
Priest, from presbyteros, elder, has come to mean sacerdos, for which no noun has formed in English, French, or German. The priest serves as Divine worship's minister, above all of its highest act, sacrifice. In this sense each religion has its priests, holding more or less lofty sacerdotal posts as go betweens linking man and God. Ages and lands show wide gaps. Lower ministers of many kinds may aid the true priest. He may belong to a class or caste, to a clergy, or stand like other citizens save in sacerdotal work. He may sit in a hierarchy, or wield a lone priesthood, like Melchisedech.

Yet through all chance gaps one root thought holds for all faiths: the priest is the man duly named to pay homage to God in society's name, and to offer Him sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-provost:
Provost, from the Latin praepositus, is the title of a senior officer of a cathedral chapter. This encyclopedia entry traces the name through an early shuffle of duties. Every chapter once had an archpriest, who deputized for the bishop and ran the choir. It also had an archdeacon, who headed the chapter and managed its property. In time the archpriest became the dean and the archdeacon took the name provost. Today the chief dignity usually goes by dean, except in England, where provost is still used.

Appointed by the Holy See under a rule of the Roman Chancery, the provost sees that chapter statutes are kept. Chapter acts need his signature beside the chapter seal to count as authentic. When the bishop pontificates, the provost serves as assistant priest. It falls to him to bring Viaticum, the last communion, to a dying bishop, and to conduct the bishop's funeral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychology-of:
Interest, the mental state that draws and holds attention, gets a careful study here. The German philosopher Herbart gave it a central place in the theory of education, and psychologists since have argued over its exact nature. Some define it as a kind of consciousness that accompanies and spurs attention. Others call it the pleasant or painful side of attending itself. Some treat interest and attention as simply the same thing.

Teaching runs through the second half. A pupil who cares about a subject attends without effort, but dull first pages still demand hard, voluntary attention. The wise teacher shows the future use of dry labour, lending it a borrowed, mediate interest. He also keeps early lessons short and varies the monotony, since straining after the uninteresting tires the mind fast. A stock of worthy interests, intellectual, aesthetic and social, emerges as one of education's finest gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-con:
The Congregation of the Holy Ghost and of the Immaculate Heart of Mary dates from Whit Sunday 1703. It trained missionaries for the most abandoned souls, Christian and pagan alike. Its founder, Claude-François Poullart des Places, gave up a lawyer's career at twenty-one for the priesthood. Drawn to neglected charity, he spent his money and his friends' gifts on poor students, gathering a dozen around him to open a seminary.

From that start the congregation spread across Africa and the islands. Its field included the diocese of Angola and eight vicariates: Senegambia, Sierra Leone, Gaboon, Ubangi, Loango, Northern Madagascar, Zanzibar, and Bagamoyo. Prefectures in Lower Nigeria, French Guinea, and Lower Congo, and missions at Bata and Kindou, followed. Beyond Africa it worked in Mauritius, Réunion, the Rodriguez Islands, Trinidad, Martinique, Guadeloupe, Haiti, and the Amazon region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-resurrection-:
Resurrection means rising again from the dead, the resumption of life, and this entry treats only the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. Its main sources are the Four Gospels and the Epistles of Saint Paul. Easter morning packs in so much incident and so many persons that its full history forms a complicated tableau. The partial accounts in each Gospel look at first hard to harmonize.

The entry weighs the fact, the theories against it, its characteristics, and its importance in turn. Jesus himself had always joined his Resurrection to predictions of his death, and the disciples, treasuring his memory with a fondness that made his loss almost unbelievable, needed only a spark. Mary Magdalen applied it, and the flame spread like a conflagration. By his Resurrection Christians acknowledge Christ as immortal God, cause of their own resurrection, and model of their new life of grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-hurst:
Richard Hurst was a Lancashire farmer put to death in 1628 after a trial the entry presents as a judicial murder. A well-off yeoman and a Catholic recusant, one who refused the state church, he was targeted for arrest by the Bishop of Chester's men. During the attempted arrest, one pursuivant's man fell in a ploughed field and broke his leg. He later died of the wound, after swearing on oath that it had been a pure accident.

The government pressed a murder charge anyway, to make an example of recusants. Friends petitioned Charles I, backed by Queen Henrietta Maria. Still, the judge privately told the jury's foreman that a guilty verdict was required. Hurst was convicted. Dragged to a Protestant sermon he refused to hear, he stopped his ears against it. Offered his life for an oath against his faith, he refused and was hanged at Lancaster.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-stany:
Richard Stanyhurst was an Irish writer whose histories, translations, and devotional works spanned a restless career across Europe. Born at Dublin in 1547, the son of a leading Protestant speaker of the Irish Commons, he studied at Oxford and law in London. There he met Edmund Campion and helped him gather material for a history of Ireland. Stanyhurst's own Description of Ireland and History of Ireland under Henry VIII appeared in Holinshed's Chronicles in 1577, offending many Irish Catholics.

After his first wife's death in 1579, he left for the Low Countries and became a Catholic. At Leyden he published a striking translation of Virgil's Aeneid into English hexameters in 1582. Later years in Spain, as an adviser on English affairs, and in Brussels, as chaplain to Archduke Albert, produced Latin histories. These covered Ireland and St Patrick. He also wrote two devotional works, Hebdomada Mariana and Hebdomada Eucharistica. He died at Brussels in 1618.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandhurst:
Sandhurst, a diocese in Victoria, Australia, suffragan of Melbourne, takes its cathedral city name from Bendigo, about a hundred miles north of Melbourne. Bendigo sits in a shallow basin ringed by gold-rich hills, where gold found in 1852 drew immigrants worldwide, among them many Irish Catholics. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a gold-rush diocese.

Father Backhaus served as first missionary. On 21 September 1874 Martin Crane, an Augustinian, was consecrated first bishop and reached his diocese early in 1875 with Fathers Maher and Reville. Reville became coadjutor in 1885 and succeeded Crane on 21 October 1901. Across Crane's twenty-five active years and beyond, the Church grew fast in spirit and in buildings, and the entry records that growth parish by parish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-arbogast:
St. Arbogast, in Gaelic Arascach, flourished about the middle of the seventh century. This entry untangles a common error about his birthplace. He has been claimed as a native of Scotland, but that rests on misunderstanding the name Scotia, which until late in the Middle Ages really meant Ireland. Like so many other missionaries, he left Ireland and settled as a hermit in a German forest.

He then went to Alsace, where his real name Arascach was changed to Arbogast. Foreigners struggled to pronounce Irish Christian names, so Moengal, Maelmaedhog, Cellach, and others were likewise transformed into Marcellus, Malachy, Gall, and the like. In Alsace Arbogast found a warm friend in King Dagobert II of Austrasia. Dagobert had been educated at Slane in Meath and was restored to his kingdom on the death of Childeric II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-the-b:
John the Baptist, precursor of Christ, is known chiefly through the Gospels, with Luke fullest on his birth and ministry. Matthew closely follows Luke on public ministry but says nothing of early life. Mark's account is meagre, adding no new detail. The fourth Gospel gives John's testimony after the Saviour's baptism. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 weighs those sources with Josephus's erratic Antiquities.

Luke tells the wonderful circumstances of the precursor's birth, and Acts alludes to his ministry in passing. An old tradition, echoed in Paul the Deacon's hymn, sends the boy John into desert caves in tender years, though the Gospel says only that he grew in the wilderness. Herod's fear for his kingdom, report said, drove the child into the desert and cost Zachary his life between temple and altar. The entry sorts Gospel, tradition, and Josephus with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-the-e:
John the Evangelist, son of Zebedee and brother of James the Greater, is called a son of thunder. With his brother he fished Galilee's lake with their father, then followed John the Baptist for a time. Christ called them from the Baptist's circle with Peter and Andrew, and they returned with him from Jordan to Galilee. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 divides his story into New Testament accounts, the alleged presbyter, later accounts, feasts, and art.

After a second return from Judea, John and companions went back to fishing until called finally. Later writings add Ephesus, where a Christian community already existed before Paul's labours, and Patmos, where Revelation's author says he was for God's word and Jesus' testimony. The second and third epistles' author calls himself the presbyter, the ancient, raising the question whether presbyter John differs from the evangelist. The entry weighs that debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephan-wiest:
Stephan Wiest, a Cistercian monk of Bavaria, taught church doctrine at Ingolstadt and wrote a vast positive work. Born at Teisbach in Lower Bavaria on 7 March 1748, he attended school at Landshut. In 1767 he entered Aldersbach, where he studied philosophy and theology. He took vows on 28 October 1768 and was ordained priest in 1772.

He continued studies at Ingolstadt. He taught philosophy and mathematics at Aldersbach from 1774 to 1780 and theology in 1780 to 1781. He then became professor of dogma at Ingolstadt in 1781, also teaching the Fathers and the history of church writings. He served as rector in 1787 to 1788, resigned his chair in 1794, and returned home.
