Mrs. Laurence Binyon collected and arranged The Mind of the Artist, thoughts and sayings of painters and sculptors on their art, published by Chatto and Windus in London in 1909. George Clausen, R.A., supplied a preface, and a Rembrandt frontispiece faces the title page. In her opening note, Binyon explains that the volume does not aim at completeness. She hopes instead that the sayings chosen fairly represent what typical artists of their race and time said about their work.

Binyon deliberately drew less on famous treatises, such as those of Leonardo and Reynolds, than on intimate avowals. Letters, diaries, working notes, and memoirs supplied her material, often after considerable research to trace it. Her acknowledgments name quotations from Burne-Jones, Whistler, Watts, D. G. Rossetti, Madox Brown, Millais, and William Morris. Translations from Durer, Cennino Cennini, Leonardo, and Corot also appear.
the-passing-of-the-frontier-a-chronicle-:
Emerson Hough wrote The Passing of the Frontier, a chronicle of the old West, published by Yale University Press in 1918. The contents list nine chapters, from The Frontier in History through the range, the cattle trails, the cowboy, the mines, the Indian wars, and the cattle kings, to The Homesteader.

Chapter One opens with a hymn to the word frontier itself. No word in English, Hough says, is more stirring or more beloved. It means all that America ever meant: the old hope of personal liberty joined to human advance. He warns that frontier tales are already turning hazy, more folklore than history, and sets out to fix them before they fade.
the-paying-guest:
George Gissing wrote The Paying Guest. Chapter One opens with Mumford, who has seen an advertisement and makes a suggestion to his wife Emmeline. She gives him a startled look and asks whether they have been extravagant. He insists not: a paying guest might simply give her company in the day, since they have plenty of room.

Emmeline weighs the matter in silence. The rent at Sutton is heavy, and her husband's season ticket costs much, though the fine air suits mother and child. A young lady's advertisement seeks a home with a respectable family near London, with excellent references. Emmeline reads it again and again, fearing people will say they take lodgers. Gissing starts a quiet comedy of pride and money.
the-people-of-the-mist: H. Rider Haggard published The People of the Mist in 1894. He dedicated it to his godsons as a record of barefaced and flagrant adventure. A dedication and a contents list are present, with no story text after them. The list promises an author's note. Chapters open with The Sins of the Father Are Visited on the Children. Otter Gives Counsel, The Tale of Soa, and The Yellow Devil's Nest follow. The Temple of Jal and The Sacrifice After the New Order close the list shown.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-rockies-or-th:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in the Rockies opens with a chapter called The Love of a Horse. Tad Butler is begging Walter Perkins for a two-minute ride on Walter's handsome new pony. He wants just a short ride down the block and back, promising not to go fast. Walter hesitates, afraid Tad will fall off. Tad scorns the idea: no pony, he boasts, could throw him.

Stacy Brown, called Chunky for his round cheeks and ample girth, backs him up. He reminds them how Tad rode a broncho saddled only once before, three times around the baseball field, its back humped like a mad cat's. Reassured, Walter drops the bridle rein over the pony's neck and slides down. He warns Tad not to hold the reins tight, since the pony is trained to run when they tighten.
the-provost:
The Provost opens with an introduction framed as a visit to the West Country. The visitors call on Mrs Pawkie, widow of a provost who served three times as chief magistrate of Gudetown. Her youngest daughter Jenny has lately married Mr Caption, a writer to the signet. Talk turns to the improvements in town and country since the visitors last came. The widow mentions a book in her late husband's handwriting, full of curious matter.

She rates it above the Annals of the Parish, which the visitors had a hand in editing. They ask to see it, expecting little from a widow's partial praise. Turning a few well-penned pages, they find it far surpasses her account. They urge her duty to publish it at once. The frame presents the provost's own record of his burgh career.
the-psalms-of-david-imitated-in-the-lang: Isaac Watts's Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament applies the psalms to Christian worship. A transcriber's note says the file derives from an 1818 London printing and omits the index and table of first lines. The opening also begins Dr. Johnson's Life of Isaac Watts, from his Lives of the Poets. The pages provided stop within that life's first lines; Watts's psalm versions themselves are not among them.
the-quadroon-adventures-in-the-far-west:
Captain Mayne Reid published his western adventure in 1856, opening with a long hymn to the Mississippi River as Father of Waters. The narrator traces the river from the land of a thousand lakes, past wild rice meadows, birch woods, Chippewa canoes, moose, and wapiti.

Moving south, the passage notes falls, bluffs, clearings, maize fields, cabins, and church spires as signs of settlement spreading along the banks. The rhapsody sets place before plot and shows Reid's feel for frontier landscape. Readers who like nineteenth-century adventure writing will find scenery treated as a character in its own right.
the-romance-of-the-coast: James Runciman dedicates his sketches to Frederick Greenwood, editor who gave him escape from political journalism, thanking him for severe discipline that trained a school of writers. Contents open with an old-school pilot, an ugly contrast, a fisherwoman, and a veteran, promising short coastal pieces. Here only the title page, dedication letter, and opening of the contents list are present, so the sketches themselves do not appear.
the-sagebrusher-a-story-of-the-west: Emerson Hough copyrighted The Sagebrusher, a story of the West, in 1919. Hough also wrote The Covered Wagon and The Broken Gate. J. Henry illustrated the Grosset and Dunlap edition shown here. Only the title page and contents are present in this portion, so the novel's chapters themselves do not appear. The contents follow Sim Gage from his home through a chapter titled Wanted: A Wife. Hearts aflame and rival consciences follow. The list closes with The Rebirth of Sim Gage and a final chapter called Sagebrushers.
the-school-of-recreation-1696-edition-or:
R. H. compiled The School of Recreation, printed at London for H. Rhodes in 1696. Rhodes sold it at the Star, at the corner of Bride Lane in Fleet-street. The title calls it a guide to the most ingenious exercises. Hunting and hawking head the list. Riding, tennis, racing, and bowling follow.

The list also names fireworks, ringing, and military discipline. Cock-fighting, fowling, defence, and angling appear as well. A preface to the reader opens the volume. The writer promises such variety of recreations in so small a book. Nothing of the nature ever appeared so accomplished in one volume, he claims. He drew on his own experience in these exercises. He also took opinions from those whose ingenuity had led them to each exercise in particular.
the-sea-witch-or-the-african-quadroon-a-: The Sea-Witch, or The African Quadroon, is credited on its title page to Lieutenant Murray. The imprint is simply New York. A sibling record of this same book carries a fuller set of the same front pages, including a preface. The pages shown here stop at the title and the start of the contents. Chapter headings begin with Outward Bound and Captain Will Ratlin. A gale, Bramble Park, a naval officer, and a wreck follow. No story text appears.
the-shadow-of-the-east:
E. M. Hull published The Shadow of the East in 1921. An epigraph from Ezekiel heads the first chapter. It warns that the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. Chapter one opens off the harbour at Yokohama. An American yacht lies there, brilliantly lit from stem to stern.

Moonlight glitters between the yacht and the shore. Countless coloured lamps transform the Japanese town into fairyland, Hull writes. Three men lie in long chairs on deck. Jermyn Atherton, the millionaire owner, lights a fresh cigar. He tells Barry, the man on his right, that he has had every official in Japan hunting for him. Two days of silence had nearly driven him to the consul, he laughs. An international affair might have followed, he jokes.
the-song-of-our-syrian-guest:
William Allen Knight published this small devotional work in 1904, with illustrations and decorative designs by Charles Copeland. It opens with the full text of Psalm XXIII, the shepherd psalm, printed before a warm salutation from the author to his early readers.

In that salutation Knight marvels that the little booklet, first sent out in scanty dress three months earlier, has been welcomed into many thousands of homes. Letters arrived from everywhere, he says, and the story has grown larger by half under that kindness. The enlarged telling centres on a Syrian guest explaining the psalm from a shepherd's own world.
the-sorrows-of-satan-or-the-strange-expe: Marie Corelli's romance tells the strange experience of Geoffrey Tempest, a millionaire, and Methuen of London first published it in November 1895. The pages present here are the title page and a long list of editions. The list runs through a thirty-second edition within 1896 and on to the forty-second by 1900. That is a record of remarkable early sales, so the story itself does not appear.
the-soul-of-the-far-east:
Percival Lowell examines Japanese life and thought in chapters on individuality, family, adoption, language, nature and art, art, religion, and imagination. His first chapter begins with the traveller's shock on setting foot at Yokohama, where the world seems to stand reversed.

Lowell recalls the boyish belief that people on the other side of the globe must stand head downwards, like flies on a ceiling. Experience corrects the picture, yet leaves something stranger: the inhabitants seem antipodal in mind, regarding intuitively in opposite ways what Westerners take for granted. That intellectual inversion, rather than any physical one, becomes his subject for the chapters that follow.
the-spanish-chest:
Edna A. Brown wrote this story for young people, illustrated by John Goss and from photographs. She dedicated it in memory of two friends, Florence and Clara, her companions for a winter in the Channel Islands. Her foreword compares the book's growth to a Japanese artist's sketch whose little painted figures came to life and walked out of the picture.

Two uninvited characters, Brown explains, insisted on joining the story, protesting that at twenty-three and a half they were not so very grown-up and still knew how to play. That playful foreword promises a tale in which its people took on lives of their own, beyond what their author first expected of them.
the-story-of-the-foss-river-ranch-a-tale: Ridgwell Cullum, author of The Law Breakers and The Watchers of the Plains, published this tale of the Northwest with the A. L. Burt Company in 1903, for his wife. Only title page and contents appear here. The contents list fourteen chapters. They open at a polo club ball. They survive a blizzard and play a big game of poker. A stray beyond the muskeg follows. Bad Man's Hollow and Lablache's coup come next. A hue and cry closes the list. The ranch story itself does not appear.
the-strolling-saint-being-the-confession: Rafael Sabatini's novel gives the confessions of Agostino D'Anguissola. He is tyrant of Mondolfo and lord of Carmina. Only the title page and a fuller contents list appear here. Two companion records of the same book show the same. That list runs through three books: The Oblate, Giuliana, and The Wilderness. The third book opens with a home-coming. A captain of justice follows. The narrative itself does not appear.
the-suitors-of-yvonne-being-a-portion-of: Rafael Sabatini's novel gives Gaston de Luynes's memoirs. A production note dates it 1902. Only its title page and contents appear here. A companion record shows the same. The list in this record runs far. It reaches a chapter on leaving Canaples. A boy's drunken indiscretion and a horse-market fight come first. Fair rescuers follow. Mazarin plays the match-maker. A woman's obstinacy, a rescue, and the hand of Yvonne close the heads. The narrative itself does not appear.
the-suppressed-gospels-and-epistles-of-t: This volume holds gospels and epistles attributed to the apostles and disciples. Archbishop Wake and others translated them. Only an elaborate title page and contents appear here. The title makes a large claim. The primitive churches venerated them for four centuries, it says, until the Nicene Council forbade them. Later New Testaments left them out. The list names Mary, the Protevangelion, and infancy gospels. Nicodemus, Christ and Abgarus, and Laodiceans follow. Paul and Seneca and the Acts of Paul and Thecla close it. The texts themselves do not appear.
the-tempest: Shakespeare's Tempest is the play named by this record, but the pages present hold a general editor's note from Michael S. Hart about early printing errors, the same note attached to several other plays in this set. It explains u and v exchanges, type packed into cliches, and scholars' attachment to the old spellings. Hart closes by presenting Shakespeare's play without naming which one in the note itself. No storm, no Prospero, and no line of the Tempest appears in what is shown here.
the-unknown-guest: Maurice Maeterlinck's The Unknown Guest is credited here in an English translation by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Nothing beyond the project header, title, author, and translator lines is present in this record, so the essay itself does not appear. Readers learn only the bare identification of the piece: a work by the Belgian writer Maeterlinck, carried into English by Teixeira de Mattos, his frequent translator. No contents list, preface, or opening passage accompanies the title lines. Anyone seeking the piece's argument will need the book itself.
the-ward-of-king-canute-a-romance-of-the: Ottilie A. Liljencrantz subtitles her Ward of King Canute a romance of the Danish conquest. The pages present here give a thirty-two-chapter contents list and an empty acknowledgment heading, so the romance itself does not appear. Early chapters trace the fall of the house of Frode and introduce Randalin, Frode's daughter. A page named Fridtjof is trained, plays the game of swords, and is taken captive. Later headings promise the Norns' decree, a foreign page, the fates cheating Randalin, and a red cloak's secret.
the-winning-of-the-west-volume-4-louisia:
Volume four of Theodore Roosevelt's The Winning of the West covers Louisiana and the Northwest from 1791 to 1807. A map accompanies the text. The book is dedicated to Francis Parkman, the historian of the American frontier. Roosevelt's preface sets out the period in plain terms. War in the Northwest opens it, and western expansion closes it.

Victories under General Wayne brought peace with Native nations in the north. Treaties with Britain and Spain fixed the young nation's boundaries. Settlers poured in year after year. Kentucky, Tennessee, and Ohio won statehood, while Louisiana, Indiana, and Mississippi organized as territories. Roosevelt presents this growth as the moment the West gained real weight in national councils.
the-zeit-geist: The Zeit-Geist by L. Dougall is represented here only by advertisements for its London series. Hutchinson and Company issued the Zeit-Geist Library of complete novels in one volume. Early volumes listed include works by Gyp and Frankfort Moore. Paper copies cost one shilling and sixpence, cloth two shillings. Each volume promised a designed title page and frontispiece. Dougall's novel itself does not appear in the pages present in this record.
told-in-the-east:
Talbot Mundy's Told in the East was first published by Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis in 1920 and later reprinted in his Romances of India omnibus. Contents name three tales: Hookum Hai, For the Salt Which He Had Eaten, and Machassan Ah. The first opens under a blood-red sun in India.

Heat shimmers over a mud wall while squirrels hunt food that is not there. A coppersmith's hammer has sounded since sunrise, driving listeners nearly mad. Sergeant William Brown, plain Bill Brown at two rupees a day, steps out to watch the sunset. Readers get British-Indian adventure fiction steeped in heat and stillness.
two-years-before-the-mast:
Richard Henry Dana Jr.'s Two Years Before the Mast appears here with an introduction and notes by Homer Eaton Keyes of Dartmouth College. The contents add a biographical note, a section on California and her missions, and a diagram of ships. Dana's later piece, Twenty-Four Years After, completes the volume.

The biographical note calls the two years at sea a mere episode in Dana's life. His services in other fields brought him small recognition and many disappointments, it says. Yet the sailor narrative became his chief claim to wide remembrance. A Coleridge motto about the rank and narrow ship heads the title page, framing a Harvard man's years as a common sailor.
vergilius-a-tale-of-the-coming-of-christ:
Irving Bacheller, author of Eben Holden, published Vergilius, a Tale of the Coming of Christ, with Harper and Brothers in 1904. Chapter one opens on Rome past her summit, looking down into a long dark valley of years. Behind her lie the graves of Caesar, Sallust, Cicero, Catullus, Vergil, and Horace. Before her stretch centuries of trampling, and around her a crowd sick of luxury, their houses full of spoil and their souls full of discontent.

Bacheller paints a city rotting in wealth: philosophers who judge life a misfortune, poets sunk to poor obscenities, priests without faith, and rich folk with no credit. Into that decay his tale brings a young Roman, Vergilius, at the moment when news of Christ begins to stir the world. Readers get a reverent period romance, written to show an empire ripe for a new faith.
wau-bun-the-early-day-in-the-northwest:
Mrs. John H. Kinzie of Chicago wrote Wau-Bun, the Early Day in the Northwest. The book came out at Philadelphia in 1873. Two mottoes at the front fix the title's sense: an Ojibway vocabulary gives wau-bun as the dawn, the break of day. Her preface takes up the apology that books of personal record are supposed to owe the public, and refuses the usual plea.

Most travellers, she notes, claim their pages began as letters to friends, dragged into print by wiser judges. No such plea serves here. Her record of events, in which she herself had no share, was preserved at the urging of a revered relative. Children and even strangers would one day care to hear them. The book keeps the early northwest as her family lived it: forts, journeys, and the first years of Chicago, at the dawn of settlement.
william-lloyd-garrison-the-abolitionist:
Archibald H. Grimke wrote a life of William Lloyd Garrison, the abolitionist, first printed in 1891. His preface states two aims. First, he hopes the record of a hero will aid brave and true living in the republic. Garrison's career, he says, rested on bravery and truth. Readers should copy that example in daily things, not only in crises.

Second, Grimke thanks the storehouse of anti-slavery material in the life of Garrison written by his children. He drew much from that work. The book follows the famed editor who fought slavery with his paper and his voice. Grimke writes as a Black leader honoring a white ally in the cause.
wine-women-and-song-mediaeval-latin-stud: The front pages here hold the title page and a dedication letter for John Addington Symonds's Wine, Women, and Song, with none of the songs shown. Chatto and Windus printed the book in London in 1884. Symonds first turned medieval Latin student songs into English verse, with an essay. He gave the book to Robert Louis Stevenson. His letter recalls past evenings when wit flowed freer than their wine. He calls the work his pastime through three anxious months at San Remo, in May 1884.
woman-on-the-american-frontier-a-valuabl:
William W. Fowler wrote this history of pioneer women in America. His preface complains that history records mostly men's deeds in war and statecraft. Women appear, when at all, as queens or schemers. The wives and mothers who crossed a continent got only scattered lines. Fowler sets out to give them a full volume instead.

He calls pioneer women soldiers, labourers, heroines, and comforters. Their endurance helped carry settlement from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The preface asks readers to honour that share in building the republic. True stories of hardship and courage form the heart of the volume.
wulf-the-saxon-a-story-of-the-norman-con:
G. A. Henty wrote this story of the Norman Conquest for young readers. His preface calls Hastings a turning point for mankind. Saxon England, he says, lagged behind Europe and split into rival regions. Strong earls acted like kings under weak rulers. Norman rule then tied England to the continent and quickened its growth.

Henty admits the conquest itself had no justice behind it, and was a curse at the time, yet later brought lasting gains. He took his facts from Freeman's history of the conquest. Readers get a Saxon hero's path through invasion, defeat, and a changing England.
wyoming-a-story-of-the-outdoor-west:
William MacLeod Raine wrote this Western novel set in the Big Horn country. Chapter one opens with a woman driving an automobile out of the hills. She stops above a vast plain and drinks in the view. Sunlight, blue sky, and distant mountains strike her as new and thrilling. The contents then promise ranch life at the Lazy D and a dance at Fraser's.

Later chapters bring a rescue, big game hunting, and a fight for a world's championship. A figure called the King of the Big Horn Country looms over the plot. The final chapter title promises lovers meeting at journey's end.
yeast:
Thomas H. Huxley gave this lecture on yeast as a simple, familiar substance with large lessons inside it. He starts with sugary liquids left alone. Fruit juice or honey water turns cloudy, foams, and drops sediment called lees. The sweet liquid gains the power to intoxicate. Bubbles rise through it the whole time. Huxley walks listeners through each change step by step.

His point reaches past brewing. A tiny living growth drives a change people had used for ages without grasping it. Careful looking at a common thing opens big questions in science. Readers get a model of clear public lecturing on biology.
